name: Fulcanelli — Le Mystère des Cathédrales
description: Terms, persons, works and places of Fulcanelli's Le Mystère des Cathédrales, as the book itself explains them (English).

0.content: This lorebook holds the terms, persons, works and places of Fulcanelli's Le Mystère des Cathédrales, as the book itself explains them. Recommended SillyTavern World Info settings: Recursive Scan on, Max Recursion Steps 2-3; Match Whole Words on and Case-sensitive off (the defaults). This entry is disabled and never sent to the model.

1.content:
[Person: A. Bonnetty]
Struck by the mystery of the Nativity narratives and unable to ascribe them to a celestial phenomenon, he asks who the Magi were and what to think of the star, blaming rationalism and ontologism for having made forgotten how the ancient peoples of the East kept the primitive traditions. Source: Documents historiques sur la Religion des Romains, t. II, p. 564.

Fulcanelli: “Who are these Magi, and what are we to think of this star?”

2.content:
[Person: Abbo]
Author of a poem on the siege of Paris by the Normans, in which, the text says, he reports several features attesting the marvellous properties of the water of the well of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

Fulcanelli: “Abbo, in his poem on the siege of Paris by the Normans, reports several features attesting the marvellous properties of the water of the well of Saint-Germain-des-Prés”

3.content:
[Person: Abbé Ansault]
Author of La Croix avant Jésus-Christ (Paris, V. Rétaux, 1894), cited as amply proving that the cross is an ancient symbol of all religions, not specially Christian.

Fulcanelli: “The cross is a very ancient symbol, used at all times, in all religions, among all peoples, and one would be wrong to consider it an emblem peculiar to Christianity, as abbé Ansault amply demonstrates.”

4.content:
[Person: Abbé Roze]
Named among those who read the Amiens wheel-fire as Ezekiel's vision. Durand prefers Roze's name Apostasy for the relief of the man leaving a church.

Fulcanelli: “it seems to us that the word Apostasy proposed by the abbé Roze fits the subject better.”

5.content:
[Person: Abbé Vilain]
Cited for the small portal of Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie, made by Flamel in 1389 and covered with figures, with an angel holding a stone circle in which Flamel set a black marble disc with a gold cross. His work is the Histoire critique de Nicolas Flamel, Paris, Desprez, 1761.

Fulcanelli: “The abbé Vilain tells us that the small portal of Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie, which the Adept had made in 1389, was covered with figures.”

6.content:
[Person: Abraham the Jew]
Author of the book of figures that came to Flamel. The text says he was also known as Eléazar and that he used the symbol of the serpent coiled on a golden rod, the image of the philosophers' Mercury. His third figure (hollow oak and fountain) is compared to the Paris relief and to a figure of Trismosin.

Fulcanelli: “Abraham the Jew, also known by the name of Eleazar, made use of it in the book that fell to Flamel”

7.content:
[Term: Absolute]
The name by which ancient alchemists designated the philosophers' stone; the text notes it is close to Absolum, name of the Cnossos labyrinth. On a ceiling panel of the Hôtel Lallemant chapel, the dead serpent below is mercury and the seal of Solomon on top of the ingots is the Absolute: a method of one way, one matter, one operation.

Fulcanelli: “Now we shall point out that this term is close to Absolu, which is the name by which the ancient alchemists designated the philosophers' stone.” / “Below, the mercury; above, the Absolute.”

Identified in the text with: Philosophers' stone

8.content:
[Term: Adept]
Interpreted: one who has achieved the Work (Canseliet speaks of the event that forced the Adept to flee the world). The Phrygian cap is the attribute of 'Adeptat' (adepthood) on the alchemist of Notre-Dame; a note calls it the distinctive sign of the Initiates. Flamel is called an Adept; Jacques Cœur had the reputation of a proven Adept. The Adept, his wish fulfilled, keeps his vow of silence: 'the Adept must forever / keep silent'. Canseliet: the new Adept aligns his destiny with his rare predecessors, like beacons along the road, and casts off the 'old man', leaving only the trace of a name; the Adept flees the world's homage.

Fulcanelli: “Wearing the Phrygian cap, attribute of Adepthood, set carelessly on the long thick-curled hair, the sage, wrapped in the light laboratory cape, leans one hand on the balustrade” / “In Science, in Good, the Adept must forever”

9.content:
[Person: Aegidius de Vadis]
Cited, inside the commentary on La Lumière sortant des Ténèbres quoted by Fulcanelli, as showing in his Dialogue de la Nature that a portion of the first Chaos remains in this world, known but despised by all and sold publicly.

Fulcanelli: “Aegidius de Vadis, in his Dialogue of Nature, shows clearly and as in letters of gold that there has remained, in this world, a portion of that first Chaos, known but despised by everyone, and sold publicly.”

10.content:
[Person: Aeneas]
In the legend recalled by Varro, Aeneas saves his father and household gods from the flames of Troy and after long wanderings reaches the fields of Laurentum, end of his voyage. From Troy onward he saw the star of Venus every day and by day until the Laurentine fields, where it disappeared, which told him these were the lands appointed by Fate. The legend opens the series of texts on the star.

Fulcanelli: “Varro, in his Antiquitates rerum humanarum, recalls the legend of Aeneas, saving his father and his household gods from the flames of Troy, and arriving, after long wanderings, at the fields of Laurentum, the end of his journey.”

11.content:
[Person: Albert Poisson]
Called 'the famous occultist'. Cited for Flamel's chapel of the Saint-Gervais hospital, covered with figures, and for the escutcheon on Flamel's first arcade at the charnel house of the Innocents, which he says imitates one attributed to saint Thomas Aquinas and appears at the end of Lagneau's Harmonie Chymique; his description of it follows. He gives a fire base of 50° rising to about 300° centigrade for the coction. His work is Histoire de l'Alchimie. Nicolas Flamel, Paris, Chacornac, 1893.

Fulcanelli: “Albert Poisson gives a base of 50° with progressive increase up to about 300° centigrade.”

12.content:
[Term: Alchemical Fortress]
On the north (Saint-Firmin) portal of Amiens a quatrefoil shows a citadel with a massive bolted door, crenellated towers, two storeys and a barred vent. Fulcanelli asks whether it symbolizes the esotericism of the other quatrefoils, or is the mother idea of the 'Forteresse alchimique' taken up and modified by Khunrath in 1609, or the closed Palace of the king of the Art spoken of by Basile Valentin and Philalèthe; citadel or royal dwelling, it seems built to keep a treasure or secret, entered only with the key. Elsewhere the Philosophers' obscurity is a wall raised as the enclosure of their citadel, and alchemical furnaces are drawn as keeps or small fortresses.

Fulcanelli: “Or should we see, in this motif of the year 1225, the mother idea of the Alchemical Fortress, taken up and modified by Khunrath in 1609?” / “Built to keep some treasure or conceal some important secret, it seems one can enter it only by possessing the key to the powerful locks that guard it against any break-in.”

13.content:
[Place: Alchemical stove of Winterthur]
Stove painted in 1702 by P. H. Pfau, kept at the Winterthur museum (Switzerland); its paintings show an angler and a fish and the straw beehive with its bees, a subject also on the Lallemant chapel ceiling.

Fulcanelli: “Not far off, a common straw beehive is shown surrounded by its bees, a subject often reproduced, particularly on the alchemical stove of Winterthur.”

14.content:
[Place: The alchemist of Notre-Dame]
A large stone old man on the second gallery of Notre-Dame de Paris, near the central axis at the re-entrant angle of the north tower, among the chimeras (pl. III). He wears the Phrygian cap, attribute of Adeptship, and a laboratory cape; one hand on the balustrade, the other stroking his beard; he does not meditate but observes, in extreme emotion and surprise. Fulcanelli reads him as the old master watching the evolution of mineral life and at last beholding the marvel his faith foresaw. Notre-Dame thus 'keeps its alchemist'.

Fulcanelli: “He is not meditating, he is observing.” / “What a splendid figure is this old master who scrutinizes and questions, anxious and attentive, the evolution of mineral life, then at last contemplates, dazzled, the marvel his faith alone let him glimpse!”

15.content:
[Term: Alchemy]
The science the book finds in the monuments. At Notre-Dame alchemy is a woman on a throne with sceptre, two books, one closed (esotericism), one open (exotericism), and the nine-step ladder; the cathedral rests on alchemical science, which studies the transformations of the original substance. It is as positive and exact as optics or geometry and must be purified of the stains its own followers left. It was also called 'celestial Agriculture', its Adepts 'Labourers'. Canseliet: for man, alchemy is the search for and awakening of the Life asleep under the envelope of beings, a purification to perfection on the planes of matter and spirit.

Fulcanelli: “The science we study is as positive, as real, as exact as optics, geometry or mechanics; its results as tangible as those of chemistry.” / “Alchemy also bore the name of celestial Agriculture, and its Adepts that of Labourers.”

16.content:
[Work: Alchemy (Alchimie)]
Book cited in notes: 'Alchimie, p. 137. J.-J. Pauvert éditeur', for Canseliet's study on the Golden Fleece; cited again on the Golden Fleece fable and on the St Marcel pillar dragon. The text implies but does not state that it is Canseliet's book.

Fulcanelli: “Cf. Alchimie, op. cit.”

17.content:
[Term: Alkahest]
A name some gave to the dissolvent whose first magnetic agent is the Green Lion; the grammar leaves open whether 'Alkaest' names the dissolvent or that agent. Stated: the 'servus fugitivus', a mineral water, solid, brittle, stone-like, easily liquefied, this coagulated water, is the Alkahest and the universal solvent. The dissolution of alchemical gold by the Alkahest solvent marks the first way; that of common gold by 'our mercury' the second. Identified with the universal solvent (e321).

Fulcanelli: “The dissolution of alchemical gold by the Alkahest Solvent marks the first way; that of common gold by our mercury indicates the second.”

Identified in the text with: Universal solvent

18.content:
[Term: Aludel]
Named only in Grillot de Givry's passage: the bishop of the right portal of Notre-Dame is perched on the aludel where the philosophical mercury, chained in limbo, is sublimed.

Fulcanelli: “the bishop perched on the aludel where the philosophical mercury, chained in limbo, is sublimed.”

19.content:
[Person: Amyraut]
Author of a Paraphrase of the First Epistle of Saint Peter (Saumur, 1646), quoted on the stone rejected by the builders that became the 'maistresse pierre du coin'.

Fulcanelli: “'The stone that the builders rejected,' writes Amyraut, 'has been made the master stone of the corner, on which the whole structure of the building rests”

20.content:
[Person: Amédée de Ponthieu]
Author of Légendes du Vieux Paris. Fulcanelli calls his explanation of Monsieur Legris the best, valuable because he was no hermetist and judged without bias; he describes the sacred monolith Phœbigène, Maître Pierre, messire Legris. The legend of Saint Christopher is transcribed from him, after Jacobus de Voragine.

Fulcanelli: “The best explanation is the one Amédée de Ponthieu gives us, and it seems all the more worthy of interest since the author, who was no hermetist, judges without bias and pronounces without preconceived idea”

21.comment: The Ancient War of the Knights (work; e309)
21.content:
[Work: The Ancient War of the Knights (Ancienne Guerre des Chevaliers)]
Work quoted for the 'poisoned worm that infects everything with its venom', which the text identifies with the serpent of Mercury. The note says it was augmented with a commentary by Limojon de Saint-Didier in the Triomphe hermétique.

Fulcanelli: “That is the 'poisoned worm which infects everything with its venom' of which the Ancient War of the Knights speaks.”

22.content:
[Term: Animated Mercury]
Stated: the single body, of middle quality and homogeneous substance, that results when the eagle (volatile) and the lion (fixed) have fought until the eagle loses its wings and the lion its head. It is achieved by the second way, the dissolution of common gold by 'our mercury'. In the animation of mercury the gold or king is dissolved little by little without violence. The dog and doves of the Paris north porch appear in the animation of the exalted mercury.

Fulcanelli: “until at last, the eagle having lost its wings and the lion its head, the antagonists make only one body, of middle quality and homogeneous substance, the Animated Mercury.”

23.content:
[Term: Ansate cross (ankh)]
With the apse added to the choir, the plan of the great churches takes the form of the Egyptian ansate cross, read ank, which designates the universal Life hidden in things; example on a Christian sarcophagus from Saint-Honorat at Arles, in the Saint-Germain-en-Laye museum. Its hermetic equivalent is the emblem of Venus or Cypris, common copper.

Fulcanelli: “takes the shape of the Egyptian hieratic sign of the ansate cross, which reads ank and designates the universal Life hidden in things.”

24.content:
[Work: Antiquities of Human Things (Antiquitates rerum humanarum)]
Work of Varro in which he recalls the legend of Aeneas saving his father and his household gods from the flames of Troy and reaching, after long wanderings, the fields of Laurentum; Venus's star, seen every day and by day, vanished there, showing him these were the lands appointed by Fate. The French gloss is the book's.

Fulcanelli: “From his departure from Troy he saw every day, and during the day, the star of Venus, until he reached the Laurentine fields, where he ceased to see it”

25.content:
[Work: Basilian Aphorisms (Aphorismes Basiliens)]
Work also called Canons Hermétiques de l'Esprit et de l'Ame, printed after the Oeuvres of R. P. de Castaigne, Paris, de la Nove, 1681. Its canon XVI is cited on the weights: the work begins with the conjunction of the three principles in a proportion where the body should equal the spirit and soul nearly by half.

Fulcanelli: “we begin our hermetic work by the conjunction of the three principles prepared in a certain proportion, which lies in the weight of the body, which must equal the spirit and the soul almost by half.”

26.content:
[Work: The Apocalypse (Apocalypse)]
Its ch. IV, v. 6–7 (the four animals before the throne) is quoted with Ezekiel for the four ages. The S of the Hendaye cross is a theoretical image of the beast of the Apocalypse, the dragon vomiting fire and sulphur at the Judgment. The alchemical books are closed like the Apocalypse by cabalistic seals, to be broken one by one.

Fulcanelli: “Your books are closed, like that of the Apocalypse, by cabalistic seals. You must break them one by one.” / “It is a theoretical image of the beast of the Apocalypse, of the dragon that spews, in the days of Judgment, fire and sulphur over the macrocosmic creation.”

27.content:
[Person: Apollo]
In Callimachus, quoted for the sublimations, the swans circled Delos seven times and Apollo was born before the eighth song. Apollo killing the monster Python with arrows is one of the fables of the combat whose chemical bodies yield the secret dissolvent. Apollo and Diana appear as brother and sister whose union makes the compost or philosophic rebis.

Fulcanelli: “It is Cadmos piercing the serpent against an oak; Apollo killing the monster Python with arrows, and Jason the dragon of Colchis”

28.content:
[Person: Apollonius of Tyana]
Said to share the Language of the Birds. The note calls him a philosopher whose legendary life seems very hypothetical; his name seems only a mytho-hermetic image of the compost or philosophical rebis, made by the union of brother and sister, Gabritius and Beya, Apollo and Diana; hence the wonders told by Philostratus are chemical.

Fulcanelli: “The name of this almost fabulous person seems to us only a mytho-hermetic image of the compost, or philosophical rebis, made by the union of the brother and the sister, of Gabritius and Beya, of Apollo and Diana.”

29.content:
[Term: Arcanum]
A hidden secret of the Work. Fulcanelli hopes to show that the meaning of the arcanum hidden under the stone bark of the cathedral can be recovered; the old masters covered the arcanum with a thick veil by mixing the qualities of the substances across the four black phases. Canseliet: the key of the 'major arcanum' is given by one of the book's figures and consists in a colour shown to the artisan at the first work; the anonymous letter says the arcanum cannot be found by reason alone; the star is a 'marvellous arcanum'.

Fulcanelli: “show lovers of the occult that it is not impossible to recover the meaning of the arcanum hidden under the petrified bark of the prodigious grimoire.”

Canseliet, in his preface: “And this key consists quite simply in a colour, shown to the craftsman from the first work.”

30.content:
[Term: Archimic]
Canseliet: the star is not peculiar to the Great Work; it can be met in many 'archimic' combinations, particular processes and lesser spagyric operations, always indicating a transformation of the bodies it settles on. Interpreted: 'archimic' designates operations of lesser rank than the Great Work, as the sentence pairs them with lesser spagyric operations.

Canseliet, in his preface: “It can be met in a host of archimic combinations, particular processes and spagyric operations of lesser importance.”

31.content:
[Term: Argonauts]
The argotiers are hermetic descendants of the argo-nautes, who sailed the Argo, spoke the argotic language, and went to Colchos to win the Golden Fleece; the 'nautes' builders knew the road to the Garden of the Hesperides. The last medallion of the Notre-Dame porch is a replica of the Argonauts' expedition: Jason by the ram with the golden fleece and the tree of the Hesperides.

Fulcanelli: “The argotiers, those who use this language, are hermetic descendants of the argo-nauts, who manned the ship Argo and spoke the argotic language — our langue verte — as they sailed toward the happy shores of Colchis to win the famous Golden Fleece.” / “Moreover, this image is a replica of the famous expedition of the Argonauts; we see Jason beside the ram with the golden fleece and the tree with the precious fruits of the Garden of the Hesperides.”

32.content:
[Term: Argot]
A language for those who wish to communicate without being understood, hence a 'spoken cabala'. Its speakers, the argotiers, are hermetic descendants of the Argonauts; all Initiates spoke it, from the truands of the Cour des Miracles with Villon to the medieval Freemasons who built the 'argotic' cathedrals. Today it is the language of the outcasts called voyous, that is, voyants. It derives from the Language of the Birds. Rabelais's Gargantua is called a 'roman d'argot'.

Fulcanelli: “Now the dictionaries define argot as 'a language peculiar to all individuals who have an interest in communicating their thoughts without being understood by those around them'. It is therefore indeed a spoken cabala.” / “Let us add finally that argot is one of the derived forms of the Language of the Birds, mother and eldest of all the others, the language of philosophers and diplomats.”

33.content:
[Person: Ariadne]
Read cabalistically: Ariane is a form of airagne, spider, by metathesis; our soul is the spider weaving our body. Via Greek αιρην it is the magnet, the virtue in the body the Sages call their magnesia; via Provençal aran/iran, iron, it is Hiram and the Ram; via αρυαν it is the Orient, the rising sun. The mystic spider left the trace of her web at Amiens. In sublimation, Theseus, manifested light, separates from Ariadne, the spider at the centre of her web, the empty husk.

Fulcanelli: “Ariane is a form of airagne (spider), by metathesis of the i.” / “αρυαν, or ariane, is therefore the Orient, by permutation of vowels.”

34.content:
[Term: Ariadne's thread]
What the artist needs to find the way out of the labyrinth of the Work and not wander among its windings. Batsdorff wrote a special treatise on it (Le Filet d'Ariadne); Fulcanelli instead offers cabalistic readings of Ariadne's name.

Fulcanelli: “It is here that Ariadne's thread becomes necessary to him, if he does not wish to wander among the windings of the work without finding the way out.”

35.content:
[Person: Aristotle]
Cited for Mercury's emblematic colour, grey or violet. In a quoted passage of the Cosmopolite he is among those who learned from the 'mirror' how the world was created. A four-petalled flower on the Saint-Marcel pillar expresses universal matter, the quaternary of first elements according to his doctrine, widespread in the Middle Ages.

Fulcanelli: “expressing universal matter, the quaternary of the first elements, according to the doctrine of Aristotle widespread in the Middle Ages.”

36.content:
[Term: Armillary sphere]
On the Lallemant chapel ceiling, an armillary sphere on a fiery ground, very like an engraving in the Azoth treatise, with the brazier in Atlas' place, is the symbol of sulphur and its extraction from the first matter.

Fulcanelli: “It is an armillary sphere, set on a burning ground, closely resembling one of the engravings of the treatise of the Azoth.”

37.content:
[Person: Arnold of Villanova]
'Maître Arnaud de Villeneuve' is quoted on the green names of the Green Lion: our water takes the names of the leaves of all trees and of everything green, to deceive the foolish.

Fulcanelli: “Our water takes the names of the leaves of all trees, of the trees themselves, and of all that takes a green colour, in order to deceive the foolish”

38.content:
[Person: Artephius]
With Pontanus and the Epistola de Igne Philosophorum, recommended for careful reading on the nature of the secret fire, the watery fire or fiery water. He and Philalèthe speak of the 'chien de Corascène' to be separated from the compost as black powder. Quoted: 'Notre Art ... est entièrement cabalistique', which Fulcanelli endorses: the cabala let him say things not found in his predecessors' books.

Fulcanelli: “'Our Art,' Artephius once said, 'is entirely cabalistic'”

39.content:
[Term: Artist]
The text's name for the alchemist who carries out the Work: on Notre-Dame the artist, after long wandering, finds the fountain and watches over the cooking of the compost. He must make his vessel himself, 'a maxim of the art'. Canseliet says the key is a colour shown to the artisan from the first work; the same preface uses 'artiste' plainly for the painter Julien Champagne.

Fulcanelli: “The artist must make his vessel himself; it is a maxim of the art.”

Canseliet, in his preface: “And this key consists quite simply in a colour, shown to the artisan from the first work.”

40.content:
[Term: Assation]
The text names assation the dry second period of the coction, begun by a second turn of the wheel and ended when the content of the egg, calcined, appears granular or powdery, as crystals, sand or ash.

Fulcanelli: “The second period, marked by dryness, or assation, then begins, with a second turn of the wheel”

41.content:
[Work: Atalanta Fleeing (Atalanta Fugiens)]
Work by Michel Maier; its 50th emblem shows a dragon entwining a woman in her grave, which Canseliet matches to the Saint Marcel legend and its two ways.

Canseliet, in his preface: “on which the dragon entwines a clothed woman, in the full bloom of her maturity and lying inert in the hollow of her grave, likewise violated.”

42.content:
[Term: Athanor]
The furnace of the Work. On Notre-Dame's porch a small crenellated tower is 'the instrument of the Great Work, the Athanor, the occult furnace with two flames, potential and virtual'; another relief shows its cross-section and the support for the philosophical egg. The Rebis lies at its centre. At Amiens the 'church' is an athanor, its tower the secret furnace holding the egg, with openings for watching; its parts are ash-pit, tower and dome, and old prints show furnaces as keeps. The St Marcel dragon grips the athanor. Canseliet quotes Grillot: a celestial ray is needed to light its fire.

Fulcanelli: “This curious keep, a castle in miniature, is the instrument of the Great Work, the Athanor, the occult furnace with two flames, — potential and virtual, — which all disciples know” / “One finds in it the parts of the alchemical furnace: ash-pit, tower and dome.”

43.content:
[Person: Avicenna]
Named only inside the Cosmopolite's passage on the mirror in the kingdom of Sulphur: whoever looks into it learns the three parts of the wisdom of the world, as Aristotle, Avicenna and many others did, who saw in this mirror how the world was created.

Fulcanelli: “he will become very learned in these three kingdoms, as were Aristotle, Avicenna and many others”

44.comment: Azoth, or the Means of Making the Hidden Gold of the Philosophers (work; e270)
44.content:
[Work: Azoth, or the Means of Making the Hidden Gold of the Philosophers (Azoth)]
Treatise attributed to Basil Valentine, which the text thinks rather the work of Senior Zadith; edition Paris, Pierre Moët, 1659. It has a woodcut of a crowned nymph or siren swimming in the sea and spurting milk from her breasts into the waves. Its second part seems to envisage the dry way: the Art learnt in under twelve hours and perfected in eight days. One of its engravings closely resembles an armillary sphere on the Lallemant ceiling.

Fulcanelli: “For this Art can be learnt in less than twelve hours, and brought to perfection within eight days, when it has its own principle within itself.” / “a woodcut showing a crowned nymph or siren swimming on the sea and spurting from her full breasts two jets of milk that mingle with the waves.”

45.content:
[Term: Babylonian Dragon]
After the pure, coloured principles have risen, the residue is ready to give the mercurial salt, volatile and fusible, which the old authors often called the Babylonian Dragon. On the Saint Anne pedestal the dragon rises from the flames, its tail seeming to come out of the human figure, and grips the athanor with its claws. The dragon is the image of mercury, and its bands of circles, the solar sign, show it can transmute in quantity after the multiplications.

Fulcanelli: “the residue is then ready to furnish the mercurial salt, volatile and fusible, to which the old authors often gave the epithet Babylonian Dragon.”

46.content:
[Person: Balaam]
The text finds the first mention of the star in Balaam's mouth; said to be born at Pethor on the Euphrates and to have lived about 1477 B.C., a prophet or Magus in Mesopotamia. His words (Num. XXIV) are quoted.

Fulcanelli: “A star rises out of Jacob and the sceptre comes forth from Israel”

47.content:
[Person: Baleus]
Voice in the Tourbe cited by Canseliet: 'the mother takes pity on her child, but the child is very hard toward her'.

Canseliet, in his preface: “Several alchemists have said, and the Turba in particular, through the voice of Baleus, that 'the mother takes pity on her child, but the child is very hard toward her.'”

48.content:
[Person: Basil Valentine]
Cited Adept, 'the monk of Erfurth'; the Azoth attributed to him may rather be by Senior Zadith. He named the Green Lion 'green Vitriol' for its hot, burning, saline nature; he counsels dissolving and feeding the true Lion with the blood of the Green Lion; he used the cock-fox in his third Key; the eagle-and-dragon combat; the body of Vitriol as 'Mirror of philosophical Science'; a white swan given to the double igneous man (weights); Saturn's lament. Lallemant is called his equal. Canseliet: Fulcanelli's first initiator.

Fulcanelli: “Dissolve and feed the true Lion with the blood of the green Lion, for they are both of the same nature.” / “Certain Adepts, Basil Valentine among them, have named it green Vitriol, to reveal its hot, burning and saline nature”

49.content:
[Term: Bath of the stars]
A small relief under the Portal of the Virgin expresses the condensation of the universal Spirit, which once materialised forms the Bath of the stars, where the chemical sun and moon must bathe, change nature and grow young. It shows a child falling from a crucible held by an archangel against a starry night sky, which Fulcanelli reads as Flamel's Massacre of the Innocents. In Abraham the Jew's fourth figure sun and moon come down to bathe in the vat of the children's blood.

Fulcanelli: “It sums up and expresses the condensation of the universal Spirit, which, once materialised, forms the famous Bath of the stars where the chemical sun and moon must bathe, change their nature and grow young again.”

50.content:
[Term: Bather]
Stated: the baigneur in the Kings' Cake is the Child Jesus carried by Offerus, 'gold in its bath'; it is also the bean (fève), the sabot, the cradle or the cross of honour, and the fish swimming in the philosophic sea. It sits in the flaky dough like a bookmark. The swaddled 'mineral child' in the flames of the Saint-Marcel pillar is likened to the porcelain baigneur of the Epiphany galette. Whoever finds the bean (fève) will never lack money, doubly king by science and fortune.

Fulcanelli: “It is the Child Jesus carried by Offerus, the servant or traveller; it is gold in its bath, the bather; it is the bean, the clog, the cradle or the cross of honour”

51.content:
[Person: Batsdorff]
Presumed author of a classic work, Le Filet d'Ariadne, which others attribute to Gaston de Claves; he wrote a special treatise on Ariadne's thread. Quoted: putrefaction appears with blackness and separates pure from impure; its stench is sensed by the understanding, not the nose. He says the Philosophers called the vessel of coction Green Lion, without giving a reason.

Fulcanelli: “It is therefore clear that by this putrefaction the separation of the pure from the impure is made.” / “Batsdorff, in his Thread of Ariadne, says the Philosophers called the vessel used for coction Green Lion, but without giving any reason.”

52.content:
[Person: Bernard Husson]
Named only in Canseliet's third preface (voice CANSELIET). He gave a date to the photograph published by Grillot de Givry and called it a daguerreotype. Following Marcel Clavelle (Jean Reyor), he recently revived, thirty-two years later, the dispute over Fulcanelli's correction of Cambriel, adopting Reyor's opinion entirely. He proposed that 'XVIe siècle' on page 407 of the Musée des Sorciers was a misprint corrected to 'XVIIe siècle' in the caption, a correction Canseliet says is not there. Canseliet says he and Clavelle were blinded by the pleasure of catching Fulcanelli in error.

Canseliet, in his preface: “of which Bernard Husson deliberately fixes the date and makes a daguerreotype”

53.content:
[Person: Bernard of Treviso]
Named among the masters of old times. The Mysterious Fountain carved at Notre-Dame is the one he describes in the final Parable of his book on the natural philosophy of metals. Quoted (La Parole délaissée) on the blackening: the compound soaked with permanent water turns like melted pitch, black as coal, and receives many names; this blackness is the key and sign of right working. The 'Fountain of Trévisan' where the King strips off his purple mantle appears in a quoted text. His parable of the old priest and the king of the country, whom the fountain attracts and engulfs, matches a Notre-Dame medallion. The Verbum dimissum of the Trévisan is the Lost Word of the medieval freemasons.

Fulcanelli: “when our compound begins to be soaked with our permanent water, then the whole compound is turned like melted pitch, and is all blackened like coal.” / “That is the Verbum dimissum of the Trévisan, the Lost Word of the medieval freemasons”

54.content:
[Person: Beya]
The sister in the brother-sister pair Gabritius and Beya, whose union makes the compost or rebis.

Fulcanelli: “made by the union of the brother and the sister, of Gabritius and Beya, of Apollo and Diana.”

55.content:
[Term: Bezants]
The restorers replaced the bezants and flowers of the Saint Anne pedestal with Romanesque scrolls. On the original pedestal, two bezants on the right side are the metallic matters or natures, subject and solvent, with which the Work must begin; on the front, changed by preliminary operations, they become rosettes; on the left, flowers with visible calyx, showing the metallic roots opened and ready to show their seed principle.

Fulcanelli: “On the cubic pedestal you will notice, on the right side, two bezants in relief, massive and circular; they are the metallic matters or natures, subject and solvent, with which the Work must begin.”

56.content:
[Work: The Bible of Amiens]
Work of Ruskin, named for his reading of the Amiens wheel-fire as Ezekiel's vision.

Fulcanelli: “Jourdain and Duval, Ruskin (The Bible of Amiens), the abbé Roze and, after them, Georges Durand”

57.comment: General Bibliography of the Occult (work; e221)
57.content:
[Work: General Bibliography of the Occult (Bibliographie générale de l'Occulte)]
Work of Pierre Dujols, quoted on Elias Schadius's inscription to Isis and on Bigarne's interpretation of Isis as the Virgo paritura and mother of the gods.

Fulcanelli: “Already, says the erudite Pierre Dujols in his General Bibliography of the Occult, the learned Elias Schadius had pointed out, in his book De dictis Germanicis, a similar inscription”

58.content:
[Term: Bird of Hermes]
Stated (Philalèthe, quoted with approval): the philosophers' Mercury is the bird of Hermes, also called Goose or Swan, sometimes Pheasant. The swans of Callimachus circling Delos seven times are the sublimations. Basile Valentin (quoted) says to give a white swan to the double igneous man, on the weights. Tollius (quoted) mocks seekers of their red 'faysan' in glass vessels. Identified with the Philosophical Mercury (e307).

Fulcanelli: “And our Philosophical Mercury is the bird of Hermes, which is also given the name of Goose or Swan, and sometimes that of Pheasant.”

Identified in the text with: Philosophical Mercury

59.content:
[Term: Black colour]
The first of the three principal colours of the Work, which go in invariable order from black to red through white. In the cooking of the Rebis it is the first appearance of decomposition and the sign of exact preparation; its symbol is the Raven. Le Breton (quoted) counts four putrefactions, in each of which blackness appears, which lets authors mix up the operations; Trévisan and Batsdorff (quoted) describe it (pitch-black compound, 'clef', sign of the good path; 'noirceur très noire' as sign of true putrefaction). Symbolically black was given to Saturn (lead, the Black Hen), is the colour of darkness, Satan, the primitive Chaos, heraldic sable, earth, night and death. Paracelsus (quoted) calls black the root of the other colours. The Virgin's blue corresponds to black. On cathedral roses the colours run from darkness, figured by absence of light and black, to ruddy light. At Bourges the death of the body shows a dark blue or black colour, given to the Raven. Fulcanelli also warns that the clear descriptions of colours of the 'régimes' are false and that one should learn how one régime differs from the next rather than one colour from another. Identified with the Raven (e282).

Fulcanelli: “It expresses, in fact, in the cooking of the philosophical Rebis, the black colour, first appearance of the decomposition that follows the perfect mixing of the matters of the Egg.” / “it is the sable of heraldry and the emblem of the element earth, of night and of death.”

Identified in the text with: Raven

60.content:
[Term: Black Hen]
The black colour was given to Saturn, who became in magic the Black Hen. On the Lallemant ceiling a 'géline' or partridge perches on the horn of Amalthea; whether the emblem is the black hen or the red partridge changes nothing to its hermetic meaning. Interpreted: through Saturn, the hen belongs to the black colour of the Work.

Fulcanelli: “The black colour was given to Saturn, who became, in spagyrics, the hieroglyph of lead, in astrology a malefic planet, in magic the Black Hen, etc.”

61.content:
[Term: Black Virgins]
Statues of Isis that became, after the coming of Christianity to Gaul, the Black Virgins, venerated in the crypts; same symbolism, same inscription Virgini parituræ. In hermetic symbolism they figure the primitive earth that the artist must choose as subject: the first matter as ore, a black, heavy, brittle substance; hence their colour and their underground dwelling. Examples: Chartres (Notre-Dame-sous-Terre, Notre-Dame-du-Pilier), Le Puy, Marseille, Rocamadour, Vichy, Quimper, and a Paris Virgin in the Observatory cellars. Only green candles were burnt in their processions, a detail called useful to the hermetist.

Fulcanelli: “In hermetic symbolism they figure the primitive earth, the one the artist must choose as the subject of his great work.” / “In the ceremonial prescribed for processions of Black Virgins, only green candles were burnt.”

62.content:
[Person: Blaise de Vigenère]
Canseliet: with Naxagoras, he wrote at length on the value of a long preliminary coction of lead, which, though dead, can be revived by being fed with igneous substance.

Canseliet, in his preface: “Blaise de Vigenère and Naxagoras, for instance, dwelt on the advisability of a long preliminary coction.”

63.content:
[Term: Brass (latten)]
Airain and laiton are names some gave to common copper, the metal of Venus, to veil the sense; all good authors repeat 'whiten the laiton and burn your books'. Bernard Trévisan (QUOTED) lists 'laton non net' (unclean latten) among the names of the blackened compost. Venus is to airain.

Fulcanelli: “'Whiten the latten and burn your books,' all the good authors repeat to us.” / “And at this point our compost is called: the black pitch, the burnt salt, the molten lead, the unclean latten, the Magnesia and John's Blackbird.”

64.content:
[Term: Brothers of Heliopolis]
Named only in Canseliet's first preface: he leaves to the Brothers of Heliopolis the joy of receiving this synthesis, set out by 'one of theirs', and thanks the illustrator in their name and his own. The text says nothing more about who they are. Interpreted: 'one of theirs' makes the author, Fulcanelli, a member; the signature 'F. C. H.' under Canseliet's name is not explained by the text.

Canseliet, in his preface: “as [I leave] to the Brothers of Heliopolis the joy of receiving this synthesis, so masterfully set out by one of their own.”

65.content:
[Place: Building on boulevard Péreire]
A building Fulcanelli saw being built when he was a student; above the door two children, boy and girl, lift a veil; on the corner a bas-relief shows the symbolic combat of the eagle and the lion, an emblem he thinks imposed on the architect by a superior will. The note places it at the corner of boulevard Péreire and rue de Monbel, 17th arrondissement, six storeys of cut stone.

Fulcanelli: “it shows the symbolic combat of the eagle and the lion, of which we have just spoken, and one easily guesses that the architect had some trouble fitting in the cumbersome emblem”

66.content:
[Term: Bull]
The Bull is the sculpted figure that follows the fox-cock on the Paris stylobate. As a zodiac sign it is the second month of the preparatory operations in the first work, and the first regimen of the elemental fire in the second. As a figure of practice it stands for Sulphur, the male principle: bull and ox are sacred to the sun as the cow is to the moon, and Hermes calls the sun the Father of the stone. Bull and cow, sun and moon, sulphur and mercury mean the same thing: the two contrary primitive natures before their conjunction, which the Art extracts from imperfect mixtures. On the Portal of the Virgin, Taurus comes after Aries among the spring signs that mark the start of the work.

Fulcanelli: “The bull and the cow, the sun and the moon, sulphur and mercury are therefore hieroglyphs of identical meaning, and denote the contrary primitive natures, before their conjunction”

67.content:
[Term: Cabala]
Fulcanelli's reading of words by sound. The origin of 'gothic' must be sought in its 'cabalistic origin' rather than its literal root; by the 'phonetic law' governing the traditional cabala regardless of spelling, art gothique is argotique; argot is a 'spoken cabala'. People of wit, punning, are cabalists unknowingly. The phonetic cabala reads Christophe as Chrysophe, 'gold-bearer'; 'Saba' or 'Caba' points to the cabalists; in cabala sabot equals cabot or chabot. Artephius: 'Our Art is entirely cabalistic'; the cabala let the author say things without lying or breaking his oath. Canseliet derives cabale from χαβάλλης or Latin caballus, horse, and distinguishes it from the Jewish kabbale.

Fulcanelli: “For us, art gothique is merely a spelling distortion of the word argotique, with which it is perfectly homophonous, in keeping with the phonetic law that governs the traditional cabala in all languages, regardless of spelling.” / “'Our Art,' Artephius once said, 'is entirely cabalistic'; the cabala has indeed always been of great use to us.”

68.content:
[Person: Cadmus]
The adept of the Fountain bas-relief disdains the bow and arrows with which, like Cadmus, he pierced the dragon. A quoted text says Philalethes describes the vessel through the fable of the serpent Python which Cadmus pierced through against an oak. The Hippocrene fountain was said to be discovered by Cadmos. Cadmos piercing the serpent against an oak is one of the fables of the combat of chemical bodies whose combination gives the secret dissolvent (and the vessel of the compound).

Fulcanelli: “It is Cadmus piercing the serpent against an oak; Apollo killing the monster Python with arrows, and Jason the dragon of Colchis”

69.content:
[Term: Caduceus]
The serpent coiled on the golden rod, image of the Philosophical Mercury on the second Paris relief; Abraham the Jew used it and the symbol runs through the Middle Ages. Stated: the serpent shows the incisive, dissolving nature of Mercury, which greedily absorbs the metallic sulphur; it is Mercury in its first state; the golden rod is the corporeal sulphur added; the resulting body keeps the image of the caduceus.

Fulcanelli: “This reptile is the type of Mercury in its first state, and the golden rod the corporeal sulphur added to it.”

70.content:
[Term: Calcination]
Personified on the Paris stylobate by a woman with flame-like hair pressing to her breast the disc of the Salamander. The spagyric image: violent fire destroys the combustible parts of a body, leaving the fixed central salt, extractable by lixiviation. The masters stress that philosophical calcination differs from common laboratory calcination: it uses no common fire or reverberatory furnace but an occult agent, a secret fire more like water than flame. Limojon (quoted): the secret fire calcines the matter, dissolves, sublimes it and resolves it into dry water. At Bourges philosophical calcination is shown as a pomegranate in a goldsmith's vase on the fire, with '3 R' marking the three reiterations; the calcination of the Sulphur must be reiterated three times to make the three works; the compound is heated in its sealed vessel until complete calcination, and this is repeated. The Paris figures follow the Elixir 'depuis sa calcination première'.

Fulcanelli: “The latter is done by no common fire, needs no reverberatory furnace, but requires the help of an occult agent, a secret fire”

71.content:
[Person: Callimachus]
Fulcanelli says Callimachus describes the sublimations in the Hymn to Delos, speaking of the swans that circled Delos seven times before Apollo was born.

Fulcanelli: “It is these sublimations that Callimachus describes in the Hymn to Delos (lines 250, 255), when he says, speaking of the swans”

72.content:
[Term: Calyougam]
The fourth and last age, of misery, misfortune and decrepitude; the text identifies it with the iron age, 'which is ours', when the cow of Virtue barely balances on one foot. Its seal is Death.

Fulcanelli: “It is the fourth and last age, the Calyougam, age of misery, misfortune and decrepitude.”

Identified in the text with: Iron age

73.content:
[Person: Camille Flammarion]
Reports a statuette of the Virgin he saw in the cellars of the Paris Observatory on 24 September 1871, placed there in 1671 and invoked as Nostre-Dame de dessoubs terre. Source: L’Atmosphère (Paris, Hachette, 1888, p. 362).

Fulcanelli: “At the corner of one of the underground galleries there is a statuette of the Virgin, placed there that same year 1671, which verses carved at her feet invoke under the name of Our Lady beneath the earth.”

74.content:
[Term: Caput mortuum (dead head)]
On a Lallemant chapel capital, a winged skull on oak leaves expresses new generation from the putrefaction after death. The body's death shows a dark blue or black colour, given to the Raven, hieroglyph of the caput mortuum of the Work: sign of dissolution, separation of the elements and future generation of sulphur. The calcined black ash then leaves its impurities and a pure salt is born.

Fulcanelli: “The death of the body lets a dark blue or black colour appear, assigned to the Raven, hieroglyph of the caput mortuum of the Work.”

75.content:
[Term: Cathars]
In Pierre Dujols's passage quoted by Fulcanelli on white: the Cathars, the sect to which the Whites of Florence belonged, were the Pure (from Greek Katharos).

Fulcanelli: “The Cathars, the sect to which the Whites of Florence belonged, were the Pure (from the Greek Katharos).”

76.content:
[Term: Celestial Agriculture]
Stated: a former name of alchemy, whose Adepts were called 'Laboureurs' (ploughmen). Interpreted: Fulcanelli's address to operators 'vous qui avez déjà tant labouré' plays on this name.

Fulcanelli: “Alchemy also bore the name of Celestial Agriculture, and its Adepts that of Ploughmen.”

77.content:
[Term: Central salt]
Stated: what the Salamander designates: the incombustible, fixed salt that keeps its nature even in the ashes of calcined metals, named by the Ancients 'Semence métallique'; in the violence of fire the combustible parts are destroyed and only the pure, unalterable parts resist, which can be extracted by lixiviation. The commentator of the Lumière sortant des Ténèbres (quoted) says the subject of the art must be sought in the mineral kingdom only, 'où réside la semence métallique'. Identified with the Salamander (e312).

Fulcanelli: “and which the Ancients named metallic Seed.”

Identified in the text with: Salamander

78.content:
[Person: Ceres]
Isis is called the Egyptian Ceres. Greeks and Egyptians kept absolute silence on the mysteries of Ceres; disclosure was punished by death and the temple barred to the uninitiated. From the four grades of her priests (Hierophant; Torch-bearer, representing the Sun; Herald, representing Mercury; Minister of the Altar, representing the Moon) Fulcanelli infers that her mysteries were of the same order as those of Hermetic Science. At Rome the Cerealia began on 12 April and lasted eight days, with an egg, symbol of the world, carried in procession. Isis, Ceres and Cybele are 'three heads under the same veil'.

Fulcanelli: “the information handed down to us on the hierarchy of the high priests allows us to think that the mysteries of Ceres must have been of the same order as those of the Hermetic Science.”

Identified in the text with: Isis

79.content:
[Person: Ch. Bigarne]
Author of Considérations sur le Culte d’Isis chez les Eduens (Beaune, 1862). He speaks of several statues of Isis under the same title as the Black Virgins. In the passage quoted from Pierre Dujols, Bigarne explains Isis before conception as the Virgo paritura, the earth before fecundation, and as mother of the gods. Fulcanelli adds that one cannot better define the esoteric sense of the Black Virgins.

Fulcanelli: “Isis before conception is, says Bigarne, in astronomical theogony, the attribute of the Virgin whom several monuments, long before Christianity, designate by the name Virgo paritura”

80.content:
[Person: Chalcidius]
A 4th-century philosopher who, according to his editor Mullachius, held that the gods of Greece, of Rome and foreign gods should be worshipped; he preserved a mention of the star of the Magi and the scholars' explanation of it, after speaking of a star the Egyptians called Ahc which announced misfortunes. He tells of a holier story in which the most learned Chaldeans saw the star at night and sought the newborn God. Source: Comm. in Timæum Platonis, c. 125; the footnote adds that Chalcidius plainly addresses an initiate.

Fulcanelli: “The most learned of the Chaldeans, having seen this star while travelling by night, as men perfectly practised in contemplating heavenly things, sought, so it is told, the recent birth of a God”

81.content:
[Term: Chaos]
The Sages' name for the confused first matter. The Arab 'Modhallan', 'dark and gloomy sea', marks the elemental confusion the Sages attribute to their Chaos or first matter; the primitive water issues from the Chaos of the Sages. Black is the colour of the primitive Chaos, where the seeds of all things are mixed. 'The metallic Chaos contains all metals and is not metal'; a portion of the first Chaos remains in this world, known but despised and sold publicly. Possessing the right subject, one has the 'Chaos of the Sages' in which all secrets are in potency (Philalèthe). Light was drawn from the dark Chaos. Canseliet: heaven and earth are confused in the original cosmic Chaos.

Fulcanelli: “The metallic Chaos produced by the hands of nature contains in itself all the metals and is not metal.” / “which clearly marks the elemental confusion the Sages attribute to their Chaos or first matter.”

Identified in the text with: First matter

82.content:
[Person: Charles Vincens]
Confirms the closeness of Isis and Cybele by describing a bas-relief of Cybele, inscribed Matri Deum, seen for centuries on the outside of the parish church of Pennes (Bouches-du-Rhône); it disappeared about 1610 but is engraved in Grosson's Recueil.

Fulcanelli: “This curious piece, he tells us, disappeared only around 1610, but it is engraved in Grosson's Recueil (p. 20).”

83.comment: Charnel house of the Innocents (place; e431)
83.content:
[Place: Charnel house of the Innocents]
Flamel built two decorative arcades there, in 1389 and 1407; the first bore, among other hieroglyphic plaques, an escutcheon that seems imitated from one attributed to saint Thomas Aquinas. Fulcanelli concludes Lagneau had his engraving copied from this arcade; of four plaques three remained in Gohorry's time, about 1572.

Fulcanelli: “Flamel also raised two decorative arcades at the charnel house of the Innocents, one in 1389, the second in 1407.”

84.content:
[Place: Chartres cathedral]
Its nave labyrinth, called 'la lieue', once showed Theseus and the Minotaur. The north portal rose renders the movements of matter excited by fire. It has two Black Virgins: Notre-Dame-sous-Terre in the crypt, inscribed Virgini parituræ, and Notre-Dame-du-Pilier; it passes for the oldest pilgrimage, originally an Isis statuette. Its figure of a man in his shirt is, for Fulcanelli, an alchemist dressed lightly for the furnace heat. Its royal portal shows the four animals around Christ.

Fulcanelli: “With its underground Virgin, Chartres is held to be the oldest of all pilgrimages.” / “As for the light dress the craftsman wears in the Chartres motif, it is explained by the heat given off by the furnace.”

85.content:
[Term: Chemical heaven]
Canseliet: the hermetic star, first admired in the mirror of the art, is then found in the chemical heaven, where it shines more discreetly; it is a nocturnal star at the pole of the hermetic heaven, the 'terrestrial heaven' of Lavinius and Tollius. Heaven and earth are one in substance in the original Chaos but differ in quality; the inert alchemical earth contains the philosophical heaven, which the artist separates with the secret fire and universal spirit, extracting light from darkness: thus one knows the 'heaven of the Sages'. Tollius's book is titled Le Chemin du Ciel Chymique.

Fulcanelli: “J. Tollius, The Road to the Chemical Heaven.”

Canseliet, in his preface: “Does not the alchemical earth, chaotic, inert and sterile, nonetheless contain the philosophical heaven?”

86.content:
[Term: Child gold]
Stated: gold dissolved in mercury and brought back to its first state is young or rejuvenated gold, 'in a word child gold'. The mercury then carries the child — the Son of the Sun, the Little King (Roitelet) — like a true mother, since gold is reborn in its bosom; hence mercury is called Fountain of Youth. The Kings' Cake with its baigneur is the popular version of this truth. At Amiens the hermetic star announces the birth of the 'fils du soleil'. Interpreted: the 'petit roi' or mineral child in the flames of the Saint-Marcel pillar is the same figure.

Fulcanelli: “This geometric pattern persists and appears more clearly once gold has been put to dissolve in the mercury to bring it back to its first state, that of young or rejuvenated gold, in a word child gold.” / “So the Philosophers speak plainly when they teach that the mercury, once the dissolution is done, carries the child, the Son of the Sun, the Little King (Roitelet), like a true mother, since gold is indeed reborn in its bosom.”

87.content:
[Place: Church of Brixen]
A small church in the Tyrol which held a painted 'replica' of the fable of the fountain whose water seemed to flow like milk from two breasts. The painting, described by Misson and reported by Witkowski, showed Jesus letting the blood of his side flow into a basin and the Virgin pressing milk from her breasts into the same vessel; the overflow fell into a gulf of flames where the souls of Purgatory received it. Fulcanelli says it seems to be the religious version of the same chemical theme. Beneath it a Latin inscription ends 'Et sit Fons Vitae, Fons et Origo boni', which the book renders as the blood and milk mingling and becoming 'la Fontaine de Vie et la Source du Bien'.

Fulcanelli: “A painted replica of the fable we have just cited was to be found in the little church of Brixen (Tyrol).” / “This curious picture, described by Misson and noted by Witkowski, seems to be the religious version of the same chemical theme.”

88.content:
[Term: Cista (basket)]
The basket of Bacchus, called Cista, carried by the Cistophores in the bacchanal processions and holding, according to Fr. Noel, what was most mysterious. It follows the fish's basket in the Catacomb painting, which is the same hieroglyph as the galette, its texture also of crossed strands.

Fulcanelli: “The basket the fish carries is the same hieroglyph as the galette; its texture likewise proceeds from crossed strands.” / “let us merely draw the attention of the curious to the basket of Bacchus, called Cista, which the Cistophori carried in the processions of the bacchanals”

89.content:
[Work: Keys of Spagyric Philosophy (Clefs de la Philosophie Spagyrique)]
Book by Le Breton, Paris, Jombert, 1722; cited at p. 282 for the four putrefactions and at p. 240 for the mineral containing fixed and volatile.

Fulcanelli: “there are four putrefactions in the philosophical Work.”

90.content:
[Term: Cock]
The monster half cock half fox on the Paris stylobate shows the extraction of the red, incombustible Sulphur; Basile Valentin (quoted, third Key): the cock will eat the fox, drown, revive by fire and be devoured by the fox in turn. Cock and fox are Basile's figure for the combat of the conjunction. At Amiens the cock is perched on an oak branch the fox tries to reach. Stated: cock and fox are one hieroglyph of two physical states of one matter; the cock is the volatile, living portion extracted from the subject (the oak), the famous source called Mercury, the dry water. The cock is emblem of Mercury among pagans and of resurrection among Christians, can become the Phoenix, and, as attribute of Saint Peter, 'crowing three times' marks the three reiterations. By galla, Gallia, gallus, the cock is emblem of Gaul and attribute of Mercury according to Tollius.

Fulcanelli: “Such is the alchemical meaning of the cock, emblem of Mercury among the pagans and of resurrection among the Christians.” / “we shall say only that the cock and the fox are but one hieroglyph covering two distinct physical states of one same matter.”

91.content:
[Term: Coction]
The cooking of the compound in the vessel. The rose window, called Rota, the wheel, is the hieroglyph of the time needed for coction and of coction itself; its steady fire is the 'wheel fire'. The black, white, red phases are specific to coction. The Regimen of the stone, its coction, contains several repetitions of one way of operating. Linear, continuous coction needs a double rotation: a humid phase (elixation) then a dry one (assation); it is 'the seal of the Great Work'; on heat degrees, Philalèthe says one must boil, else it is digestion. The Amiens 'apostate' scene is read as coction and its furnace. Canseliet: a long preliminary coction revives dead lead.

Fulcanelli: “Now the wheel is the alchemical hieroglyph of the time needed for the coction of the philosophical matter and, by extension, of coction itself.” / “In fact, linear and continuous coction requires the double rotation of one and the same wheel, a movement impossible to render in stone, which justified the need for two wheels interlocked so as to form only one.”

92.content:
[Term: Cohobation]
The text makes the first lower medallion of Paris, a horseman thrown from a fiery horse, the allegory of the rectification of the spirit obtained and its cohobation on the heavy matter. At each cohobation the horse (the spiritual substance) throws its rider (the weight of the coarse metallic body): the volatile leaves the fixed, until the exhausted animal consents to carry the burden. The work needs much patience and frequent repetition of pouring the water on the earth, the spirit on the body; only so is the occult salt of the Red Lion extracted with the spirit of the Green Lion. In the rose window the rider of the Cohobation is a crowned prince in white jacket and red stockings.

Fulcanelli: “At each cohobation, the horse throws its rider, the volatile leaves the fixed”

93.content:
[Term: Colours of the Work]
On the Notre-Dame base, Evolution holds an oriflamme with three pennants, the triplicity of the Colours of the Work. There are three, in invariable order black, white, red; many passing intermediate hues matter little, while the essential colours last longer and colour the mass itself, marking a change of state. Each received a symbolic meaning, giving a language of colours found again in Gothic windows: black for Saturn, chaos, earth, night and death; white for purity and the Initiates; red for fire, exaltation and the finished stone. The three roses of a cathedral display them in a circle from black to red through white. Fulcanelli then warns, citing Etteilla and Tollius, that the clear descriptions of colours are not to be trusted literally; one must learn how one regime differs from the next.

Fulcanelli: “These colours, three in number, develop in the invariable order that goes from black to red by way of white.” / “Learn, then, not how one colour differs from another, but rather how one regime is distinguished from the next.”

94.content:
[Term: Common mercury (of the Philosophers)]
The Philosophers' common mercury, which they call 'our' mercury to distinguish it from the fluid metal it comes from; one cartouche shows a rarely used dissolution of common quicksilver meant to obtain it, an operation Fulcanelli calls hazardous if not sophistic. The dissolution of common gold by 'our mercury' marks the second path, which yields the animated mercury. At the Hôtel Lallemant the vase with dolphins and lily-like flower on the left capital refers to the solvent or common mercury of the Philosophers, the principle contrary to sulphur.

Fulcanelli: “It is that of common quicksilver, in order to obtain from it the common mercury of the Philosophers, which they call 'our' mercury, to distinguish it from the fluid metal from which it comes.”

95.content:
[Term: Compost]
The mixed matter of the Work, ready to be cooked. A Notre-Dame relief shows the cooking of the philosophical compost in the athanor. The black colour is the sign of its exact preparation. Per Bernard Trévisan (QUOTED), soaked in the permanent water it turns black like pitch and receives many names. A six-rayed star, Star of the Magi, shines on its surface, above the crib of the Child-King. Apollonius's name images the compost or rebis, union of brother and sister. REBIS designates the compost ready for its metamorphoses by fire. The text identifies it with the Rebis.

Fulcanelli: “It is a radiate figure with six points (digamma), called Star of the Magi, which shines on the surface of the compost, that is, above the crib where Jesus, the Child-King, lies.” / “Note, then, that when our compost begins to be soaked with our permanent water, the whole compost is turned into something like molten pitch and is all blackened like coal.”

Identified in the text with: Rebis

96.content:
[Term: Conjunction]
The union of the two contrary natures, sulphur and mercury. The griffin (eagle and lion) is the hieroglyph of the 'première conjonction', achieved only little by little through the labour the philosophers call their 'eagles'; the series of operations ending in the intimate union of sulphur and mercury is also called Sublimation. A violent combat precedes 'our conjunction': eagle and lion fight until they make one body, the Animated Mercury. The Sages say violent storms arise in the Conjunction; some figure it as fights of unlike animals: eagle and lion (Flamel), cock and fox (Basile Valentin), and, best of all, the Remora and the Salamander of Cyrano Bergerac. Le Breton (quoted) speaks of a first and a second conjunction, each with a putrefaction. On the Paris zodiac Leo usurping the place of Cancer indicates the conjunction of the philosophical ferment (Lion) with the mercurial compound towards the end of the fourth month of the first Work. Bull and cow, sun and moon, sulphur and mercury designate the contrary natures 'avant leur conjonction'. The escutcheon said to be of Saint Thomas Aquinas reveals the secrets of extracting mercury and of its conjunction with sulphur.

Fulcanelli: “We find in this image the hieroglyph of the first conjunction, which is achieved only little by little, in the course of that painful and tedious labour the Philosophers have called their eagles.” / “The sages said on this point that in the Conjunction violent storms arose, great tempests”

key: Cult of Isis among the Aedui
97.comment: Considerations on the Cult of Isis among the Aedui (work; e219)
97.content:
[Work: Considerations on the Cult of Isis among the Aedui (Considérations sur le Culte d'Isis chez les Eduens)]
Work of Ch. Bigarne (Beaune, 1862), cited for statues of Isis bearing the same title as the Black Virgins.

Fulcanelli: “Ch. Bigarne tells us of several statues of Isis designated under the same title.”

98.content:
[Person: Constantine]
Around the luminous cross he saw in a dream appeared the words he had painted on his labarum: In hoc signo vinces.

Fulcanelli: “Let us not forget that around the luminous cross seen in a dream by Constantine appeared the prophetic words he had painted on his labarum: In hoc signo vinces; by this sign you will conquer.”

99.content:
[Term: Cornerstone]
Through the sign of the Cross the church plan leads, for alchemists, to the First stone, cornerstone of the Great Work; Jesus built his Church on it. Before being cut the rough stone was given the devil's image. At Notre-Dame the devil figure Maistre Pierre du Coignet was the symbol of 'our cornerstone', 'pierre du coin', 'maîtresse pierre du coignet'; its cutting means its preparation, shown on a relief by the rue du Cloître-Notre-Dame. The parvis monolith called Maître Pierre, 'Pierre maîtresse, pierre de pouvoir', is identified with it.

Fulcanelli: “which leads, for the alchemists, to obtaining the First stone, cornerstone of the philosophical Great Work.” / “As for the cutting of this cornerstone — we mean its preparation — it can be seen rendered in a very pretty bas-relief of the period”

Identified in the text with: Monsieur Legris

100.content:
[Person: Cosmopolite]
An alchemical author quoted often, works cited as Nouvelle Lumière chymique with treatises on Sulphur, Mercury and Salt. The wise will find the stone in dung. In Sulphur's kingdom is a mirror in which the whole world is seen. On weights; the solar tree of the Parable, whose water Saturn draws; planetary virtues descend, Mars turns into Venus. The one Green Lion opens the seven seals; the fish Echinéis swims in the philosophical sea; he calls the subject Son of Saturn. Water rare in the island; acier and aimant in Aries.

Fulcanelli: “'The wise man will find our stone even in the dung-heap,' writes the Cosmopolite, 'while the ignorant will not be able to believe it is in gold.'” / “In his kingdom there is a mirror in which one sees the whole world.”

101.comment: Course of Hermetic Philosophy or Alchemy in Nineteen Lessons (work; e086)
101.content:
[Work: Course of Hermetic Philosophy or Alchemy in Nineteen Lessons (Cours de Philosophie hermétique ou d'Alchimie en dix-neuf leçons)]
Book of L. P. François Cambriel, Paris, Lacour et Maistrasse, 1843. On its p. 33 Cambriel says the St Marcel bishop puts a finger to his mouth to say 'be silent'; an engraving accompanies the text. Canseliet: its cover states it was finished in January 1829.

Fulcanelli: “This bishop puts a finger to his mouth, to say to those who see him and come to learn what he represents… be silent, say nothing of it!…”

102.content:
[Term: Cross]
Gothic churches are mostly laid out as a Latin cross, and 'the cross is the alchemical hieroglyph of the crucible'. Its three nails image the three purifications by iron and fire. It is not specifically Christian. Through the sign of the Cross the plan reveals the qualities and preparation of the first matter, leading to the first stone. On the tympanum of the north portal of Notre-Dame, as in spagyric notation, the four crosses represent the imperfect metals. At Hendaye, the upper cross is the divine one, the lower the cross of the globe locating the northern pole; INRI is read Igne Natura Renovatur Integra.

Fulcanelli: “Now, the cross is the alchemical hieroglyph of the crucible” / “Remember too, alchemists my brothers, that the cross bears the imprint of the three nails used to sacrifice the Christ-matter, image of the three purifications by iron and by fire.”

103.content:
[Place: Cross of Hendaye]
A plain stone cross by the south transept of Hendaye's parish church, moved from the cemetery in 1842; origin unknown, dated by Fulcanelli not before the late 17th or early 18th century. He calls it the most singular monument of primitive millenarianism; its rough reliefs show deep science. On the Greek cross: OCRUXAVES / PESUNICA, read as a deliberate sign; on the front INRI. The pedestal bears the sun, the moon, a large star and a circle quartered by two diameters with an A in each sector, the four ages of the world.

Fulcanelli: “Whatever its age, the cross of Hendaye, by the decoration of its pedestal, is indeed the most singular monument of primitive millenarianism, the rarest symbolic rendering of chiliasm, that we have ever met.”

104.content:
[Term: Crucible]
The cross is its hieroglyph; low-Latin crucibulum has the root crux, cross. In it the first matter suffers the Passion, dies and rises purified. The dry way cooks the Celestial Salt with a metallic body in a crucible on a naked fire; the Regime of Saturn needs only a crucible instead of glass; Elias showed the stone stuck to crucible shards. A relief shows a child falling from a crucible held by an archangel, the Massacre of the Innocents.

Fulcanelli: “It is indeed in the crucible that the first matter, like Christ himself, suffers the Passion; it is in the crucible that it dies, to rise again afterwards, purified, spiritualized, already transformed.” / “The cooking of the Work, instead of requiring a glass vessel, calls only for a simple crucible.”

105.content:
[Term: Crypt]
The set of hidden passages beneath the church floor, named from the Greek for 'hidden'. A low, damp, cold place giving the sense of power joined to darkness, the dwelling of the dead; its massive pillars express a real but occult force working in secret. Formerly the underground chambers of temples housed statues of Isis, which became the Black Virgins; since these figure the black primitive earth, the subject of the Work, it is fitting that they live in the underground places of temples. Chartres's Notre-Dame-sous-Terre sits in the crypt.

Fulcanelli: “Taken together, they extend beneath the floor of the church and make up the crypt (from the Greek kryptos, hidden).” / “A real but occult force, which works in secret, develops in the shadow, and acts unceasingly in the depth of the work's substructures.”

106.content:
[Term: Crédayougam]
In Hindu myth as given by the text, the first age, the age of innocence, answering to the Greeks' golden age: the cow of Virtue stands firmly on all four feet.

Fulcanelli: “In the first age, which answers to the golden age of the Greeks and is called Crédayougam or age of innocence, Virtue stands firm on the earth: the cow rests fully on its four feet.”

107.content:
[Work: With the light, salvation (Cum luce salutem)]
Latin legend of a painting at the Franciscan convent of Cimiez showing the two stars; Canseliet says it expresses the saving virtue of nocturnal starlight.

Canseliet, in his preface: “'Cum luce salutem; with the light, salvation.' (French gloss is the book's.)”

108.content:
[Work: Curiosities of Paris (Curiositez de Paris)]
Published in 1716 by Saugrain the elder; cited for the schools of the Angelic Doctor beside the Jacobins' church.

Fulcanelli: “The Curiosities of Paris, published in 1716 by Saugrain the elder”

109.content:
[Person: Cybele]
The epithet 'mother of the gods' applied to Isis also applied to Rhea or Cybele; Fulcanelli inclines to see them as different expressions of one principle. Charles Vincens describes a bas-relief of Cybele at Pennes inscribed Matri Deum. Cybele was worshipped at Pessinus in Phrygia as a black stone said to have fallen from the sky, which the text calls a singular hermetic analogy; Phidias showed her enthroned between two lions with a mural crown and a veil; sometimes she holds a key and seems to draw aside her veil. The sceptre with which Rhea strikes Mount Dindymus is one of several images of the hidden matter of the Philosophers.

Fulcanelli: “Cybele was worshipped at Pessinus, in Phrygia, in the form of a black stone said to have fallen from the sky.”

Identified in the text with: Isis

110.content:
[Person: Cyliani]
Author cited from the Preface of his book (Hermès dévoilé, Paris 1832): two matters of one origin, one volatile, one fixed; two ways, dry and humid; he follows the humid 'by duty', though the dry, made with a single matter, is familiar to him. He described the combat of the alchemist and the dragon. Canseliet: Cyliani opened the door of the labyrinth to him in 1915; meditating the Adepts' words on the two stars gives 'the key with which Cyliani opens the lock of the temple'.

Fulcanelli: “I follow the latter by preference, out of duty, though the former is very familiar to me: it is done with a single matter.”

111.content:
[Person: Cyprian Piccolpassi]
For making the vessel, the potter's craft is more instructive than glassmaking; among Piccolpassi's plates is a dove whose feet are tied to a stone. The footnote cites 'Claudius Popelin, Les Trois Livres de l’Art du Potier, du cavalier Cyprian Piccolpassi' (Paris, Librairie Internationale, 1861).

Fulcanelli: “look at Piccolpassi's plates; you will find one showing a dove whose feet are tied to a stone.”

112.content:
[Person: Cyrano Bergerac]
Called 'the great philosopher'; his description of the duel of the Remora and the Salamander is, for Fulcanelli, the best and most initiatic account of the violent reaction in the Conjunction. Canseliet cites him for calling the matrix language 'the instinct or voice of Nature'.

Fulcanelli: “But in our opinion the best description, — the most initiatic above all, — is the one the great philosopher de Cyrano Bergerac left us of the dreadful duel fought before his eyes by the Remora and the Salamander.”

113.content:
[Place: Dampierre-sur-Boutonne]
Site of one of two soffits with initiatic subjects comparable to the Lallemant chapel ceiling: sculpted, 16th century, with a reference to Les Demeures Philosophales.

Fulcanelli: “Two priceless soffits with initiatic subjects can be compared with it: one at Dampierre-sur-Boutonne, likewise sculpted, of the 16th century (Les Demeures Philosophales)”

114.content:
[Person: David de Planis-Campy]
Cited as saying that Jacques Cœur possessed 'the precious gift of the stone to the white'.

Fulcanelli: “David de Planis-Campy indeed cites him as possessing 'the precious gift of the stone to the white', in other words of the transmutation of base metals into silver.”

115.content:
[Work: On German Sayings (De dictis Germanicis)]
Book of Elias Schadius, in which he reported an inscription to Isis analogous to Virgini parituræ; the book's French gloss of the inscription stands in a footnote.

Fulcanelli: “To Isis, or to the Virgin from whom the Son will be born.”

116.content:
[Person: de Laborde]
Called 'the sagacious de Laborde', whose attention the hermetic emblem of the Saint Anne porch had already drawn in the seventeenth century. His work is Explications de l'Enigme trouvée à un pilier de l'Eglise Notre-Dame de Paris, Paris, 1636.

Fulcanelli: “The hermetic emblem of Notre-Dame, which had already, in the seventeenth century, held the attention of the sagacious de Laborde”

117.content:
[Work: On the Philosophical Stone (De Lapide Philosophico)]
Work of Pontanus, Frankfurt ('Francofurti'), 1614, given as the reference for Pontanus on the secret fire.

Fulcanelli: “Pontanus, On the Philosophical Stone. Frankfurt, 1614.”

118.content:
[Person: De Nuysement]
Author of the Poème philosophic de la Vérité de la Phisique Minéralle, in the Traitez de l’Harmonie et Constitution generalle du Vray Sel (Paris, 1620 and 1621, p. 254). The verses on the wheel and the even heat that the artist must keep, neither too high nor too low, are cited from him.

Fulcanelli: “Only mark the tracks of my wheel.”

119.content:
[Person: Denys Zachaire]
He tells that the alchemists' weekly meetings at Notre-Dame de Paris still went on in 1539, on Sundays and feast days. Named with 'messire Bernard, comte de Trévise' and Flamel as of a time now past.

Fulcanelli: “Denys Zachaire tells us that the custom still held there in the year 1539, 'on Sundays and feast days'”

key: Des choses qui arrivèrent en Perse
Des choses qui arriverent en Perse
120.comment: Of the Things that Happened in Persia at the Birth of Christ (work; e202)
120.content:
[Work: Of the Things that Happened in Persia at the Birth of Christ (Des choses qui arrivèrent en Perse)]
Legend attributed to Julius Africanus, of uncertain date. In a temple of Juno built by Cyrus, a priest announces that Juno has conceived; the statues dance; a star descends and announces the birth of a Child Principle and End; the statues fall face down; the Magi announce the Child born at Bethlehem; Bacchus foretells that the Child will drive out the false gods; the Magi, guided by the star, salute Mary, have her portrait with the Child painted and dedicate it 'to Jupiter Mithra' (glossed 'to the sun god') and to King Jesus.

Fulcanelli: “A star descends and announces the birth of a Child who is Beginning and End.”

121.content:
[Work: On Symbolic Colours (Des Couleurs Symboliques)]
Book by Frédéric Portal, Paris, Treuttel et Würtz, 1857, p. 2, the reference for the language of colours.

Fulcanelli: “Frédéric Portal, On Symbolic Colours. Paris, Treuttel et Würtz, 1857, p. 2.”

122.content:
[Work: Two Alchemical Dwellings (Deux Logis alchimiques)]
Work in which Canseliet ('we') wrote on the centaur, the man-horse of Plessis-Bourré; a note cites it for the painted soffit of Plessis-Bourré.

Fulcanelli: “the other, at Plessis-Bourré, made of paintings, of the 15th century (Two Alchemical Dwellings).”

Canseliet, in his preface: “after the brief remarks we offered on the centaur, the man-horse of Plessis-Bourré, in Two Alchemical Dwellings”

123.content:
[Work: Dialogue of Nature (Dialogue de la Nature)]
Work of Ægidius de Vadis, cited (through the commentator of La Lumière sortant des Ténèbres) for the statement that a despised, publicly sold portion of the first Chaos remains in the world.

Fulcanelli: “Aegidius de Vadis, in his Dialogue of Nature, shows clearly and as in letters of gold that there has remained, in this world, a portion of that first Chaos”

124.content:
[Work: Dictionary of Fable (Dictionnaire de la Fable)]
Noel's dictionary (Paris, Le Normant, 1801), cited for the fountain Libéthra and for the Cista.

Fulcanelli: “Fr. Noel, Dictionary of Fable. Paris, Le Normant, 1801.”

125.content:
[Work: Dictionary of Christian Antiquities (Dictionnaire des Antiquités chrétiennes)]
Martigny's dictionary, article Eucharistie, 2nd ed., p. 291, source of the Catacomb fish-and-basket image.

Fulcanelli: “Martigny, Dictionary of Christian Antiquities, art. Eucharist, 2nd ed., p. 291.”

key: Dictionnaire des Arts et des Sciences
126.comment: Dictionary of Arts and Sciences (work; e404)
126.content:
[Work: Dictionary of Arts and Sciences (Dictionnaire des Arts et des Sciences)]
Work cited for its article Rose-Croix, Paris, Coignart, 1731, as the source of Thomas Corneille's statement on the Brothers of the Cooked Dew.

Fulcanelli: “Dictionary of Arts and Sciences, article Rose-Croix. Paris, Coignart, 1731.”

127.content:
[Work: Mytho-Hermetic Dictionary (Dictionnaire Mytho-Hermétique)]
Pernety's dictionary, noted for not citing the term 'Miroir de l'Art'.

Fulcanelli: “Pernety, in his Mytho-Hermetic Dictionary, did not cite this term, either because he did not know it or because he left it out on purpose.”

128.content:
[Term: Dijon Infantry]
Processions and banquets called the last echo of the Feast of Fools, with their Mère Folle (Mother Fool), Rabelaisian diplomas and a banner with two brothers head to tail showing their buttocks.

Fulcanelli: “the processions and banquets of the Dijon Infantry, last echo of the Feast of Fools, with its Mother Fool, its Rabelaisian diplomas, its banner on which two brothers, head to tail, delight in baring their buttocks”

129.content:
[Person: Diodorus of Tarsus]
Quoted as more positive still than Chalcidius: the star of the Nativity was not one of the stars of the sky but a certain virtue or force that took the form of a star to announce the birth of the Lord of all. Source: Du Destin, in Photius, cod. 233.

Fulcanelli: “this star was not one of those that people the sky, but a certain virtue or force (dynamis), urano-diurnal (theioteran), which had taken the form of a star to announce the birth of the Lord of all”

130.content:
[Term: Diplomatics]
