The Language of the Birds is the language of philosophers and diplomates; the ancient Incas called it Language of the court because it gave diplomates the key to a double science, sacred and profane. At Hendaye the inscription must be read in the language of the gods or birds by the rules of the Diplomatique: read the Latin as written in French, 'langue des diplomates', permuting vowels.

Fulcanelli: “The ancient Incas called it the Language of the court, because it was familiar to the diplomats, to whom it gave the key to a double science: sacred science and profane science.” / “and that its meaning must be discovered with the help of the rules of Diplomatics.”

key: Discours philosophique sur les Trois Principes
Philosophical Discourse on the Three Principles
131.comment: Philosophical Discourse on the Three Principles (work; e383)
131.content:
[Work: Philosophical Discourse on the Three Principles (Discours philosophique sur les Trois Principes)]
Work of Sabine Stuart de Chevalier, also titled Clef du Sanctuaire philosophique, Paris, Quillau, 1781; the source of the passage on dissolving common mercury that Fulcanelli rejects.

Fulcanelli: “Sabine Stuart de Chevalier, Philosophical Discourse on the Three Principles, or the Key of the Philosophical Sanctuary. Paris, Quillau, 1781.”

132.content:
[Work: Dialogue with Trypho (Dispute avec Tryphon)]
Work the text attributes to Saint Augustine (ch. 40), quoted on the lamb, its roasting in the form of a cross, and the believers who dye their dwellings, that is themselves, by faith.

Fulcanelli: “in his Dispute with Trypho (Dialogus cum Tryphone, 40)”

133.content:
[Term: Dissolution]
In the philosophical Dissolution the volatile parts extract the fixed, central and pure parts; the horseman thrown by his horse on the first lower medallion of Paris stands for it. The lower medallions as a group show the points that vary in the practice of the Solution, which alone identifies the path followed: dissolving alchemical gold with the Alkahest marks the first path, dissolving common gold with 'our mercury' the second. A second solution, that of the red or white Sulphur by the philosophical water, is the subject of the twelfth medallion. The reign of Saturn is the emblem of radical dissolution, decomposition and the black colour. In the Conjunction, the dissolution of the gold is gentle in one path and violent, like an effervescence, in the other. A footnote gives the name Key to any radical alchemical dissolution.

Fulcanelli: “The dissolution of alchemical gold by the Alkahest Solvent characterises the first path; that of common gold by our mercury indicates the second.”

134.content:
[Term: Dog of Corascene]
The dog carved on the base of the Portal of the Virgin belongs to the animation of the exalted mercury; it is the dog of Corascene spoken of by Arthépius and Philalethes, which must be separated from the compost in the state of black powder.

Fulcanelli: “this dog of Corascene, of which Arthepius and Philalethes speak, which one must know how to separate from the compost in the state of black powder”

135.content:
[Term: Dolphin (Dauphin)]
The dolphin was a 'royal fish'; the name was symbolic, since the kings' eldest son bore the title Dauphin. The fishermen of the Mutus Liber try to net a dolphin; dolphins appear on the Hôtel Lallemant (corner turret window, a pillar capital, the credence). On the chapel capital a vase flanked by two dolphins stands for the dissolvent or common mercury of the Philosophers; two symmetrical dolphins, tied at their ends along the axis, crown the credence.

Fulcanelli: “since the kings' eldest son, the one who was to wear the crown, always bore the title of Dauphin, the name of a fish and, better still, of a royal fish.” / “It is, moreover, a dolphin that the fishermen in a boat in the Mutus Liber try to catch with net and hook.”

136.comment: The Twelve Keys of Philosophy (work; e016)
136.content:
[Work: The Twelve Keys of Philosophy (Douze Clefs de la Philosophie)]
Work of Brother Basile Valentin (Paris, Moët, 1659; reissued 1956). Its third key uses the cock-and-fox figure for the extraction of the red sulphur; one figure of the 'Livre des Douze Clefs' shows the vessel with smoke rising to a window showing sun and moon, the origin of the mercurial water. Fulcanelli warns against taking literally its saying that whoever has the matter will find a pot to cook it. Canseliet wrote an Introduction to it and quotes its two stars given to man by the Gods.

Fulcanelli: “Do not trust what Basil Valentine says in his Twelve Keys, and beware of taking his words literally when he claims that 'whoever has the matter will surely find a pot to cook it in'.”

137.content:
[Work: Twelve Gates (Douze Portes)]
Work of 'Ripleus Anglois', cited inside a quotation from the commentary on La Lumière sortant des Ténèbres: at its beginning Ripley says the same as that author about the essence in which the sought spirit lives. The 'first gate of Ripley' is named as the first step of practice.

Fulcanelli: “the same thing is said by Ripley the Englishman at the beginning of his Twelve Gates”

138.content:
[Term: Doves of Diana]
The two doves on the base of the Portal of the Virgin, described in the animation of the exalted mercury, are the Doves of Diana, a 'despairing enigma' under which the spiritualisation and sublimation of the philosophical mercury are hidden.

Fulcanelli: “these Doves of Diana, another despairing enigma, under which the spiritualisation and sublimation of the philosophical mercury are hidden.”

139.content:
[Person: Dr Evans]
Of Oxford; discovered in 1902 the labyrinth of Cnossos in Crete, which was called Absolum.

Fulcanelli: “that of Cnossos in Crete, which was discovered in 1902 by Dr Evans of Oxford, was called Absolum.”

140.content:
[Term: Dragon]
In the motif of the Saint-Anne porch, after the pure principles rise, the residue yields the volatile, fusible mercurial salt that old authors call the 'Dragon babylonien'; the sculpted dragon emerges from the flames and clasps the athanor. The dragon is the image of mercury, on which the nourishing of the Sulphur or Elixir should be sought; covered with solar circles, it can transmute in quantity, but only after further cookings with the Sulphur, the multiplications. Basil Valentine teaches the making of the Green Lion under the fight of eagle and dragon; this combat of chemical bodies yields the secret dissolvent and recurs in Cadmos, Jason, Saint Michael, Saint George, Saint Marcel. Whoever knows the dragon knows how to defeat it. In the third preface Canseliet sees in Saint Marcel's dragon legend the two ways, dry and wet.

Fulcanelli: “It is therefore on the dragon, image of mercury, that we should look for the symbol representing the nourishment and progression of the Sulphur or Elixir.” / “the residue is then ready to yield the mercurial salt, volatile and fusible, to which the old authors often gave the epithet Babylonian Dragon.”

key: water that does not wet the hands
141.content:
[Term: Dry water]
From the combination of the primitive water from the Chaos of the Sages with a second water comes a third water 'that does not wet the hands', called Mercury or Sulphur according to its quality or aspect. Limojon de Saint-Didier, citing the Cosmopolite, says the secret fire resolves the stone into dry water. The servus fugitivus needed is a solid, brittle, stone-like mineral water, easily melted; this coagulated water is the Alkaest and Universal Dissolvent. The water needed is dry, does not wet the hands and gushes under Aaron's rod; though wholly volatile, it can be made fixed, the water becoming earth and the mercury sulphur.

Fulcanelli: “For the water we need is dry, does not wet the hands, and gushes forth under the stroke of Aaron's rod.” / “It is this water, coagulated in the form of a stony mass, that is the Alkahest and the Universal Dissolvent.”

142.content:
[Term: Dry way]
Of the two ways of the Work, the short and easy one; few alchemists admit there are two. The south (Saint-Anne) porch of Notre-Dame describes the shortest practice. Per the 18th-century Encyclopedia (QUOTED), it is less esteemed and consists in cooking the Celestial Salt, mercury of the Philosophers, with an earthly metallic body in a crucible on a naked fire for four days; other authors give eight days or a week. The Sages named it the Regime of Saturn; it needs only a crucible instead of a glass vessel. Cyliani (QUOTED): it is done with a single matter; Henckel imagines keeping the matters long in strongest fluidity by violent fire. At the fourth degree of fire in the dry way about 1200° is required. Canseliet finds both ways in the Saint Marcel legend.

Fulcanelli: “Few alchemists consent to admit the possibility of two ways, one short and easy, called the dry way, the other longer and more thankless, called the wet way.” / “This shortened way, but covered with a thick veil, was named by the Sages the Regime of Saturn.”

143.content:
[Person: Du Cange]
Cited for the etymology that low-Latin crucibulum, crucible, has as root crux, crucis, cross. His glossary gives orarium as the stole.

Fulcanelli: “in low Latin, crucibulum, crucible, has as its root crux, crucis, cross, according to Ducange”

144.content:
[Term: Durandal]
At Rocamadour, beside a giant Saint Christopher and an old iron-bound coffer, a rough sword fragment fixed in the rock by a chain is said by legend to belong to Durandal, the sword Roland broke opening the breach of Roncevaux. The sword that opens the rock, Moses's rod, Rhea's sceptre and Atalanta's javelin are one hieroglyph of the hidden matter; Saint Christopher shows its nature and the iron-bound coffer its result.

Fulcanelli: “are one and the same hieroglyph of that hidden matter of the Philosophers, whose nature Saint Christopher indicates and whose result the iron-bound coffer shows.”

145.content:
[Term: Eagle]
The Sages figured the two natures by the Eagle and the Lion, equal in power but opposite in complexion: the eagle is the aerial, volatile force, the lion the earthly, fixed force. They fight until the eagle loses its wings and the lion its head, making one body, the Animated Mercury. The griffin has the head and breast of the eagle. Eagle and lion are Nicolas Flamel's figure for the combat of the conjunction. Basile Valentin teaches the making of the Green Lion under the fight of the eagle and the dragon. In one legend the star of the Magi had the form of an eagle.

Fulcanelli: “The lion expresses the earthly and fixed force, while the eagle expresses the aerial and volatile force.”

[Term: Eagles]
Stated: the philosophers' name for the painful, tedious labour by which the first conjunction is achieved little by little; the reiteration of the Eagles is philosophical Sublimation. To 'make the eagle fly' is to bring the light out of the tomb to the surface, the mark of every true sublimation. Philalèthe (quoted): the exact preparation of the flying Eagles is the first degree of perfection; the Sages lead their eagles to devour the lion; at least seven eagles, even nine, are needed. The seven circuits of Callimachus's swans round Delos and Joshua's seven rounds of Jericho are variants. Identified with Sublimation (e345).

Fulcanelli: “To make the eagle fly, in the hermetic expression, is to bring the light out of the tomb and carry it to the surface, which is the mark of every true sublimation.” / “But to perfect our work, no fewer than seven eagles are needed, and one should even use as many as nine.”

Identified in the text with: Sublimation

146.content:
[Term: Echinéis]
Stated: the Cosmopolite's famous fish, Echinéis, is the sea urchin (echinus), the bear cub, the Little Bear, the constellation of the pole star; hence Limojon de Saint-Didier tells seekers to steer 'by the sight of the north star'. The pole star is among the names of the Sign on the prepared mercury.

Fulcanelli: “Let us add that the Cosmopolite's famous fish, which he calls Echinéis, is the sea urchin (echinus), the bear cub, the Little Bear, the constellation in which the pole star lies.”

147.content:
[Person: Elias Schadius]
Called 'the learned'; in his book De dictis Germanicis he reported an inscription to Isis similar to Virgini parituræ, as cited by Pierre Dujols. The footnote gives its French rendering.

Fulcanelli: “To Isis, or to the Virgin from whom the Son will be born (following the book's French gloss)”

148.content:
[Person: Elias the artist]
Named in Henckel's passage: the artist Elias, cited by Helvétius, claims the preparation of the stone begins and ends in four days and showed the stone still stuck to the crucible shards.

Fulcanelli: “the artist Elias, cited by Helvetius, claims that the preparation of the philosophers' stone is begun and finished in four days' time”

149.content:
[Person: Elijah]
Arab authors, the text reports, teach that the waters of the fountain they call Holmat gave the prophet Elijah immortality; the text glosses his name with the Greek for sun (Ηλιος). In the reading of the Virgin as matter, the text writes 'Elie, le Soleil Dieu le Père' as the emblem of the vital spirit that animates the passive substance (Mary, the form). In the Hendaye chapter, the elect who will be saved in the cyclic catastrophe are called 'enfants d'Elie'; a list of initiatory orders includes 'Chevaliers du Cygne, institués par Elie'. The text also names 'l'artiste Elias, cité par Helvétius' (quoting Henckel), who claimed the stone is begun and finished in four days and showed it still stuck to the crucible shards; the text does not say whether this Elias is the prophet.

Fulcanelli: “they teach us, moreover, that its waters gave immortality to the prophet Elijah (Helios, sun).” / “Mary, Virgin and Mother, therefore represents the form; Elijah, the Sun, God the Father, is the emblem of the vital spirit.”

150.content:
[Term: Elixation]
The text names elixation the wet phase of the linear coction, the first turn of the wheel, in which the compound stays molten until a light skin forms and thickens. It is followed by assation.

Fulcanelli: “The first wheel corresponds to the wet phase of the operation, called elixation, in which the compound remains molten until a light film forms”

151.content:
[Term: Elixir]
The Notre-Dame base lets one follow the work of the Elixir from first calcination to final coction. The philosophic Mercury needs only graduated cooking to become red sulphur, then Elixir, then Universal Medicine. Mercury carries nascent gold to the power of the Elixir. The green lion is 'the stone of our Elixir'; the despised subject becomes the Tree of Life, Elixir or Philosophers' Stone. The second of three identical operations gives the Elixir, medicine of the second order, differing from Sulphur in quality, not nature. Its multiplication needs the mercury. The text thus uses Elixir both as a stage and, loosely, as a name of the finished stone.

Fulcanelli: “the second operation, exactly like the first, yields the Elixir, or medicine of the second order, which differs from the Sulphur only in quality and not in nature” / “the vitriolated egg, which needs only a graduated cooking to be turned first into red sulphur, then into Elixir, then, in the third period, into Universal Medicine.”

Identified in the text with: Philosophers' stone, Tree of Life

152.content:
[Term: Emerald of the Philosophers]
One of the names some Adepts gave to the Green Lion, with May Dew, Saturnian Herb and Vegetable Stone. Arnold of Villanova (quoted) explains such green names: 'our water' takes the names of leaves, trees and all green things to deceive the foolish.

Fulcanelli: “others, Emerald of the Philosophers, May Dew, Saturnian Herb, Vegetable Stone, etc.”

153.content:
[Work: The Encyclopedia (Encyclopédie)]
The eighteenth-century Encyclopédie is cited as a second proof that the Great Work can be done by two paths, the wet path, longer but more esteemed, and the dry path, less valued, in which the Celestial Salt, the Philosophers' mercury, is cooked with an earthly metallic body in a crucible on a bare fire for four days.

Fulcanelli: “to cook the Celestial Salt, which is the mercury of the Philosophers, with an earthly metallic body, in a crucible and on a bare fire, for four days”

key: Entrée au Palais fermé du Roy
Entree au Palais ferme du Roy
Entrée au Palais Fermé de Roy
Entree au Palais Ferme de Roy
154.comment: Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King (work; e041)
154.content:
[Work: Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King (Entrée ouverte au Palais fermé du Roi)]
Work of Philalèthe. The seventh Notre-Dame medallion (an old man entering the mysterious Palace) is 'the Entrée au Palais fermé du Roy of Philalèthe': the first step of practice, discovering the agent that reincrudates the fixed body. Cited in Lenglet-Dufresnoy's Histoire de la Philosophie Hermétique. Canseliet: the book where he dwelt most on practice.

Fulcanelli: “It is the Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King, of Philalethes, the first gate of Ripley and of Basil Valentine, which one must know how to open.”

155.comment: Letter on the Fire of the Philosophers (work; e319)
155.content:
[Work: Letter on the Fire of the Philosophers (Epistola de Igne Philosophorum)]
A 'petit ouvrage' recommended, with Artephius and Pontanus, for precious indications on the nature of the secret fire; a manuscript of the Bibliothèque nationale, no. 19969.

Fulcanelli: “and of the little work entitled: Letter on the Fire of the Philosophers.”

156.comment: Letter on the Philosophical Stones (work; e463)
156.content:
[Work: Letter on the Philosophical Stones (Epistola de Lapidibus Philosophicis)]
Haymon's treatise, no. 192 in vol. VI of the Theatrum Chemicum (Argentorati, 1613); the source of the quoted passage on where to find the first agent.

Fulcanelli: “Haymon, Epistola de Lapidibus Philosophicis. Treatise 192, vol. VI of the Theatrum Chemicum. Argentorati, 1613.”

157.comment: Escutcheon of Saint Thomas Aquinas (place; e433)
157.content:
[Place: Escutcheon of Saint Thomas Aquinas]
Hermetic coat of arms on a window of the chapel of Saint-Thomas-d'Aquin at the Jacobins' convent, existing until the Revolution and drawn in 1787 by Chaudet. Flamel's version at the Innocents and Lagneau's engraving derive from it. Its blazon: an inverted gold matrass in a crown of thorns above; a gold cross with three blue globes and a red heart with a green branch, on which silver tears from the matrass gather and fix; a field of stars and rays, an earth with ears of corn, a violet cloud with three arrows, three silver serpents. Fulcanelli says it reveals the secrets of extracting mercury and joining it with sulphur.

Fulcanelli: “This fine emblem is all the more important to us because it unveils the secrets relating to the extraction of mercury and its conjunction with sulphur”

158.content:
[Term: Esotericism]
The hidden meaning of an image, opposed to its exoteric, public sense. Alchemy on Notre-Dame holds a closed book (esotericism) and an open one (exotericism); the cathedral's teaching is outwardly lay and exoteric. A careless restoration leaves 'l’ésotérisme éteint'; the rose window's glass lets 'l’ésotérisme' regain its purity. Canseliet says Champagne's plates wrap the book's austere esotericism.

Fulcanelli: “while the right hand holds two books, one closed (esotericism), the other open (exotericism).” / “but its symbol is truncated, the science mutilated, the key lost, the esotericism extinguished.”

159.content:
[Person: Esprit Gobineau de Montluisant]
A predecessor in interpreting Notre-Dame, named with Cambriel. His book, written on 20 May 1640, states that the king on the Saint-Anne pillar wears a triple crown. Canseliet calls him a gentleman of Chartres and an eyewitness whose description proves the original statue stood on the middle pillar in 1640.

Fulcanelli: “But we fortunately have the text of Esprit Gobineau de Montluisant, whose book was written 'on Wednesday 20 May 1640, eve of the glorious Ascension of Our Saviour Jesus Christ', and which tells us positively that the king wears a triple crown.” / “After Gobineau de Montluisant, Cambriel and tutti quanti, we shall undertake the pious pilgrimage, speak to the stones and question them.”

160.content:
[Person: Etteilla]
Quoted on the Magi's table: a book of gold leaves (the book of Thoth) and a vase full of celestial-astral liquor, where the secret lay. He preserved the legends of a hermetic painting he is said to have owned (said to date from the mid-17th century), among them the advice not to rely too much on colour, which Fulcanelli calls worth following.

Fulcanelli: “Do not rely too much on the colour.” / “The secret, the mystery, was in the vase.”

161.content:
[Person: Eugène Canseliet]
Fulcanelli's disciple and the writer of the prefaces: the first is signed 'E. CANSELIET, F. C. H.', October 1925; the third 'Savignies, juillet 1964. Eugène CANSELIET'; the second is dated Savignies, August 1957. He received initiation orally from Fulcanelli, after Cyliani had 'opened the door of the labyrinth' to him in 1915; he wrote an Introduction to the Douze Clefs and a Preface to the Demeures philosophales, and a study on the Golden Fleece in Alchimie. He met Fulcanelli ten years after Champagne did, i.e. 1915.

Canseliet, in his preface: “For the disciple it is a thankless and awkward task to present a work written by his own Master.”

162.comment: Gospel according to Saint Luke (work; e209)
162.content:
[Work: Gospel according to Saint Luke (Evangile selon saint Luc)]
Cited (II, 1–7 as given) among the texts on the sign of the Nativity: shepherds in the fields at night, an angel, a divine light around them, the Good News, and the sign of a Child wrapped in swaddling clothes lying in a manger.

Fulcanelli: “and this shall be the sign for you: you will find a Child wrapped in swaddling clothes and lying in a manger.”

163.comment: Gospel according to Saint Matthew (work; e210)
163.content:
[Work: Gospel according to Saint Matthew (Evangile selon saint Matthieu)]
Cited (II, 1–11) on the Magi from the East who saw the star, which went before them until it stopped above the place where the Child was; they offered gold, incense and myrrh. In the Hendaye chapter it is the Gospel of the age of iron: Matthæus is derived from the Greek for science, making it the Gospel according to Science, which teaches that, save a few elect, mankind must collectively perish; hence the angel attributed to Saint Matthew.

Fulcanelli: “and behold, the star they had seen in the East went before them, until it came and stopped above the place where the Child was.” / “It is the Gospel according to Science, the last of all, but the first for us”

164.content:
[Term: Evolution]
The fifth figure of the Paris stylobate, which shows the oriflamme with three pennants, the threefold Colours of the Work. The colours go from black to red through white. The Green Lion is metallic youth 'sur laquelle l'Evolution n'a pas ouvré' but containing a latent germ. Interpreted: Evolution names the progressive maturing of the matter, marked by the colours.

Fulcanelli: “Evolution follows and shows the oriflamme with three pennants, the threefold Colours of the Work, which are described in all the classic works”

165.comment: Very Curious Explanation of the Enigmas and Hieroglyphic Figures (of the great portal of Notre-Dame de Paris) (work; e105)
165.content:
[Work: Very Curious Explanation of the Enigmas and Hieroglyphic Figures (of the great portal of Notre-Dame de Paris) (Explication très curieuse des Enigmes et Figures hiéroglyphiques)]
Work by Esprit Gobineau de Montluisant on the figures of the great portal of Notre-Dame de Paris, written 20 May 1640. Canseliet cites its description of the bishop putting his crosier in the dragon's mouth, with a triple-crowned king in the waves, as proof against Grillot de Givry.

Fulcanelli: “Very curious Explanation of the Enigmas and Hieroglyphic, Physical Figures which are on the great portal of the Cathedral and Metropolitan Church of Notre-Dame de Paris.”

Canseliet, in his preface: “On the pillar which is in the middle and separates the two doors of this Portal is also the figure of a Bishop, who puts his Crosier into the mouth of a dragon”

166.comment: Explanations of the Enigma Found on a Pillar of Notre-Dame de Paris (work; e419)
166.content:
[Work: Explanations of the Enigma Found on a Pillar of Notre-Dame de Paris (Explications de l'Enigme trouvée à un pilier de l'Eglise Notre-Dame de Paris)]
Work of De Laborde, Paris, 1636, on the emblem of the Saint Anne pillar.

Fulcanelli: “De Laborde, Explanations of the Enigma Found on a Pillar of the Church of Notre-Dame de Paris. Paris, 1636.”

167.content:
[Person: Ezekiel]
Several authors read the Amiens wheel-fire as Ezekiel's prophecy: he saw four winged creatures and wheels within each other; Fulcanelli rejects this, since the figure has open eyes, no cloud border, and does not face the phenomenon. In the Hendaye chapter Ezekiel's vision of the four creatures with faces of man, lion, ox and eagle is quoted as agreeing with saint John's.

Fulcanelli: “found its meaning in the prophecy of Ezekiel, who, says G. Durand, 'saw four winged creatures, as saint John later did, then wheels one within the other.”

168.content:
[Term: Feast of Fools]
A medieval ceremony held in the cathedral, called also Feast of the Wise; Fulcanelli calls it a hermetic processional fair and a satire of an ignorant clergy subject to 'disguised Science'. It had a chariot of the Triumph of Bacchus drawn by a centaur and centauress, Olympian deities at mass, and a mass composed by the initiate Pierre de Corbeil according to pagan ritual, with the bacchanal cry Evohé. The Dijon Infantry was its last echo.

Fulcanelli: “There was the Feast of Fools — or of the Wise — a hermetic processional fair, which set out from the church with its pope, its dignitaries, its devotees, its people” / “Hilarious satire of an ignorant clergy, subject to the authority of disguised Science, crushed under the weight of an indisputable superiority.”

169.content:
[Term: Feast of the Ass]
A ceremony almost as lavish as the Feast of Fools, with the triumphal entry of 'master Aliboron' into the church and an office exalting the asinine power that brought the Church the gold of Arabia and the incense and myrrh of Saba. Fulcanelli reads it as a parody by the 'mystifiers of the land of Saba, or Caba', the cabalists, which the priest accepted without understanding. Per Witkowski (QUOTED), a capital in the nave of Notre-Dame de Strasbourg shows it as the Procession of the Fox; an identical illuminated scene is in manuscript 5055 of the Bibliothèque nationale.

Fulcanelli: “A grotesque parody that the priest, unable to understand, accepted in silence, head bowed under the ridicule poured out to the brim by these mystifiers of the land of Saba, or Caba, the cabalists in person!” / “It is the Procession of the Fox, or of the Feast of the Ass”

key: Symbolic Figures of Abraham the Jew
170.comment: Symbolic Figures of Abraham the Jew (work; e277)
170.content:
[Work: Symbolic Figures of Abraham the Jew (Figures symboliques d'Abraham le Juif)]
Figures whose book, it is said, belonged to Nicolas Flamel, who kept them displayed in his scrivener's shop. The note cites a 'Recueil de Sept Figures peintes', Bibliothèque de l'Arsenal no. 3047. Fulcanelli quotes the descriptions of the third figure (a walled garden, an old hollow oak with a rose-bush of golden leaves and white and red roses, at whose foot a fountain bubbles which blind seekers cannot find, except one who weighs it in his hand) and the fourth (a red-clad king, soldiers killing children, a vat of blood in which sun and moon bathe). The man weighing the fountain is the subject of the Notre-Dame relief. A figure of Trismosin closely resembles the third. The anonymous Clef du Cabinet hermétique says Flamel paints in these figures the hollow oak with its fountain, the oak signifying the oak barrel in which the water must be corrupted. Abraham used the serpent on the golden rod 'dans le livre qui échut à Flamel'.

Fulcanelli: “Among the descriptions accompanying the Symbolic Figures of Abraham the Jew, whose book, it is said, belonged to Nicolas Flamel” / “And at the foot of the said hollow oak bubbles a fountain clear as silver, which goes losing itself in the earth”

171.content:
[Term: First matter]
The substance with which the Work begins. In the crucible it suffers the Passion like Christ, dies and rises again purified; the cruciform church plan reveals its qualities and preparation. The devil figure Maistre Pierre du Coignet represents the 'matière initiale' as Lucifer. The Black Virgins figure it as the primitive earth the artist must choose, the first matter as ore, a black, heavy, brittle substance. The Sages' Chaos is their first matter, an elemental confusion. Called Mirror of Art; this despised subject later becomes the Tree of Life, Elixir or Philosophers' Stone. It is the 'sujet' that contains the indispensable agent; the dead trees of an Amiens quatrefoil refer to the 'matières premières', metallic planets killed by fire and made inert by fusion, like trees in winter. Expressed by a book, open or closed, and by the globe held by God, Jesus and monarchs. The text links it with the subject (sujet), Chaos and Mirror of Art.

Fulcanelli: “It is the first matter in the state of ore, as it comes out of the metal-bearing deposits, deeply buried under the rock mass.” / “All the descriptions the Philosophers have left us of their subject, or first matter which contains the indispensable agent, are very confused and most mysterious.”

Identified in the text with: Mirror of the Art, Chaos

172.content:
[Term: First stone]
By the sign of the Cross the plan of the church reveals the qualities and preparation of the first matter, which leads to the 'First stone', cornerstone of the Great Work; on this stone Jesus built his Church, and the medieval freemasons followed the example; before being cut, the rough stone was often given the image of the devil. At Notre-Dame this was the devil figure called Maistre Pierre du Coignet, symbol of 'our cornerstone'. In the practice, after the second coagulation of the cock-fox operation 'the first stone' is born, neither wholly fixed nor wholly volatile, to be perfected by a third reiteration. Canseliet: all truth, philosophy and religion rest on this 'unique and sacred stone'.

Fulcanelli: “which leads, for the alchemists, to obtaining the First stone, cornerstone of the philosophical Great Work.” / “Thus will be born the first stone, neither absolutely fixed nor absolutely volatile, yet fairly permanent in the fire, very penetrating and very fusible”

173.content:
[Term: Fish]
Stated: the fish is the hieroglyph of the Philosophers' stone in its first state, because the stone, like the fish, is born and lives in water; it is the fish 'that swims in our philosophic sea' of the Cosmopolite, to be caught with a net, image of the crossed lines on the galette. The Cosmopolite's fish Echinéis leads to the pole star. A porcelain sole once replaced the baigneur in a cake: 'sole' from Latin Sol, the sun. The fish found in the cake is the 'royal fish'; the dolphin, royal fish, gave the heir's title Dauphin; the Greek Ichtus has the same origin.

Fulcanelli: “The fish is the hieroglyph of the Philosophers' stone in its first state, because the stone, like the fish, is born in water and lives in water.” / “In place of the bather a porcelain fish had been put, and this fish was a sole (Lat. Sol, solis, the sun).”

174.content:
[Term: Fish eyes]
Stated (in the Clef du Cabinet hermétique, quoting Philalèthe): one sign of the first putrefaction is that the matter looks like fish eyes, that is, small bubbles on its surface, as if it were foaming, a mark that it ferments and boils; this fermentation is long and done by the secret fire.

Fulcanelli: “Philalethes says it must look like fish eyes, that is, little bubbles on the surface, and that it should seem to foam”

175.content:
[Term: Flamboyant Gothic]
Name given to the style of the 14th and 15th centuries; the text explains it by the predominance of the fiery symbol in the last period of medieval art, following its reading of rose windows as images of fire and of matter moved by fire.

Fulcanelli: “In the architecture of the 14th and 15th centuries, the predominance of the fiery symbol, which clearly marks the last period of medieval art, caused the style of that time to be called Flamboyant Gothic.”

176.content:
[Term: Flogging of the Alleluia]
A yearly custom in Langres cathedral, among those in which 'a hermetic sense, often very pure' shows through: the choirboys drove their humming tops out of the nave with whips.

Fulcanelli: “such as the Flogging of the Alleluia, in which the choirboys drove their humming tops with great lashes of the whip out of the naves of Langres cathedral”

177.content:
[Term: Foliated earth]
Stated: the prepared mercury is a stony, friable, flaky mass whose crystalline plates lie like the leaves of a book; hence the names terre feuillée, terre des feuilles, livre aux feuillets. The Kings' Cake's flaky dough confirms this. The Cosmopolite says the weight of the water must be plural and that of the white or red foliated earth singular.

Fulcanelli: “The crystalline plates composing its substance are indeed stacked like the leaves of a book; for this reason it received the epithet of foliated earth, earth of leaves, book of leaves, etc.” / “The weight of the water, he says, must be plural, and that of the white or red foliated earth must be singular.”

178.content:
[Term: Forest of Morois]
The setting of the Tristan and Yseult corbel. Later the text calls it the forest 'de Mort-Roi', strange because the tree behind Tristan is laden with huge fruits, and would liken it to the Garden of the Hesperides. The text gives no further comment on the spelling Mort-Roi.

Fulcanelli: “A strange forest indeed, that of Mort-Roi, and how inclined we would be to liken it to the fabulous and marvellous Garden of the Hesperides!”

179.content:
[Term: Fountain of Life]
The Brixen inscription has the blood of Christ and the Virgin's milk mingle 'et sit Fons Vitae'; the book's French gives 'la Fontaine de Vie et la Source du Bien'. The text says the esoteric tradition of the 'Fontaine de Vie ou Fontaine de Jouvence' was materialised in the sacred wells of medieval Gothic churches, whose water was held to heal. In the Bourges chapter the text states why mercury is called the Fountain of Youth: when gold is dissolved in it to bring it back to its first state, 'young' or 'child' gold, the gold is reborn in its womb. Stated: the Fontaine de Jouvence is the philosophers' mercury in which gold is rejuvenated. Interpreted: the name ties this entry to the occult fountain sculpted on the Paris portal (the dissolvent).

Fulcanelli: “That is why mercury, the loyal servant and Seal of the earth, is called the Fountain of Youth.” / “Let us say finally that the esoteric tradition of the Fountain of Life or Fountain of Youth is found materialised in the Sacred Wells”

Identified in the text with: Mercury

180.comment: Four ages of the world (term; e533)
180.content:
[Term: Four ages of the world]
On the Hendaye pedestal a circle cut by two perpendicular diameters bears an A in each sector, the four ages of the world; the four great centuries, with their rulers Alexander, Augustus, Charlemagne, Louis XIV, figure them historically. In the Middle Ages the four phases are shown by the four evangelists or four animals around Christ. Hindu myth figures them by the cow of Virtue standing on four, three, two, then one foot: Crédayougam, Trédayougam, Touvabarayougam, Calyougam; ours is the iron age.

Fulcanelli: “These bear an A that marks them as the four ages of the world, in this complete hieroglyph of the universe, formed of the conventional signs of heaven and earth”

181.content:
[Term: Fox]
Stated: the fox, 'notre renard hermétique' or goupil, is the state of provisional fixity the volatile cock (mercury) must take when held long in the fire; then the water has become earth and the mercury sulphur. This dry earth must be redissolved in its own water so the fox regains the wings and tail of the cock; repeated, the process yields the first stone, and a third reiteration is needed. On the Paris stylobate a cock-fox monster shows the extraction of the red, incombustible Sulphur; at Amiens the fox tries to reach the cock on the oak.

Fulcanelli: “It then changes its emblem, and its endurance in the fire, its heavy quality, cause the fox to be given it as the sign of its new nature.”

182.content:
[Person: Fr. Noel]
Author of the Dictionnaire de la Fable (Paris, Le Normant, 1801), cited on the Cista of Bacchus and as reference for the fountain Libéthra.

Fulcanelli: “in which, Fr. Noel tells us, was enclosed what was most mysterious”

183.content:
[Place: Franciscan convent of Cimiez]
Canseliet: one of the small alchemical paintings of this convent shows the two stars, with the Latin legend Cum luce salutem expressing the saving virtue of nocturnal starlight.

Canseliet, in his preface: “Are these not the two stars shown us by one of the small alchemical paintings of the Franciscan convent of Cimiez, with the Latin legend expressing the saving virtue inherent in the nocturnal, starry radiance:”

184.content:
[Person: François Cambriel]
Author of the Cours de Philosophie hermétique (1843). He solved the enigma of the St Marcel pillar exactly, at least in part; Fulcanelli's reading broadly agrees with his, but rejects his extending the symbolism to the statue and his claim that multiplication is not shown. His engraving is called faked: bearded bishop, short crosier, finger to lips, a gesture 'entirely from his excessive imagination'. Canseliet defends this verdict against Grillot de Givry and Jean Reyor.

Fulcanelli: “This enigma of the alchemical work, solved exactly, — at least in part, — by François Cambriel, earned him a mention by Champfleury in his Excentriques and by Tcherkapoff in his Fous littéraires.” / “As for the famous gesture of the figures of the Mutus Liber and of Harpocrates, it came entirely from Cambriel's excessive imagination.”

185.content:
[Person: François Rabelais]
Author of the Life of Gargantua and Pantagruel, an esoteric work and a 'roman d'argot'; the curé de Meudon shows himself a great initiate and a first-rank cabalist.

Fulcanelli: “The good curé of Meudon reveals himself there as a great initiate and a cabalist of the first order besides.”

186.content:
[Person: François Villon]
The poet Villon was at the head of the truands of the Cour des Miracles, who, like the medieval Frimasons, expressed themselves in argot, as all Initiates did. Canseliet's third preface opens with lines from his Testament, stanzas XXXVI and XXXVII.

Fulcanelli: “All the Initiates expressed themselves in argot, the vagabonds of the Court of Miracles, — the poet Villon at their head, — as much as the Frimasons, or freemasons of the Middle Ages”

187.content:
[Term: Freemasons]
The medieval Frimasons or freemasons, 'logeurs du bon Dieu', built the argotic masterpieces, spoke argot like all Initiates, and knew the road to the Garden of the Hesperides. They followed symbolically the divine example of building on the stone. The cathedrals were built by them to transmit hermetic symbols and doctrine. Their 'Lost Word' is the Verbum dimissum. Canseliet: Freemasonry still seeks it.

Fulcanelli: “Built by the medieval Frimasons to ensure the transmission of the hermetic symbols and doctrine, our great cathedrals exerted from their appearance a marked influence on many humbler examples of civil or religious architecture.”

188.content:
[Person: Frédéric Portal]
Author of Des Couleurs Symboliques (1857), cited for the language of colours united to religion. Within Pierre Dujols's quoted passage, Portal says the black Osiris at the beginning of the funerary Ritual represents the soul passing from night to day, death to life.

Fulcanelli: “The black Osiris, who appears at the beginning of the funerary Ritual, says Portal, represents that state of the soul passing from night to day, from death to life.”

189.content:
[Person: Fulcanelli]
The author of the book, Canseliet's Master. Canseliet: he 'is no more'; he disappeared when the Sign was accomplished; in 1922 he had not yet received the Gift of God but was close to it, and kept anonymity; the name is a pseudonym 'wanted by the Tradition'; he received initiation orally; Basile Valentin was his first initiator, an anonymous letter-writer his true one; he knew Julien Champagne in 1905. The epigraph signed FULCANELLI repeats the author's own words on dissecting words. In the main text he says the problem of the secret fire stopped him for more than twenty years.

Fulcanelli: “What wonders, what unsuspected things would we not discover if we knew how to dissect words, break their bark and free the spirit, the divine light they enclose!”

Canseliet, in his preface: “Fulcanelli is no more.”

190.content:
[Person: G. J. Witkowski]
Author of L'Art profane à l'Eglise, quoted repeatedly as a source on church imagery (QUOTED: Witkowski): the satirical procession on a capital at Strasbourg; the window of the Conception of Saint Romain at Saint-Jean, Rouen, where a star on the coverlet figured conception; Notre-Dame-du-Pilier at Chartres; a stone Isis at Saint-Etienne, Metz; the Brixen painting of Christ's blood and the Virgin's milk.

Fulcanelli: “The conception was figured by a star shining on the coverlet in contact with the woman's belly…” / “This stone figure of Isis, writes the author, measuring 0.43 m high by 0.29 m wide, came from the old cloister.”

191.content:
[Person: Gabritius]
Named with Beya as the brother and sister whose union produces the compost or philosophical rebis, paralleled with Apollo and Diana.

Fulcanelli: “made by the union of the brother and the sister, of Gabritius and Beya, of Apollo and Diana.”

192.content:
[Term: Gall (oak-gall)]
The oak bears galls (noix de galle, Latin galla). The text sets galla, Gallia, gallus side by side — gall, Gaul, cock — the cock being emblem of Gaul and attribute of Mercury. Stated: the gall gives the name of the raw mercurial matter, while the kermès names the prepared substance. The Golden Fleece hangs on the oak like gall and kermes. Greek gala means milk, and mercury is called Lait de Vierge.

Fulcanelli: “Now, if we bring together three words of the same Latin family, galla, Gallia, gallus, we obtain gall, Gaul, cock.” / “However, while the gall gives the name of the raw mercurial matter, the kermes (Arabic girmiz, which dyes scarlet) characterizes the prepared substance.”

193.content:
[Term: Garden of the Hesperides]
The medieval builder 'nautes' knew its road. Pegasus carried Perseus to the Hesperides. The last Notre-Dame medallion shows the tree with the precious fruits of the Garden beside Jason and the ram. Fulcanelli would liken the fruit-laden forest of Mort-Roi in the Tristan group to it.

Fulcanelli: “They themselves, these builder-sailors, knew the road to the Garden of the Hesperides…” / “A strange forest indeed, that of Mort-Roi, and how inclined we would be to liken it to the fabulous and wondrous Garden of the Hesperides!”

194.content:
[Person: Gaston de Claves]
Named only as the author to whom 'others' attribute the classic work (Le Filet d'Ariadne) of which Batsdorff is the presumed author.

Fulcanelli: “Batsdorff, presumed author of a classic work which others attribute to Gaston de Claves”

195.content:
[Person: Geber]
Huginus à Barma says the old masters, Geber, Lully and Paracelsus, each had his own process. Geber is quoted praising the Most High for creating this Mercury, without which the alchemists' work would be useless. The threefold calcination of the Sulphur yields the three philosophical works 'according to the doctrine of Geber'. He is called Magister magistrorum, with whom Jean Lallemant deserves to commune.

Fulcanelli: “Blessed be the Most High, cries Geber, who created this Mercury and gave it a nature that nothing resists!”

196.content:
[Work: Genesis (Genèse)]
Hermetic philosophy, the text says, often invokes Genesis as an analogy for the first work of the Work. As day succeeds night in Genesis, light succeeds darkness, and its signature is the white colour. Interpreted: the same analogy is drawn without naming the book where the Spirit moving on the waters and the six days of God's 'Grand Œuvre' are recalled, and where many authors liken the forming of the philosophical compound to the genesis of the world.

Fulcanelli: “Hermetic Philosophy frequently invokes the testimony of Genesis to serve as an analogy for the first labour of the Work”

197.content:
[Person: Georges Aurach]
Georges Aurach of Strasbourg wrote and painted by his own hand, in 1415, the manuscript Le Très précieux Don de Dieu. It shows a glass matras half full of a green liquor and says its name shows its colour, in the discussion of the vessel called Lion vert; the third figure of the Toison d'Or is almost identical.

Fulcanelli: “G. Aurach's manuscript shows a glass matras half filled with a green liquor, and adds that its very name indicates its colour.”

198.content:
[Person: Georges Durand]
Author of the Monographie de l'Eglise Cathédrale d'Amiens. With others he reads the Amiens wheel-fire quatrefoil as Ezekiel's vision of the wheels; Fulcanelli finds two errors in this. He calls another relief a replica of Paris's seventh medallion and prefers for it the name Apostasy proposed by the abbé Roze. On the cock and fox he notes the dogs of the fable are missing.

Fulcanelli: “Naively taking the text literally, the artist has reduced the vision to its simplest expression.”

199.content:
[Term: Gift of God]
The final grace of achieving the Work. Canseliet: in 1922 Fulcanelli had not yet received the Gift of God but was so close to 'supreme Illumination' that he chose to wait and remain anonymous. The letter of his master congratulates the recipient on having truly had the gift of God, a great and rare Grace; he now possesses 'the treasure of treasures'. Distinct from the manuscript title Le Très précieux Don de Dieu of Georges Aurach.

Canseliet, in his preface: “This time you have truly had the gift of God; it is a great Grace, and for the first time I understand how rare this favour is.”

200.content:
[Term: Goetic art]
A view Fulcanelli reports (QUOTED: 'quelques auteurs perspicaces'): struck by the likeness of gothique and goétique, some authors linked Gothic art with goetic or magical art. He calls them perspicacious but gives his own reading, argotique.

Fulcanelli: “Some perspicacious and less superficial authors, struck by the similarity between gothique and goétique, thought there must be a close connection between Gothic Art and Goetic or magical Art.”

201.content:
[Term: Golden age]
From the promised land where life takes refuge, the elect will witness the return of the golden age; finding its location is left to us. In the Hindu scheme the first age, Crédayougam or age of innocence, answers to the Greeks' golden age.

Fulcanelli: “As for the geographical position of this promised land, from which the elect will witness the return of the golden age, it is for us to seek it.”

202.content:
[Term: Golden Fleece]
The fable is a complete enigma of the hermetic work leading to the Philosophers' Stone. In the Adepts' language the Golden Fleece is both the matter prepared for the Work and the final result, differing only in purity, fixity and maturity. The Hôtel Lallemant chapel relief shows the ram's fleece guarded by a dragon among oaks; oak and ram are one thing under two aspects, and the Fleece hangs on the oak like the gall and the kermes. The Argonauts sailed to win it. Canseliet recalls his own study titled Toison d'Or on the star.

Fulcanelli: “The fable of the Golden Fleece is a complete enigma of the hermetic work that is to end in the Philosophers' Stone.” / “In the language of the Adepts, Golden Fleece is the name for the matter prepared for the Work, as well as for the final result.”

203.content:
[Term: Gothic art]
The French art of the 12th to 15th centuries. Fulcanelli rejects derivations from the Goths or from 'barbarous' and says the people kept 'Art gothique' against the Academy's 'Art ogival'; the explanation lies in the word's cabalistic origin. For him 'art gothique' is a spelling distortion of 'argotique': the cathedral is a work of 'art goth' or argot. Gothic art is also 'art got ou cot', the art of Light or of the Spirit. The fire symbol gave the late style the name Flamboyant Gothic.

Fulcanelli: “For us, art gothique is only a spelling distortion of the word argotique, with which it is perfectly homophonous” / “Gothic art is, indeed, the art got or cot (Χο), the art of Light or of the Spirit.”

204.content:
[Term: Gothic cathedral]
The book's object. The cathedral is a sanctuary of Tradition, Science and Art, not only a monument to Christianity; an encyclopedia of medieval knowledge; 'books of images' with pages of stone. 'Gothic' is read cabalistically as argotique: the cathedral is a work of 'art goth' or argot. Its cross plan is the hieroglyph of the crucible. The whole cathedral is a mute glorification of the science of Hermes, the alchemical temple par excellence; it was built by the medieval Frimasons to transmit hermetic symbols and doctrine. Canseliet: thanks to Fulcanelli it gives up its secret.

Fulcanelli: “For the whole cathedral is nothing but a mute, yet pictured, glorification of the ancient science of Hermes, of which it has moreover kept one of the old craftsmen.” / “The cathedral is a work of art goth, or of argot.”

205.content:
[Person: Grasset d’Orcet]
Cited as having stated the rules of the 'Diplomatique' clearly enough, in his analysis of the Songe de Polyphile published by the Revue Britannique, that Fulcanelli need not repeat them.

Fulcanelli: “Some authors, and particularly Grasset d'Orcet, in the analysis of the Dream of Poliphilo published by the Revue Britannique, have given them clearly enough to spare us from speaking of them after them.”

206.content:
[Term: Great Book of Nature]
The first matter of the Work is shown as a book, open or closed according as it has been worked or only extracted from the mine; closed, sometimes sealed with seven bands, the seven successive operations that open it. Such is the Great Book of Nature, of simple style, easy to read once found and opened. On Notre-Dame, Alchemy holds two books, one closed (esotericism), one open (exotericism). The Lallemant ceiling shows a child with an open book beside a dead serpent, and an open book devoured by fire.

Fulcanelli: “Such is the Great Book of Nature, which holds in its pages the revelation of the profane sciences and that of the sacred mysteries.” / “So we see the first matter of the Work expressed symbolically by a book, sometimes open, sometimes closed, according as it has been worked or only extracted from the mine.”

207.content:
[Term: Great Days of Solomon]
Canseliet: the separation of the pure, luminous parts from the dense, dark parts of the alchemical earth, extracting light from darkness, is the work of the first of the Great Days of Solomon. The text gives no further explanation. Interpreted: this parallels Fulcanelli's remark that in God's Great Work light was separated on the first of six days.

Canseliet, in his preface: “Now this separation must be accomplished, which consists in extracting light from darkness and carrying out the work of the first of the Great Days of Solomon.”

208.content:
[Term: Great Work]
The alchemical operation as a whole, ending in the Philosophers' Stone. The alchemy figure on the Notre-Dame trumeau is 'the seal of the lay Great Work on the brow of the Christian Great Work'; God took six days to complete 'his Great Work', light being separated on the first. Its cornerstone is the First stone. Its colours run black, white, red; it may be done by two ways, dry and humid; three identical operations give Sulphur, Elixir and Stone. The fable of the Golden Fleece is a complete enigma of it. Canseliet: the letter gives an idea of the 'sublime domain' of the Great Work; the artist imitates Nature and the divine Great Work.

Fulcanelli: “the imprint, the seal of the lay Great Work on the brow of the Christian Great Work.” / “Finally, remember that God took six days to complete his Great Work; that the light was separated on the first day”

209.content:
[Term: Green Lion]
Stated: the first magnetic agent used to prepare the dissolvent; called green not so much for its colour as because it has not acquired the mineral characters of the adult state: a green, sour fruit, metallic youth with a latent germ, the embryo of our stone. Other names: Green Vitriol (Basile Valentin), Emerald of the Philosophers, May Dew, Saturnian Herb, Vegetable Stone. The Red Lion is the same matter brought to the quality of hermetic gold. The occult salt of the Red Lion is extracted with the spirit of the Green Lion; the old man and the Palace are a variant of the Green and Red Lions, the dissolvent and the body to dissolve. Tristan 'de Léonois' figures the making of the Green Lion. The secret vessel too is called Green Lion; authors (Batsdorff, the Cosmopolite, G. Aurach, Ripley) are quoted on it without a clear reason being given. Identified with Vitriol and May Dew (e358, e359).

Fulcanelli: “is called Green Lion, not so much because it has a green colour as because it has not acquired the mineral characters that chemically distinguish the adult state from the nascent state.” / “Generally, it is called philosophical egg and Green Lion.”

Identified in the text with: Vitriol, May Dew

210.content:
[Person: Gregory of Tours]
Cited as the authority that the water of the well of Saint-Marcel in Paris, dug inside the church near the bishop's tombstone, was a powerful remedy for several ailments.

Fulcanelli: “proved, according to Gregory of Tours, a powerful specific for several ailments.”

211.content:
[Term: Grey]
In the quoted account of the Parvis monolith, it was called messire Legris when gris meant fire, particularly firedamp, will-o'-the-wisp. The colossal Saint Christopher of Notre-Dame was painted grey. According to Aristotle, grey or violet is the emblematic colour of Mercury, which the text says explains why statues of Saint Christopher were coated in that tone. In the rose window one of the two quarrelling children is violet grey.

Fulcanelli: “According to Aristotle, Mercury has grey or violet as its emblematic colour, which is enough to explain why the statues of Saint Christopher were given a coating of the same tone.” / “it was also named Messire Legris, at a time when gris meant fire, and particularly firedamp, will-o'-the-wisp”

212.content:
[Term: Griffin]
The eighth figure of the Paris stylobate. Stated: a monster with the head and breast of the eagle and the rest of the lion, it teaches the contrary qualities that must be joined in the philosophical matter; it is the hieroglyph of the first conjunction. In it the Lion is the fixed, basic part, which loses its head (its form) on contact with the opposing volatility.

Fulcanelli: “The mythological monster whose head and breast are those of the eagle, and which borrows the rest of its body from the lion, initiates the seeker into the contrary qualities that must be joined in the philosophical matter”

213.content:
[Person: Gril]
In Helvetius's account translated by Canseliet: a goldsmith of The Hague, practised in alchemy but very poor; he poured a specially prepared spirit of salt on lead in a glass jar; after two weeks a silver Star floated on it, which he took for the visible star of the Philosophers, probably learned from Basile Valentin; after cupellation a pound of the lead gave twelve ounces of silver, and from these two ounces of gold. Canseliet cites it to show the star accompanies internal changes of bodies treated philosophically, but warns that two essential data are missing.

Canseliet, in his preface: “Whereupon Gril, filled with immense joy, told us he had already seen the visible star of the Philosophers, about which he had probably learned in Basil (Valentine).”

214.content:
[Person: Grillot de Givry]
Author of Le Grand Œuvre (1907), quoted: the bishop on the Notre-Dame south portal stands on the aludel where philosophical mercury sublimes; the door kept closed all year shows the 'non-vulgar way'. Canseliet: in his Musée des Sorciers he claimed a third, 16th-century statue to excuse Cambriel, which Canseliet rejects as baseless; he died a week before it appeared.

Fulcanelli: “'See,' says Grillot de Givry, 'carved on the right portal of Notre-Dame de Paris, the bishop perched on the aludel where the philosophical mercury sublimes, chained in limbo.”

215.content:
[Person: Guillaume de Paris]
Some saw his features in the Parvis monolith, which he was said to have erected together with the portal of Notre-Dame. Foreseeing the damage of time, he had the medallions of the great porch reproduced in the glass of the central rose, which preserves their colours. A legend says he hid the philosophers' stone in one of the pillars of the nave, its place fixed by the gaze of the carved raven; Victor Hugo is quoted on him. His hermetic work influenced the decoration of the great porch of Amiens.

Fulcanelli: “As a far-sighted master, he had the subjects of the medallions reproduced in detail in the glass of the central rose.” / “is said to have hidden the philosophers' stone in one of the pillars of the immense nave.”

216.content:
[Person: Gérard Dubois of Orléans]
Father Gérard Dubois of Orléans reports, in his History of the Church of Paris, the legend of Saint Marcel and the serpent, counted among the bishop's last deeds; Canseliet summarizes and translates it from the Latin.

Canseliet, in his preface: “which is reported by Father Gérard Dubois of Orléans (Gerardo Dubois Aurelianensi)”

217.content:
[Work: Chemical Harmony (Harmonie Chymique)]
Work of Lagneau, published by Claude Morel in 1601, at whose end the escutcheon copied from Flamel's arcade appears.

Fulcanelli: “the Harmonie chymique appeared from Claude Morel in 1601.”

218.content:
[Person: Harpocrates]
Named for his 'famous gesture', shared with figures of the Mutus Liber, which Cambriel wrongly gave to the St Marcel statue. Interpreted: the gesture is the finger to the lips commanding silence, as the same passage describes Cambriel's drawing.

Fulcanelli: “As for the famous gesture of the figures of the Mutus Liber and of Harpocrates, it came entirely from Cambriel's excessive imagination.”

219.content:
[Person: Haymon]
Author of the Epistola de Lapidibus Philosophicis (treatise 192, vol. VI of the Theatrum Chemicum, Argentorati, 1613). Fulcanelli quotes him as an example of the symbolic language describing where the first agent is found.

Fulcanelli: “To obtain the first agent, one must go to the hinder part of the world, where one hears the thunder roll, the wind blow, the hail and rain fall”

220.content:
[Person: Henckel]
J.-F. Henckel, author of the Traité de l'Appropriation. Cited for his reflection that, since the artist Elias claimed the stone is begun and finished in four days and showed it still stuck to the crucible shards, the alchemists' 'great months' might be days, and a method might consist in keeping the matters long in the highest fluidity by a violent fire with bellows.

Fulcanelli: “it seems to me it would not be so absurd to ask whether what the alchemists call great months might not be so many days”

221.content:
[Person: Henri de Linthaut]
Cited as a witness for the dry path: the secret lets one reach a great projection in little time, without much care or work, and he refers to Isaac Hollandois. Fulcanelli regrets he is no more forthcoming than others. The footnote spells him H. de Lintaut and gives his work L'Aurore, an Arsenal manuscript.

Fulcanelli: “This secret here surpasses all the secrets of the world, for you can in little time, without great care or labour, arrive at a great projection”

222.content:
[Person: Hermes]
Cited as an authority of the Art. According to Hermes, sun and moon, sulphur and mercury, are the parents of the stone; he calls the sun metaphorically the Father of the stone. Trévisan quotes him: having seen the blackness, believe you have followed a good path. The king born of fire must rejoice in the marriage 'afin, dit Hermès, que les choses occultes deviennent manifestes'. In his Emerald Table he says the wind carried it in its belly; the text glosses the wind as the winged, volatile mercury. The 'termes' were busts of Hermes (Mercury). Kermès has in the Gay Science the same meaning as Hermès, both meaning Mercury. Maia was mother of Hermes. Alchemy is 'l'antique science d'Hermès'.

Fulcanelli: “since the sun is called metaphorically, by Hermes, the Father of the stone.”

223.content:
[Term: Hermeticist]
A student of the hermetic science. Hermeticists know that the king of metals is figured by the solar sign; a detail of the Black Virgin processions (green candles only) is 'useful for the hermeticist'; Amédée de Ponthieu 'was no hermeticist' and so judged without bias; Chaudet, who drew the escutcheon of St Thomas Aquinas, was one. Canseliet: hermeticists will find in the book that from the confrontation of the Book and the Building the Spirit emerges and the letter dies.

Fulcanelli: “Now, hermeticists know that the king of metals is figured by the solar sign, that is, a circle with or without a central point.”

224.content:
[Work: Hermes Unveiled (Hermès dévoilé)]
Book of Cyliani, Paris, F. Locquin, 1832. Its Preface is cited for the two paths, dry and wet: Cyliani follows the wet 'by duty', though the dry, done with a single matter, is very familiar to him.

Fulcanelli: “I follow the latter, by preference, out of duty, although the former is very familiar to me: it is done with a single matter.”

225.content:
[Person: Herodotus]
Quoted on the yearly feast of Isis at Busiris, where an ox was sacrificed and myriads of men and women beat themselves, for a god he refused to name as an impiety; cited to show the mysterious nature of her cult.

Fulcanelli: “For which god they strike themselves, I judge it would be an impiety on my part to say.”

226.content:
[Term: Hieroglyph]
The text's term for a carved or painted image standing for an alchemical thing or operation. Examples stated: the cross is the alchemical hieroglyph of the crucible; the wheel that of the time of coction and of coction itself; the Raven that of the black colour; the fish that of the stone in its first state. Cathedral sculpture is called a 'prodigieux grimoire' read through such signs. Canseliet quotes Cambriel's 'hiéroglyphe' of the bishop with a finger to his lips, which Fulcanelli showed to be invented.

Fulcanelli: “Now, the cross is the alchemical hieroglyph of the crucible, formerly called cruzol, crucible and croiset” / “Now, the wheel is the alchemical hieroglyph of the time needed for the coction of the philosophic matter and, consequently, of coction itself.”

227.content:
[Person: Hiram]
Reached through Provençal aran/iran, iron: the Masonic Hiram, the divine Ram, the architect of Solomon's Temple.

Fulcanelli: “It is the Masonic Hiram, the divine Ram, the architect of Solomon's Temple.”

228.comment: Critical History of Nicolas Flamel (work; e428)
228.content:
[Work: Critical History of Nicolas Flamel (Histoire critique de Nicolas Flamel)]
Work of the abbé Vilain, Paris, Desprez, 1761, source of the description of Flamel's portal at Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie.

Fulcanelli: “Abbé Vilain, Critical History of Nicolas Flamel. Paris, Desprez, 1761.”

229.content:
[Work: History of Alchemy (Histoire de l'Alchimie)]
Work of Albert Poisson, with the subtitle Nicolas Flamel, Paris, Chacornac, 1893; source of the passages on Flamel's buildings.

Fulcanelli: “Albert Poisson, History of Alchemy. Nicolas Flamel. Paris, Chacornac, 1893.”

key: History of the Church of Paris
230.comment: History of the Church of Paris (work; e098)
230.content:
[Work: History of the Church of Paris (Histoire de l'Eglise de Paris)]
Work by Father Gérard Dubois of Orléans, from whose Latin text Canseliet summarizes the legend of Saint Marcel taming the serpent that defiled a noblewoman's tomb.

Canseliet, in his preface: “in his History of the Church of Paris (in Historia Ecclesiae Parisiensis)”

231.content:
[Work: History of Hermetic Philosophy (Histoire de la Philosophie Hermétique)]
Work of Lenglet-Dufresnoy, Paris, Coustelier, 1742. Its volume II contains Philalèthe's 'L'Entrée au Palais Fermé de Roy', source of the passage on the flying Eagles, and the 'Règles du Philalèthe', source of the passage on the degree of heat and on boiling.

Fulcanelli: “Lenglet-Dufresnoy, History of Hermetic Philosophy. The Entry into the Closed Palace of the King, vol. II, p. 35. Paris, Coustelier, 1742.”

232.content:
[Term: Holmat]
Name of the Mysterious Fountain among the Arab authors, whose waters gave immortality to the prophet Elias; they place it in the Modhallan.

Fulcanelli: “Among the Arab authors this fountain bears the name Holmat; they teach us, moreover, that its waters gave immortality to the prophet Elias”

233.content:
[Term: Holy Earth]
Names of the raw subject of the Work: Magnesia lunarii; 'more sincerely' Plomb des Sages, Saturnie végétable; for Philalèthe, Basile Valentin and the Cosmopolite, Son or Child of Saturn; for all, Terre sainte; its celestial hieroglyph is Aries. The names refer to its magnetic attraction of sulphur or its easy fusibility. Opening this matter and isolating its pure part gives the Kermès or tinging mercury.

Fulcanelli: “For all of them it is the Holy Earth (Terra sancta); and this mineral has for celestial hieroglyph the astronomical sign of the Ram (Aries).” / “As for the gross subject of the Work, some call it Magnesia lunarii; others, more sincere, call it Lead of the Sages, vegetable Saturnia.”

234.content:
[Term: Holy Grail]
Named once: Jean Lallemant, alchemist and knight of the Round Table, deserves a place around the Holy Grail with Geber and Roger Bacon. The Round Table romances are called traditional hermetic legends.

Fulcanelli: “Jean Lallemant, alchemist and knight of the Round Table, deserves to take his place around the Holy Grail”

235.content:
[Term: Hooligans (seers)]
The epithet given to the minority who speak argot outside received laws; the text reads voyous as voyants (seers) and adds the name Sons or Children of the Sun.

Fulcanelli: “to whom the epithet voyous is applied, that is to say voyants (seers), and the even more expressive one of Sons or Children of the sun.”

236.content:
[Term: Horn of Amalthea]
On the second lower medallion of Paris the Initiator holds a mirror and raises the horn of Amalthea, beside the Tree of Life; the mirror marks the beginning of the work, the tree its end, the horn of plenty its result. The Stone, Elixir or Tree of Life gives its owner knowledge, fortune and health: it is the horn of plenty, the unfailing source of material happiness. On the chapel ceiling of the Hôtel Lallemant a horn of Amalthea overflowing with flowers and fruits is a perch for a hen or partridge.

Fulcanelli: “The mirror symbolises the beginning of the work, the tree of life marks its end, and the horn of plenty the result.”

237.content:
[Person: Huginus à Barma]
Author of Le Règne de Saturne changé en Siècle d’or (Paris, 1780). In its Pratique he describes the matter of the Great Work, on which the star appears, in the same terms as Saint Ignatius uses for the star. His Sigillum Sapientum shows the artist holding a balance in which one pan outweighs the other in an apparent ratio of one to two, which the text links to Basil Valentine's 'white swan' and the question of weights. Against Pernety, he affirms that the old masters, Geber, Lulle, Paracelsus, each had a process of his own.

Fulcanelli: “Take true earth, he says, well impregnated with the rays of the sun, the moon and the other stars.”

238.content:
[Work: Hymn to Delos (Hymne à Délos)]
Poem of Callimachus, lines 250 and 255, quoted in Greek with the book's French: the swans circled Delos seven times and had not yet sung the eighth time when Apollo was born. Fulcanelli reads it as the sublimations (the eagles) and compares Joshua's seven circuits of Jericho.

Fulcanelli: “(The Swans) circled Delos seven times... and they had not yet sung the eighth time when Apollo was born. (the book's French rendering of the Greek)”

239.content:
[Place: Hôtel Lallemant]
A modest bourgeois house in Bourges, perfectly preserved, unrestored and unmutilated. Its so-called kitchen is read as an alchemical laboratory, and the 'pestle' of its corbel as a long-necked matras; laboratory and vessel make it one of the rarest 'demeures philosophales'. The loggia holds a painted Saint Christopher; the chapel's decoration is wholly hermetic: the Golden Fleece relief, the emblem ceiling, the credence with RERE, RER. Its archives show Jean Lallemant belonged to the alchemical Fraternity of the Knights of the Round Table.

Fulcanelli: “the laboratory and the vessel of the Work, the place where the Adept toils and the one where nature acts, are the two certainties that strike the initiate at the start of his visit” / “All the ornament is profane; all the motifs that decorate it are borrowed from hermetic science.”

240.content:
[Term: Image-maker]
The medieval carvers of images. Their chisel confirms the burlesque festivals; the 'tailleur d'imaiges' decorated the projecting parts while the ceramist did the floor. At Notre-Dame the imaigier transposed Leo and Cancer in the zodiac to signal the conjunction of the philosophical ferment with the mercurial compound. Fulcanelli stresses their scrupulous exactness in translating their thought; they isolated supernatural attributes with a band of clouds.

Fulcanelli: “The image-maker thus meant to indicate, by this skilful transposition, the conjunction of the philosophical ferment — or Lion — with the mercurial compound” / “we know well enough the conscientiousness, the care, the scruple of exactness that the image-makers of old brought to the rendering of their thought”

241.content:
[Work: The Imitation of Christ (Imitation de Jésus-Christ)]
Cited (book II, ch. 1, v. 6) to close the quotations on the first matter: its thought matches an anonymous author's remark that the Philosophers rightly hid the mystery of the Matter, which God took pleasure in hiding in things that seem useful to men.

Fulcanelli: “He who values things for what they are worth, and does not judge them by men's merit or esteem, possesses true Wisdom.”

242.content:
[Term: Initiate]
White is the colour of the Initiates, because the man leaving darkness for light passes from the profane state to that of Initiate, of pure; Dujols (quoted) makes 'bienheureux' a synonym of Initiate and says the Initiates were in white. All Initiates spoke argot, from the truands of the Cour des Miracles to the medieval Frimasons. The Phrygian bonnet was the distinctive sign of the Initiates and, in Dujols's account, 'la marque suprême de l'Initiation'. Isis alone dispenses Revelation and Initiation. Philosophical calcination is the one 'que l'Initié opère'.

Fulcanelli: “White is the colour of the Initiates, because the man who leaves darkness to follow the light passes from the profane state to that of Initiate, of pure one.”

243.content:
[Term: INRI]
Carved on the front arm of the Hendaye cross, matching the cycle diagram on the base. Exoterically it reads Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudæorum; from the cross it takes its secret meaning Igne Natura Renovatur Integra, for our hemisphere will soon be tried by and in fire, and as fire parts gold from impure metals the good will be separated from the wicked at the Judgment.

Fulcanelli: “That is what the inscription INRI teaches, which is rendered exoterically as Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum, but which takes from the cross its secret meaning: Igne Natura Renovatur Integra (by fire Nature is renewed whole).”

244.content:
[Term: Iron age]
Our age, the fourth, identified with the Calyougam. Its only seal is Death; its hieroglyph the skeleton with Saturn's attributes, the empty hourglass and the scythe, the latter reproduced in the figure seven, number of transformation and annihilation. Its Gospel is Saint Matthew's, the Gospel according to Science.

Fulcanelli: “The iron age has no other seal than that of Death.”

Identified in the text with: Calyougam

245.content:
[Person: Isaac the Hollander]
Named only by Henri de Linthaut as speaking at length of the secret by which a great projection is reached in little time.

Fulcanelli: “on which see Isaac the Hollander, who speaks of it at length.”

246.content:
[Person: Iseult]
On the Jacques-Cœur corbel she wears a crown she steadies with her right hand. As queen she is wife both of the old king and of the young hero, keeping the hermetic tradition that makes king, queen and lover the mineral triad of the Great Work.

Fulcanelli: “Let us note too that the queen is wife at once of the old man and of the young hero, so as to keep the hermetic tradition that makes the king, the queen and the lover the mineral triad of the Great Work.”

247.content:
[Person: Isis]
Statues of Isis once dwelt in the underground chambers of temples and became, with Christianity in Gaul, the Black Virgins, with identical symbolism and the same inscription Virgini parituræ. Quoting Bigarne via Dujols: Isis before conception is the Virgo paritura, the earth before its fecundation, and also the mother of the gods. Uncristianized statuettes are rarer still, e.g. one at Metz with red skin and black drapery. Isis is the Egyptian Ceres; her cult was mysterious and its mysteries were of the same order as those of Hermetic Science. Isis, Ceres and Cybele are taken as expressions of one principle, 'three heads under the same veil'. Fulcanelli states that Isis is mother of all things and sole dispenser of Revelation and Initiation.

Fulcanelli: “Isis, Ceres, Cybele, three heads under the same veil.” / “the goddess Isis is the mother of all things, she bears them all in her womb, and she alone is the dispenser of Revelation and of Initiation.”

Identified in the text with: Ceres, Cybele

248.content:
[Person: J. F. Golfs]
Author of La Filiation généalogique de toutes les Ecoles gothiques (Paris, Baudry, 1884). Fulcanelli quotes him with approval ('avec beaucoup de vérité') on the language of stones of Gothic art, clear and sublime, speaking to the humblest and the most cultivated.

Fulcanelli: “'The language of stones that this new art speaks,' says J. F. Golfs with much truth, 'is at once clear and sublime.'”

249.content:
[Person: Jacobus de Voragine]
Reveals Saint Christopher's primitive name, Offerus. His text and the Lallemant loggia bas-relief of Saint Christopher are said to contain the same hermetic sense; the legend is transcribed as reported by Amédée de Ponthieu after him.

Fulcanelli: “It therefore seems beyond doubt that the subject of this masterpiece and the text of Jacobus de Voragine contain the same hermetic meaning, with, in addition, a certain detail found nowhere else.”

250.content:
[Person: Jacobus Tollius]
Author of Le Chemin du Ciel Chymique, translation of the Manuductio ad Coelum Chemicum (1688). He mocks the puffers who seek their colours (black raven, white dove, yellow eagle, red pheasant) in their glass vessels; for him a fixed thing will not penetrate metals; foul odour denotes fixation, pleasant odour volatility. He says the cock is the attribute of Mercury; Fulcanelli takes his advice to seek the magistery in a volatile thing. Canseliet quotes his commentary 'opening' the chemical Heaven.

Fulcanelli: “Go, and withdraw at once, you who seek with extreme diligence your various colours in your glass vessels.” / “The cock is the emblem of Gaul and the attribute of Mercury, as Jacob Tollius expressly says”

251.content:
[Person: Jacques Cœur]
Grand argentier of Charles VII, builder of the Bourges palace in the 15th century, reputed a proven Adept; David de Planis-Campy credits him with the 'pierre au blanc', perhaps the origin of his title argentier. He multiplied symbols to accredit his quality of 'philosophe par le feu'. Fulcanelli reads his motto cabalistically and concludes that he practised alchemy or saw the white stone made; scallop and heart, paired on his house, may be a rebus or steganographic signature of his name.

Fulcanelli: “Our conviction, then, is that Jacques Cœur practised alchemy himself, or at least saw the stone to the white made before his eyes from 'essencified' iron cooked three times.”

252.content:
[Person: Jason]
The twelfth Paris medallion is a replica of the Argonauts' expedition: Jason beside the ram with the golden fleece and the tree with precious fruits of the Garden of the Hesperides. Jason killing the dragon of Colchis is one of the fables of the combat of the chemical bodies that yield the secret solvent. In the Golden Fleece relief of the Hôtel Lallemant, Jason was shown at the foot of an oak, a part now detached.

Fulcanelli: “we see Jason there beside the ram with the golden fleece and the tree with the precious fruits of the Garden of the Hesperides.”

253.content:
[Person: Jean Lallemant]
Documents in the Hôtel Lallemant archives show he belonged to the alchemical Fraternity of the Knights of the Round Table. Interpreted: he is the learned hermetist who commissioned the Saint Christopher relief and the author of the Hôtel's emblems, who left no known book but entrusted his science to stone. Fulcanelli places him with Geber and Roger Bacon around the Holy Grail, equal to Basile Valentin and Flamel in knowledge and above them in modesty and sincerity.

Fulcanelli: “Jean Lallemant, alchemist and knight of the Round Table, deserves to take his place around the Holy Grail, to commune there with Geber (Magister magistrorum) and Roger Bacon (Doctor admirabilis).” / “he surpasses them in the expression of two qualities, eminently scientific and philosophical, which he carried to the highest degree of perfection: modesty and sincerity.”

254.content:
[Person: Jean Liébaut]
The woodcuts of the Pyrotechnie that he put in his treatise show furnaces as keeps with glacis, battlements and loopholes, supporting the reading of the athanor as a tower. His treatise is the Quatre Livres des Secrets de Médecine et de la Philosophie Chimique.

Fulcanelli: “in particular the woodcuts of the Pyrotechnie that Jean Liébaut put in his treatise, will not be mistaken.”

255.content:
[Person: Jean Reyor (Marcel Clavelle)]
Named in Canseliet's third preface (voice CANSELIET). Marcel Clavelle, alias Jean Reyor, published in the Voile d'Isis of November 1932 an opinion that Canseliet calls presumptuous. Quoted (QUOTED: Jean Reyor): Fulcanelli was hasty in accusing Cambriel; a third, unfaithful Saint-Marcel pillar existed, replaced about 1860, and Cambriel described it in good faith. Reyor said Grillot de Givry ignored Fulcanelli's correction 'innocently'; the 'known occultist' he cites is Grillot de Givry. To escape the 1640 testimony he had to date the statue to Louis XIV's reign. Canseliet rejects his view.

Canseliet, in his preface: “The fact is that there exists a third Saint-Marcel pillar, an unfaithful reproduction of the original pillar, and it is this pillar that was replaced around 1860 by the more honest copy we see today.”

256.content:
[Person: Jean-Frédéric Helvetius]
