Author of the Veau d'Or (Vitulus Aureus). Henckel cites the artist Elias, quoted by Helvétius, who claimed to make the stone in four days and showed it stuck to crucible shards. Canseliet translates Helvetius's account of the goldsmith Gril's star of silver on spirit of salt and lead, and warns that it omits two essential data.

Fulcanelli: “When I think, writes Henckel, that the artist Elias, cited by Helvetius, claims that the preparation of the philosophers' stone is begun and finished in four days”

257.content:
[Person: Jean-Gaspard Knôttner]
In Helvetius's account: his greatest friend, a cloth dyer, from whom the goldsmith Gril asked a specially prepared spirit of salt; Knottner asked whether it would be used on metals.

Canseliet, in his preface: “asked my greatest friend, that is Jean-Gaspard Knôttner, dyer of cloth, for spirit of salt prepared in no common way.”

258.content:
[Person: Jean-Jacques Pauvert]
Canseliet: the publisher who reissued Le Mystère des Cathédrales, with care for both quality and price, and illustrated it with photographs of the sculptures drawn by Julien Champagne; publisher of Alchimie.

Canseliet, in his preface: “Through Jean-Jacques Pauvert, it is done”

259.content:
[Term: Jesse]
Mary was of the stem of Jesse; the text states that Hebrew Jes means fire, sun, divinity, so to be of Jesse's stem is to be of the race of the sun, of fire; hence the name Jesus means fire, sun, God. At Bourges the central tree rises from the stone as the tree of Jesse rises from the Patriarch's breast.

Fulcanelli: “Now the Hebrew word Jes means fire, the sun, divinity. To be of the stem of Jesse is thus to be of the race of the sun, of fire.”

260.content:
[Person: Jesus]
From the union of the Virgin (form) and the solar spirit comes living matter: Jesus, the incarnate spirit, fire corporified in things; his name read as fire, sun, God. In the crucible the first matter, like Christ, suffers the Passion, dies and rises purified; the cross bears the three nails that sacrificed the Christ-matter; Jesus built his Church on the stone. The Star of the Magi shines above the crib where Jesus, the Child-King, lies. Saint Christopher is the hieroglyph of solar sulphur (Jesus). The Child Jesus carried by Offerus is 'gold in its bath'. Jesus spoke only in parables and revealed the Language of the Birds to his apostles.

Fulcanelli: “It is then Jesus, the incarnate spirit, the fire corporified in things as we know them here below” / “It is indeed in the crucible that the first matter, like Christ himself, suffers the Passion”

261.content:
[Person: Jonathan Swift]
Canseliet: 'the singular Dean of Saint-Patrick' knew thoroughly the Gaye Science, the Language of the Gods or of the Birds, and practised it in his own way.

Canseliet, in his preface: “The very ones that Jonathan Swift, the singular Dean of Saint Patrick's, knew thoroughly and practised in his own way, with such learning and virtuosity.”

262.content:
[Person: Jourdain and Duval]
Named among those who read the Amiens wheel-fire as Ezekiel's vision. Durand reports they called a relief 'Inconstance'. They see in the cock and fox the prototype of the fable of the crow and the fox. Fulcanelli rejects these readings.

Fulcanelli: “Messrs Jourdain and Duval had called Inconstancy this vice opposed to Perseverance”

263.content:
[Person: Julien Champagne]
The painter to whom Fulcanelli entrusted the illustration of the book; Canseliet credits him with its original plates. Three more drawings of his were added to the second edition. He knew Fulcanelli from 1905, ten years before Canseliet; the third edition prints photographs of the sculptures he drew, which Canseliet says prove his conscientiousness.

Canseliet, in his preface: “It is indeed to the sincere and meticulous talent of the painter Julien Champagne that The Mystery of the Cathedrals owes the superb mantle of original plates wrapping its austere esotericism.”

264.content:
[Person: Julius Africanus]
A 3rd-century chronographer to whom the legend Des choses qui arrivèrent en Perse, lors de la naissance du Christ is attributed, though its real date is unknown. Cited as Julius Africanus in the Patr. grecque, t. X.

Fulcanelli: “The following legend, titled Of the things that happened in Persia at the birth of Christ, is attributed to Julius Africanus, a chronographer of the 3rd century”

265.content:
[Term: Jupiter]
In the verse on the planetary metals Jupiter is the figure of tin. The Cosmopolite places Jupiter second below Saturn and says Jupiter turns easily into Mercury, being higher. On the Notre-Dame sarcophagus Jupiter and Mercury follow Saturn and the Moon from the ends inward.

Fulcanelli: “So Jupiter is easily transmuted into Mercury, because Jupiter is higher than Mercury”

266.content:
[Term: Kabbalah]
Fulcanelli dismisses 'doctors in kabbalah', so-called Jewish or Christian cabalists whose illusory combinations lead to nothing positive. Canseliet: the Jewish kabbale works by transpositions, inversions, substitutions and arbitrary calculations; the word comes from Hebrew Kabbalah, 'tradition', and must not be confused with cabale, the phonetic cabala.

Fulcanelli: “Let us then leave these doctors in kabbalah to their ignorance and return to our subject, characterised hermetically by the oak.”

Canseliet, in his preface: “the second, from the Hebrew Kabbalah, which means tradition.”

267.content:
[Term: Kermes]
The oak also gives kermès, which in the Gaye Science means the same as Hermès, the initial consonants being interchangeable; both mean Mercury. Stated: kermès names the prepared mercurial substance, as galle names the raw one; the Philosophers' mercury must have the power to dye, gained only by first preparations. Isolating the pure part of the subject gives 'le Kermès, l’Hermès, le mercure teingeant' that carries mystic gold.

Fulcanelli: “Not only does the oak supply the gall, it also gives Kermes, which in the Gay Science has the same meaning as Hermes, the initial consonants being interchangeable.” / “and you will have the Kermes, the Hermes, the tinging mercury that carries the mystic gold within it, just as Saint Christopher carries Jesus and the ram its own fleece.”

Identified in the text with: Mercury

268.content:
[Term: Key]
Stated: 'Clef' is the name given to any radical (i.e. irreducible) alchemical dissolution, sometimes extended to the menstrua or solvents able to effect it. In Trévisan's text (quoted) the blackened mass is 'la clef', the beginning and sign of the method of the second régime. The text also uses the word in its ordinary sense (e.g. the key that opens the doors, held by Cybele).

Fulcanelli: “The name Key is given to any radical (that is, irreducible) alchemical dissolution, and the term is sometimes extended to the menstrua or solvents able to effect it.”

269.content:
[Person: Khunrath]
Named once: the Amiens citadel quatrefoil of 1225 may be the mother idea of the 'Forteresse alchimique' that Khunrath took up and modified in 1609.

Fulcanelli: “Or should we see, in this motif of the year 1225, the mother idea of the Alchemical Fortress, taken up and modified by Khunrath in 1609?”

270.content:
[Person: King Mark]
On the corbel his crowned head is hidden in the foliage of the central tree, which rises from the stone as the tree of Jesse from the Patriarch's breast. Uncle and nephew (Tristan) are chemically one thing; gold loses its crown with its colour for a time and later inherits a second, nobler one — hence the old king stays hidden while Tristan and Yseult stand out.

Fulcanelli: “In fact, uncle and nephew are, chemically speaking, but one same thing, of the same kind and of similar origin.”

271.content:
[Term: Kings' Cake]
The cake shared on Epiphany is the secret version of the truth that mercury carries the reborn gold-child. Its galette is 'signed' like the matter itself with crossed lines (the mesh of the net) and holds the baigneur; its dough is flaky (feuilletée), like the foliated prepared mercury, the baigneur inserted like a bookmark. Attending to the galette des Rois points to the subject to choose. 'Avoir de la galette' means being rich; who finds the bean is doubly king, by science and fortune. The cake sometimes holds a sabot instead of a bean; the swaddled mineral child is like its porcelain baigneur. Once Fulcanelli saw an oak drawn on its crust and a porcelain sole in place of the baigneur.

Fulcanelli: “Now, we find the secret version of this positive truth in the Kings' Cake, which it is customary to share in the family on Epiphany” / “Our galette is signed like the matter itself and holds in its dough the little child popularly called the 'bather'.”

272.comment: Profane Art in the Church (work; e115)
272.content:
[Work: Profane Art in the Church (L'Art profane à l'Eglise)]
Work by G. J. Witkowski, Paris, Schemit, 1908, cited in two volumes, 'Etranger' and 'France'.

Fulcanelli: “G. J. Witkowski, Profane Art in the Church. France. Paris, Schemit, 1908, p. 382.”

273.content:
[Work: The Atmosphere (L'Atmosphère)]
Work of Camille Flammarion (Paris, Hachette, 1888, p. 362), source of the account of the Virgin in the Observatory cellars.

Fulcanelli: “The colossal building of Louis XIV, he writes, which raises the balustrade of its terrace twenty-eight metres above the ground, goes down below in foundations of the same depth: twenty-eight metres.”

274.content:
[Work: The Dawn (L'Aurore)]
Work of H. de Lintaut, manuscript of the Arsenal library, S. A. F. 169, no. 3020; the source of the passage on the dry path.

Fulcanelli: “H. de Lintaut, The Dawn. Manuscript, Arsenal library, S. A. F. 169, no. 3020.”

275.content:
[Work: The Intellective Cabala (La Cabale Intellective)]
Manuscript of the Bibliothèque de l'Arsenal, S. et A. 72, p. 15, the source of the verse on the seven planetary metals.

Fulcanelli: “The Intellective Cabala. Manuscript of the Arsenal library, S. et A. 72, p. 15.”

276.comment: The Key of the Hermetic Cabinet (work; e299)
276.content:
[Work: The Key of the Hermetic Cabinet (La Clef du Cabinet hermétique)]
An anonymous 18th-century manuscript, called 'précieux'. Quoted on the first putrefaction and its signs: acidity and a smell of the sepulchre (Morien), 'fish eyes' (Philalèthe), fermentation by the secret fire. Quoted at length on the water that holds all the virtues of heaven and earth, the 'Dissolvant général de toute la Nature', the bath of King and Queen, the Fountain of Trévisan, the steel and magnet in Aries, Flamel's hollow oak, and a vessel of old oak like a barrel; the water is 'notre vinaigre mercuriel'. Fulcanelli adds that it is useful if read with prudence: the spirit gives life, the letter kills. Also quoted on why philosophers hid the Matter.

Fulcanelli: “The water we use, writes the anonymous author of the Key of the Hermetic Cabinet, is a water that contains all the virtues of heaven and earth”

277.comment: The Cross before Jesus Christ (work; e155)
277.content:
[Work: The Cross before Jesus Christ (La Croix avant Jésus-Christ)]
Work by abbé Ansault, Paris, V. Rétaux, 1894, on the cross as a pre-Christian symbol.

Fulcanelli: “Abbé Ansault, The Cross before Jesus Christ. Paris, V. Rétaux, 1894.”

278.comment: The Genealogical Filiation of All the Gothic Schools (work; e108)
278.content:
[Work: The Genealogical Filiation of All the Gothic Schools (La Filiation généalogique de toutes les Ecoles gothiques)]
Work by J. F. Golfs, Paris, Baudry, 1884, source of the quotation on the language of stones.

Fulcanelli: “J. F. Golfs, The Genealogical Filiation of All the Gothic Schools. Paris, Baudry, 1884.”

279.content:
[Work: The Great Encyclopedia (La Grande Encyclopédie)]
Source of Berthelot's definition of the labyrinth: article Labyrinthe, vol. XXI, p. 703.

Fulcanelli: “The Great Encyclopedia. Article Labyrinth. Vol. XXI, p. 703.”

key: Lumière sortant par soy-mesme des Ténèbres
Lumiere sortant par soy-mesme des Tenebres
280.comment: Light Coming Forth by Itself from the Darkness (work; e451)
280.content:
[Work: Light Coming Forth by Itself from the Darkness (La Lumière sortant par soy-mesme des Ténèbres)]
A classic work, Paris, d'Houry, 1687. Its anonymous commentator is cited on the coction: the philosopher cooks in a single vessel a single vapour that thickens little by little. The commentator is also cited on the essence in which the spirit dwells and on seeking the subject in the mineral kingdom alone.

Fulcanelli: “it is therefore in the mineral kingdom only, where the metallic seed dwells, that we must seek the subject proper to our art”

281.content:
[Work: Nature Uncovered (La Nature à découvert)]
Book by the Chevalier Inconnu, Aix, 1669, source of the quotation on the second operation and the Raven's Head.

Fulcanelli: “Nature Uncovered, by the Unknown Knight. Aix, 1669.”

282.content:
[Work: The Forsaken Word (La Parole délaissée)]
Book of Bernard Trévisan, Paris, Jean Sara, 1618, p. 39, source of the long description of the black compound ('poix noire', 'Merle de Jean', black cloud in the vessel, the black mass as 'clef' and sign of the second régime).

Fulcanelli: “Bernard Trévisan, The Forsaken Word. Paris, Jean Sara, 1618, p. 39.”

283.content:
[Work: The Golden Fleece (La Toyson d'Or)]
Salomon Trismosin's book, Paris, Ch. Sevestre, 1612. Cited for the figure of the crowned oak and the raven, and for the short way (Régime de Saturne) using an earthen vessel instead of glass. Interpreted: the 'Toison d'Or' whose third figure shows a philosopher in red under a purple cloak and green cap holding a glass matras with a green liquid, nearly identical to G. Aurach's image of the Lion vert, is probably this book; the text does not name its author there. It comments the ludus puerorum, figured identically on the Lallemant ceiling (a child on a wooden horse). Not to be confused with Canseliet's study on the Golden Fleece or the myth of the Toison d'or.

Fulcanelli: “I will stir up your body in an earthen vessel where I will bury it” / “The third figure of the Golden Fleece is almost identical to G. Aurach's image.”

284.comment: The Life of Gargantua and Pantagruel (work; e139)
284.content:
[Work: The Life of Gargantua and Pantagruel (La Vie de Gargantua et de Pantagruel)]
Rabelais's work, called esoteric and a novel in argot; the note is attached to 'Dive-Bouteille', one of the medieval names of the Language of the Birds.

Fulcanelli: “The Life of Gargantua and Pantagruel, by François Rabelais, is an esoteric work, a novel in argot.”

285.content:
[Term: Labour of Hercules]
The text names 'our preparation' a labour of Hercules: the warrior of the twelfth Paris medallion is the artist who has just finished it. Once the hard labours of Hercules are done, the work is reduced to the ludus puerorum, the keeping of the fire.

Fulcanelli: “As for the warrior, he represents the artist who has just accomplished the labour of Hercules that our preparation is.”

286.content:
[Term: Labyrinth]
Traced on cathedral floors at the crossing of nave and transepts (Sens, Reims, Auxerre, Saint-Quentin, Poitiers, Bayeux); Amiens's had a gold rising sun at its centre; Chartres's, called 'la lieue' (for 'le lieu'), showed Theseus and the Minotaur, proof of a mytho-hermetic sense. Berthelot calls the 'labyrinth of Solomon' a cabalistic figure at the head of alchemical manuscripts. It is emblematic of the whole Work, with two difficulties: reaching the centre where the two natures fight, and getting out, for which Ariadne's thread is needed. The Cnossos labyrinth was called Absolum. The black phases form a 'ténébreux labyrinthe'.

Fulcanelli: “The image of the labyrinth thus presents itself to us as emblematic of the entire labour of the Work, with its two major difficulties: that of the way one must follow to reach the centre — where the hard combat of the two natures is fought” / “As for the labyrinth of Chartres, commonly called la lieue (for le lieu, the place), drawn on the pavement of the nave, it consists of a whole series of concentric circles folding into one another with infinite variety.”

287.content:
[Term: Ladder of the Philosophers]
On the trumeau of the central portal, the figure of alchemy holds between her knees a ladder of nine rungs, the scala philosophorum, hieroglyph of the patience her followers need through the nine successive operations of the hermetic labour (pl. II). Valois is quoted: patience is the Philosophers' ladder and humility the gate of their garden.

Fulcanelli: “stands the ladder of nine rungs, scala philosophorum, hieroglyph of the patience her faithful must have during the nine successive operations of the hermetic labour” / “Patience is the ladder of the Philosophers, Valois tells us, and humility is the gate of their garden”

288.content:
[Person: Lagneau]
Author of the Harmonie Chymique, at the end of which, per Albert Poisson, the escutcheon imitated by Flamel appears. Fulcanelli concludes Lagneau had his image copied from the arcade of the charnel house, though it would have been better to use the type escutcheon of saint Thomas.

Fulcanelli: “This account, matching Lagneau's engraving, allows us to conclude that he had his image copied from the arcade of the charnel house.”

289.content:
[Term: Lamb]
Quoting the Dialogue with Trypho: the paschal lamb was the figure of Christ, and roasted whole it formed a cross. On the base of the north portal of Notre-Dame the lamb is the emblem of the sweetening (edulcoration) of the arsenical principle of the Matter. Dujols (QUOTED): the blessed, washed in the blood of the Lamb, wear white.

Fulcanelli: “The lamb, emblem of the edulcoration of the arsenical principle of the Matter” / “'The mystery of the lamb that God had ordered to be sacrificed at Passover,' he says, 'was the figure of Christ”

290.content:
[Term: Language of colours]
The coloured phases of the coction always served as symbolic prototype; each was given a precise meaning; thus there existed in all times, as Portal says, a language of colours closely joined to religion, which reappears in the Middle Ages in the stained glass of Gothic cathedrals.

Fulcanelli: “Thus there existed, in all times, a language of colours, closely joined to religion, as Portal says”

291.content:
[Term: Language of the Birds]
The sacred language behind the phonetic cabala. Argot derives from it, the mother of all languages, language of philosophers and diplomats; Jesus gave it to the apostles with the Holy Spirit; it teaches the mystery of things; the Incas called it 'Langue de cour'; in the Middle Ages 'Gaie science', 'Gay sçavoir', 'Langue des dieux', 'Dive-Bouteille'; spoken before Babel; traces survive in argot, Picard, Provençal, the gypsies' dialect. Tiresias knew it, taught by Minerva. Initiates in the 'language of the gods' hold all keys; in the Gaye Science Kermès equals Hermès. The Hendaye inscription is to be read in it, in French, by the rules of 'Diplomatique'. Canseliet: the 'langue matrice'; Fulcanelli recovered its lost key.

Fulcanelli: “Let us add finally that argot is one of the derived forms of the Language of the Birds, mother and eldest of all the others, the language of philosophers and diplomats.” / “It is this language that teaches the mystery of things and unveils the most hidden truths.”

292.content:
[Person: Lassus]
One of the architects who restored Notre-Dame. Canseliet: with Viollet-le-Duc he replaced the St Marcel statue with a copy; Grillot de Givry names him in the restoration.

Fulcanelli: “And if art owes some gratitude to the eminent architects Toussaint, Geffroy Dechaume, Bœswillwald, Viollet-le-Duc and Lassus who restored the basilica, odiously profaned by the School, Science will never recover what it has lost.”

293.content:
[Term: Latomi (stonemasons)]
Durand's reading of the wheel-fire shows an incomplete study of the traditional technique, the formulas the latomi respected in carrying out their symbols.

Fulcanelli: “The first shows an incomplete study of the traditional technique, of the formulas the latomi respected in carrying out their symbols.”

294.content:
[Term: Laurentum]
The fields of Laurentum are the end of Aeneas's journey, where the star of Venus he had seen daily ceased to appear, showing him the lands appointed by Fate. A footnote reads the name cabalistically as 'or enté', grafted gold; the text gives no further development of this reading.

Fulcanelli: “Cabalistically, grafted gold (or enté), engrafted.”

295.content:
[Person: Le Breton]
Author of the Clefs de la Philosophie Spagyrique. Quoted for the four putrefactions of the Work (first separation, first conjunction, second conjunction of the heavy water with its salt, fixation of sulphur), each with blackness, and for a mineral known to the true learned, hidden under various names, which contains abundantly the fixed and the volatile.

Fulcanelli: “'There is,' says Le Breton, 'a mineral known to the true Learned, who hide it in their writings under various names, which contains abundantly the fixed and the volatile.'”

296.comment: The Path to the Chemical Heaven (work; e342)
296.content:
[Work: The Path to the Chemical Heaven (Le Chemin du Ciel Chymique (Manuductio ad Coelum Chemicum))]
J. Tollius's work, a translation of the Manuductio ad Coelum Chemicum, Amsterdam, 1688. Quoted for its apostrophe to the 'souffleurs' who seek colours in their glass vessels (black raven, white dove, yellow eagle, red pheasant), and for the black Earth, white Water, and the smell marking fixation or volatility. Cited for the cock as attribute of Mercury.

Fulcanelli: “You who weary my ears with your black raven, you are as mad as that man of antiquity who used to applaud in the theatre though he was alone there”

297.content:
[Work: The Poor Man's Penny (Le Denier du Pauvre)]
Work of Etteilla, cited once as in the Sept nuances de l’Oeuvre philosophique (1786), p. 57, and once as le Denier du Pauvre ou la Perfection des métaux (Paris, about 1785), p. 58. Source of the passage on the Magi's vase and of the legends of a hermetic painting.

Fulcanelli: “a vase full of a celestial-astral liquor, made of one third wild honey, one part earthly water and one part heavenly water”

298.content:
[Work: Ariadne's Thread (Le Filet d'Ariadne)]
Paris, d'Houry, 1695; ascribed to Batsdorff or to Gaston de Claves. Quoted on the signs of true putrefaction and its names (Occident, Darkness, Eclipse, Leprosy, Raven's Head, Death, Mortification of Mercury). Batsdorff in it says the philosophers called the vessel of coction 'Lion vert' without giving a reason. Interpreted: it is the special treatise Batsdorff wrote to teach what Ariadne's thread is.

Fulcanelli: “Batsdorff, in his Ariadne's Thread, says the Philosophers called the vessel used for the coction Green Lion, but without giving any reason.”

299.content:
[Work: The Great Work (Le Grand Œuvre)]
Work of Grillot de Givry, Paris, Chacornac, 1907, p. 27. Cited for its passage on the bishop of the right portal of Notre-Dame standing on the aludel and the door kept shut all year, the non-vulgar path.

Fulcanelli: “Grillot de Givry, The Great Work. Paris, Chacornac, 1907, p. 27.”

300.content:
[Work: The Museum of Sorcerers (Le Musée des Sorciers)]
Book of Grillot de Givry, which Canseliet says claimed a 16th-century replacement statue of St Marcel; dated Paris 20 November 1928, it came out in February 1929, a week after its author's sudden death; its p. 407 reads 'XVIe siècle'.

Canseliet, in his preface: “Indeed, this first book of Fulcanelli had been out since June 1926 when — dated Paris, 20 November 1928 — The Museum of Sorcerers came out in February 1929, a week after its author's sudden death.”

301.comment: The Mystery of the Cathedrals (work; e001)
301.content:
[Work: The Mystery of the Cathedrals (Le Mystère des Cathédrales)]
The book itself, presented by Canseliet as the work of his Master Fulcanelli; through it the Gothic cathedral gives up its secret. Written in 1922; first printing of 1926 in 300 copies; a second edition added three drawings by Julien Champagne and original notes of Fulcanelli, unchanged; it had appeared by June 1926. Its plates are by Julien Champagne; Jean-Jacques Pauvert reissued it with photographs of the sculptures Champagne drew; Canseliet calls the edition of PREF3 the third. Canseliet's claim for its merit: it brought the phonetic cabala back to light. Canseliet also states that the key of the major arcanum is given by one of its figures.

Canseliet, in his preface: “this book has brought back into full light the phonetic cabala, whose principles and their application had fallen into the most complete oblivion.”

302.content:
[Work: The Psalter of Hermpophile (Le Psautier d’Hermpophile)]
An anonymous 18th-century manuscript in 'Traités de la Transmutation des Métaux', strophe XXV, source of the plain statement that the metallic Chaos contains all metals and is no metal.

Fulcanelli: “The metallic Chaos produced by the hands of nature contains in itself all the metals and is not metal.”

303.comment: The Reign of Saturn Changed into a Golden Age (work; e205)
303.content:
[Work: The Reign of Saturn Changed into a Golden Age (Le Règne de Saturne changé en Siècle d'or)]
Work of Huginus à Barma (Paris, Derieu, 1780). In its Pratique the author tells the reader to take a true earth impregnated with the rays of sun, moon and stars, which Fulcanelli relates to the star of the Nativity.

Fulcanelli: “Huginus à Barma, in the Practice of his work, uses the same terms to express the matter of the Great Work on which the star appears”

304.comment: The Secret Book of Artephius (work; e315)
304.content:
[Work: The Secret Book of Artephius (Le Secret Livre d'Artephius)]
Printed in 'Trois Traitez de la Philosophie naturelle', Paris, Marette, 1612; the reference given for Artephius on the secret fire.

Fulcanelli: “The Secret Book of Artephius, in Three Treatises of Natural Philosophy. Paris, Marette, 1612.”

305.content:
[Work: The Testament (Le Testament)]
Poem of François Villon, stanzas XXXVI and XXXVII of which serve as epigraph to the third preface. The text does not comment on it.

Canseliet, in his preface: “'Better to live under coarse homespun”

306.comment: The Most Precious Gift of God (work; e486)
306.content:
[Work: The Most Precious Gift of God (Le Très précieux Don de Dieu)]
Manuscript of Georges Aurach of Strasbourg, written and painted by his own hand in 1415, cited for its image of the green-filled matras.

Fulcanelli: “The Most Precious Gift of God. Manuscript of Georges Aurach, of Strasbourg, written and painted by his own hand, in the year of the Salvation of redeemed Humanity, 1415.”

307.content:
[Person: Lenglet-Dufresnoy]
Author of the Histoire de la Philosophie Hermétique (1742), whose volume II gives Philalèthe's Entrée au Palais Fermé du Roy and his Règles. In his Remarks on chapter XIX of the Introitus he says the short way is done by the double philosophical mercury in eight days, against nearly eighteen months for the first way.

Fulcanelli: “By this means, he adds, the Work is accomplished in eight days, whereas nearly eighteen months are needed for the first way”

308.content:
[Work: The Philosophers' Dwellings (Les Demeures philosophales)]
A further work, for which Canseliet wrote a Preface, where he had called Basile Valentin Fulcanelli's 'true' initiator, later corrected to 'first'. Canseliet says a long-pondered question of the Master, to which the added notes relate, will be discussed apropos of it. A note cites it for the sculpted 16th-century soffit at Dampierre-sur-Boutonne, comparable to the Lallemant chapel ceiling. The text does not state its author outright.

Fulcanelli: “one at Dampierre-sur-Boutonne, likewise sculpted, of the 16th century (The Philosophers' Dwellings)”

key: Trois Livres de l’Art du Potier
Trois Livres de l'Art du Potier
Three Books of the Potter's Art
Three Books of the Potter’s Art
309.comment: The Three Books of the Potter's Art (work; e520)
309.content:
[Work: The Three Books of the Potter's Art (Les Trois Livres de l’Art du Potier)]
Work of the cavalier Cyprian Piccolpassi, cited under Claudius Popelin's name (Paris, Librairie Internationale, 1861), whose plates include the dove tied to a stone.

Fulcanelli: “Claudius Popelin, The Three Books of the Potter's Art, by the cavalier Cyprian Piccolpassi. Paris, Librairie Internationale, 1861.”

310.content:
[Term: The letter S]
On the Hendaye cross, the S, serpent-shaped, corresponds to the Greek khi (X) and takes its esoteric meaning: the helical track of the sun at the zenith of its curve at the cyclic catastrophe, a theoretical image of the beast of the Apocalypse. Its deliberate displacement shows the inscription must be read in the language of the gods or of the birds.

Fulcanelli: “The letter S, which borrows the sinuous form of the serpent, corresponds to the khi (X) of the Greek language and takes on its esoteric meaning.”

311.content:
[Term: Libethra]
Mythology's name for the Mysterious Fountain: a fountain of Magnesia with a neighbouring spring called the Rock, both issuing from a great rock shaped like a woman's breast, so that the water seemed to flow like milk from two breasts. Since the old authors call the matter of the Work 'our Magnesia' and its liquor Virgin's Milk, Fulcanelli sees 'an indication' here. Source: Noël, Dictionnaire de la Fable.

Fulcanelli: “Mythology names it Libethra and tells us it was a fountain of Magnesia, which had near it another spring named the Rock.”

312.content:
[Person: Limojon de Saint-Didier]
Cited author; commentator of the Ancienne Guerre des Chevaliers in the Triomphe hermétique. The secret fire is prepared by the artist; it is not actually hot but an igneous spirit put into a subject of the Stone's nature, which calcines, dissolves, sublimes and resolves it into dry water. The reborn gold receives a second crown 'infinitely nobler than the first'. He advises steering 'by the sight of the north star'. His epigraph: knowledge of the magistery comes from Heaven's inspiration.

Fulcanelli: “This fire is not actually hot, but it is an igneous spirit introduced into a subject of the same nature as the Stone” / “That is why Limojon de Saint-Didier advises seekers to set their course 'by the sight of the north star'.”

313.content:
[Term: Lion]
A complex symbol on the Paris stylobate, whose original colour is lost, so Fulcanelli cannot settle on one reading. In the griffin it is the fixed, basic part of a compound; with the eagle it figures the earthly, fixed force of one of the two natures. Stated: in general the Lion is the sign of gold, alchemical and natural; texts also give the name to the matter that receives the Universal Spirit, the secret fire, in making the dissolvent; in both cases it means power, incorruptibility, perfection. On the Paris zodiac Leo, put in place of Cancer, is 'the philosophical ferment' to be joined with the mercurial compound. The Sages lead their eagles to devour the lion (Philalèthe, quoted).

Fulcanelli: “In general, the Lion is the sign of gold, both alchemical and natural; it therefore expresses the physico-chemical properties of these bodies.”

314.content:
[Work: Book of Seth (Livre de Seth)]
A legend drawn from a work titled Livre de Seth is related by a 6th-century author (cited as the Opus imperfectum in Mattheum, joined to the works of Saint John Chrysostom). A people of the Far East on the shores of the Ocean had a Book attributed to Seth foretelling the star and the gifts for the Child; twelve of the wisest, called Magi, climbed each year the Mount of Victory, with a cave cut in the rock, prayed in silence three days, until the star appeared there as a small child bearing the figure of a cross, spoke, instructed them and sent them to Judea. The star led them two years.

Fulcanelli: “there was a Book attributed to Seth, which spoke of the future appearance of this star and of the gifts that were to be brought to the Child”

315.content:
[Work: Book of Hieroglyphic Figures (Livre des Figures hiéroglyphiques)]
A work of Nicolas Flamel. Of the hollow oak from which the fountain springs, Flamel says there only 'Note ce chêne'. In his 'Figures Hiéroglyphiques' Flamel describes the parabolic pilgrimage he made to ask 'Monsieur Jacques de Galice' for help, light and protection, which Fulcanelli takes as the journey every alchemist begins with.

Fulcanelli: “'Note this oak,' Flamel simply says in the Book of Hieroglyphic Figures.”

316.content:
[Work: Book of Images (Livre des Images)]
Work of Paracelsus quoted on the successive colorations of the Work and on tincture.

Fulcanelli: “Paracelsus, in the Book of Images, speaks thus of the successive colorations of the Work”

317.content:
[Term: Lorraine glass]
Some authors advise it for the egg's walls, which must be thick to resist internal pressure. Stated: the term once distinguished moulded from blown glass; moulding allowed very thick, regular walls.

Fulcanelli: “The term Lorraine glass once served to distinguish moulded glass from blown glass.”

318.content:
[Term: Lost Word]
The 'Lost Word' of the medieval freemasons, which all hermetic fraternities hoped to recover; Fulcanelli equates it with the Verbum dimissum of the Trévisan and with the highest secret, the extraction of May Dew. Canseliet: Freemasonry still seeks it, while the Church, which possesses this Word, is abandoning it. The text identifies it with Verbum dimissum (e003).

Fulcanelli: “That is the Verbum dimissum of the Trévisan, the Lost Word of the medieval freemasons, the one all hermetic Fraternities hoped to recover, and whose search was the aim of their labours and the reason for their existence.”

Canseliet, in his preface: “While Freemasonry still seeks the lost word (verbum dimissum), the universal Church (katholiké), which possesses this Word, is itself about to abandon it in the devil's ecumenism.”

Identified in the text with: Verbum dimissum (the abandoned Word)

319.content:
[Person: Louis David]
Named as the composer of the French flag, whose colours repeat the three of the Work: dark blue or black for the bourgeoisie, white for the people, red for royalty. The text calls him 'le maçon écribouille Louis David' and gives no gloss of 'écribouille'.

Fulcanelli: “These are the national colours of the French flag, which, moreover, was composed by the mason 'écribouille' Louis David.”

320.content:
[Person: Lucifer]
The devil figure called Maistre Pierre du Coignet at Notre-Dame represented the initial matter of the Work humanized as Lucifer, the light-bearer or morning star, and was the symbol of the cornerstone. Before being cut, the rough stone was often given the image of the devil.

Fulcanelli: “Now this figure, meant to represent the initial matter of the Work, humanized in the guise of Lucifer (who bears the light — the morning star), was the symbol of our cornerstone”

Identified in the text with: Morning star

321.content:
[Term: Ludus puerorum (children's play)]
The text states its meaning: once the labours of Hercules are done, the artist's work is reduced to the ludus puerorum of the texts, that is, maintaining the fire, which a woman spinning could do. On the chapel ceiling of the Hôtel Lallemant it appears as a child riding a wooden horse, whip raised, as in Trismosin's Toison d'Or.

Fulcanelli: “his labour is reduced to the ludus puerorum of the texts, that is, to the keeping of the fire, which a woman spinning at her distaff can easily undertake and carry through.”

322.content:
[Work: Legends of Old Paris (Légendes du Vieux Paris)]
Work of Amédée de Ponthieu (Bachelin-Deflorenne, 1867), cited at p. 91 for the Parvis monolith and at p. 106 for the legend of Saint Christopher after Jacobus de Voragine.

Fulcanelli: “Before becoming a Christian, Christopher was named Offerus; he was a kind of giant, a very thick-witted fellow.”

323.content:
[Term: Magi]
In the legend from the Book of Seth, the twelve wise men awaiting the star were called Magi in their tongue because they glorified God in silence and in a low voice; the star appeared to them on the Mount of Victory as a small child with a cross. Other legends: a thirteen-day journey with a star in the form of an eagle surmounted by a cross; in Persia the Magi announce the Child born at Bethlehem; Chalcidius speaks of the most learned Chaldeans who saw the star; Matthew's Gospel of Magi from the East following his star. Tradition says a star guided them to the Saviour's cradle, the announcing sign; the Epiphany cake keeps a hidden version of this. Canseliet cites Saint Chrysostom that the sign that led the Magi rested on the Saviour's head.

Fulcanelli: “In their language they were called Magi, because they glorified God in silence and in a low voice.” / “Tradition holds that the Magi were guided to the Saviour's cradle by a star, which was for them the announcing sign, the Good News of his birth.”

324.content:
[Term: Magistery]
The accomplished Work, or its object. Read cabalistically, Jacques Cœur's motto yields 'the three reiterations indispensable to the total perfection of the two Magisteries'. Ripley: one unclean body, the Green Lion, enters 'our magistery'. Following Tollius, the magistery is to be sought in a volatile thing, hence the need for a vessel. The letter to Fulcanelli: to make the Work by mercury alone is to have accomplished the Magistery; Limojon's epigraph: knowledge of the magistery comes from Heaven's inspiration. The text does not say what the two Magisteries are.

Fulcanelli: “3rd, the three reiterations indispensable to the total perfection of the two Magisteries (the three cuers).” / “Must you not, following the excellent advice of Tollius, seek and find the magistery in a volatile thing?”

325.content:
[Term: Magnesia]
A name for the matter of the Work: old authors call it 'notre Magnésie', and the liquor drawn from it the Virgin's Milk. The magnet (αιρην) is the virtue in the body the Sages call their magnesia. Bernard Trévisan (QUOTED) names the blackened compost Magnesia. At Amiens the dew falls on a mass that may be the mineral called Magnesia or philosophical Magnet, showing its attractive virtue; the nostoc symbolizes the Sages' mineral Magnesia. Some call the raw subject Magnesia lunarii.

Fulcanelli: “Now we have seen that the ancient authors call the matter of the Work our Magnesia, and that the liquor extracted from this magnesia is called Virgin's Milk.” / “So αιρην is the magnet, the virtue enclosed in the body that the Sages call their magnesia.”

326.content:
[Term: Magnet]
The attractive virtue in the matter. By Greek etymology, Ariadne's name leads to αιρην, 'what takes, attracts', the magnet, the virtue enclosed in the body the Sages call their magnesia. Adepts call their steel from Aries their magnet. The spirit spread over the globe needs an attractive receptacle: the magnet in the belly of Aries, to be taken at its birth; the water of the Work is a magnet drawing all celestial influences. The first magnetic agent for the dissolvent is the Green Lion. At Amiens the dew falls on a body that may be Magnesia or philosophical Magnet, showing an attractive virtue. Philalèthe's recipe: nine parts of 'our Magnet'.

Fulcanelli: “So αιρην is the magnet, the virtue enclosed in the body the Sages call their magnesia.” / “That is this magnet shut in the belly of Aries, which must be taken at the moment of its birth, with as much dexterity as skill.”

327.content:
[Person: Marcellin Berthelot]
Quoted from La Grande Encyclopédie on the 'labyrinth of Solomon': a cabalistic figure at the head of some alchemical manuscripts, part of the magical traditions attributed to Solomon, a series of broken concentric circles.

Fulcanelli: “'a cabalistic figure found at the head of certain alchemical manuscripts, and which forms part of the magical traditions attributed to the name of Solomon.”

328.content:
[Person: Marie-Guillame Devergie]
Canseliet: physician and toxicologist who, with Orfila, observed the slow decomposition of the human body, whose stench finally turns almost aromatic.

Canseliet, in his preface: “the famous physicians, toxicologists besides, Mathieu-Joseph Orfila and Marie-Guillame Devergie, on the slow and progressive decomposition of the human body.”

329.content:
[Term: Mars]
Planetary name of iron: 'And of iron Mars is the figure'. The Cosmopolite: Mars converts easily into Venus but not the reverse, the virtues of planets descending. On the sarcophagus of the north portal, Mars and Venus stand on either side of the Sun. Canseliet quotes Philalèthe: the purgation succeeds 'if Saturn has seen his image in the mirror of Mars'; the text does not explain this.

Fulcanelli: “And Mars of iron [is] the figure.” / “even experience teaches us that Mars is easily converted into Venus, and not Venus into Mars, as being lower by one sphere.”

330.content:
[Person: Martigny]
Author of the Dictionnaire des Antiquités chrétiennes (art. Eucharistie, 2nd ed., p. 291), who reproduces a Catacomb painting of a fish carrying a basket of loaves and a red object; the basket is the same hieroglyph as the galette.

Fulcanelli: “Martigny indeed reproduces a curious painting from the Catacombs showing a fish swimming in the waves and carrying on its back a basket holding loaves and a red object”

331.content:
[Person: Martyrius]
An Armenian bishop and traveller of the 15th century whose text attests that cathedrals were gilded and painted; he said the porch of Notre-Dame de Paris shone like the entrance to paradise, with purple, rose, azure, silver and gold.

Fulcanelli: “This author says that the porch of Notre-Dame de Paris shone like the entrance to paradise.”

332.content:
[Term: Massacre of the Innocents]
Abraham the Jew's fourth figure shows soldiers killing children of two mothers, the blood gathered in a vat where sun and moon come to bathe; there are seven innocents dead. Fulcanelli recognises in the Bath of the stars relief the simplified allegory of the Massacre of the Innocents dear to Flamel. Its meaning: the universal Spirit, as Sulphur, is the agent of metallic tinctures; this red 'blood' of the children is had only by breaking down what nature joined, so the body must die to release its soul. A window of the Sainte-Chapelle on this subject is given as a specimen.

Fulcanelli: “But this Spirit, this red blood of the children, can only be obtained by decomposing what nature had first assembled in them.”

333.content:
[Term: Master Pierre du Coignet]
A devil figure with a huge mouth, under the rood-screen at the corner of the choir enclosure of Notre-Dame, where the faithful put out their candles; the people's name for it puzzled archaeologists. It represented the initial matter as Lucifer and was the symbol of the cornerstone, 'maîtresse pierre du coignet'.

Fulcanelli: “The people called this image Master Pierre du Coignet, which never failed to puzzle the archaeologists.”

334.content:
[Person: Mathieu-Joseph Orfila]
Canseliet: famous physician and toxicologist who, with Devergie, at the start of the Second Empire, observed the slow decomposition of the human body, ending in a residue with an almost aromatic smell; Canseliet compares this with the old masters' passage from stench to perfume.

Canseliet, in his preface: “the famous physicians, toxicologists besides, Mathieu-Joseph Orfila and Marie-Guillame Devergie, on the slow and progressive decomposition of the human body.”

335.content:
[Term: Matrass]
At the Hôtel Lallemant, what the guide calls a pestle held by the figure in the 'kitchen' is in fact a long-necked matrass, like chemists' balloons. This secret vessel is called philosophical egg and Green Lion; G. Aurach's manuscript and the third figure of the Toison d'Or show a glass matrass half full of green liquor. An inverted gold matrass, dropping silver tears, crowns the escutcheon of saint Thomas Aquinas.

Fulcanelli: “what the figure in question holds is in reality a long-necked matrass, like those our chemists use”

336.content:
[Term: Matter]
The cathedral rests on alchemy, which studies the transformations of the original substance, elementary Matter, a word the text derives from Latin materea, root mater, mother. The Virgin-Mother, without her veil, personifies the primitive substance used by the creative Principle. An anonymous author quoted says the Philosophers were right to hide this mystery from those who value things only by their uses, for if they knew the Matter, which God took pleasure in hiding in things that seem useful to them, they would no longer esteem it.

Fulcanelli: “For the Virgin-Mother, stripped of her symbolic veil, is nothing other than the personification of the primitive substance which the creative Principle of all that is used to carry out its designs.”

337.content:
[Term: May Dew]
Stated: the name the Sages gave to the condensation of the universal spirit, the mineral blood needed to animate the fixed body of gold, because it forms in humid form only at night, under a clear sky and calm air, and most abundantly in the earth's spring. The text adds that Maia was mother of Hermes and May the month of Mary, and that this dew is easily extracted from a particular, abject, despised body; this is the highest secret, the Verbum dimissum of the Trevisan, the Lost Word of the medieval freemasons. The soul extracted from the dying body is called 'vie métallique et Rosée céleste'. Thomas Corneille says the Rose-Croix masters were called Brothers of the Cooked Dew. May Dew is one name of the Green Lion. At Amiens an Adept watches the celestial dew fall on a mass (fleece, or Magnesia, the philosophical Magnet). Identified with the Green Lion (e357).

Fulcanelli: “the Sages, for these combined reasons, gave it the name of May Dew.” / “the mineral blood they needed to animate the fixed and inert body of gold was only a condensation of the universal spirit, soul of all things”

Identified in the text with: Green Lion

338.content:
[Person: Melampus]
Said to have shared the Language of the Birds with Tiresias; called a fictitious person whose name speaks eloquently. Named again among the few able to understand.

Fulcanelli: “But for some self-styled cabalists, Jewish or Christian, richer in pretension than in knowledge, how many Tiresiases, Thaleses or Melampuses are there able to understand these things?”

339.content:
[Term: Mercury]
The volatile principle and, prepared, the philosophers' water. The serpent on the golden rod figures Mercury 'in its first state' absorbing the bodily sulphur; the result, keeping the name Philosophical Mercury, needs only graduated cooking to become red sulphur, Elixir, universal Medicine. Mixing two waters yields a third that does not wet the hands, called Mercury or Sulphur. The cock is the volatile portion drawn from the subject (the oak), named Mercury though unlike common quicksilver; a dry water. 'Our' mercury differs from vulgar quicksilver; the old man of the seventh medallion is 'our Mercury', the secret agent, identified with Saturn. Kermès equals Hermès, i.e. Mercury; the prepared mercury must have the power of tinting. The scallop designates the principle Mercury, called Traveller or Pilgrim. Canseliet: star first seen in the 'mirror of the art or mercury'.

Fulcanelli: “That is our famous spring whose clear water flows at the foot of the sacred tree so venerated by the Druids, and which the ancient philosophers named Mercury, though it has no appearance of common quicksilver.” / “This reptile is the type of Mercury in its first state, and the golden rod the bodily sulphur added to it.”

Identified in the text with: Fountain of Life, Kermes

340.content:
[Term: Mercury alone]
Maxim that the Work can be done by mercury alone. 'In our Work, the Philosophers affirm, Mercury alone suffices'. Mercury contains in itself everything needed for the work and is the only matter required. On a Lallemant ceiling panel (mercury below, the Absolute above) Fulcanelli reads a simple procedure of one way, one matter, one operation, and cites 'He who knows how to make the Work by mercury alone has found what is most perfect' as the claim of the most famous authors. The same sentence closes the letter to Fulcanelli, adding 'that is, has received the light and accomplished the Magistery'.

Fulcanelli: “'In our Work,' the Philosophers affirm, 'Mercury alone suffices.'” / “It is important, before undertaking the practice, to know that mercury contains in itself all that is necessary for the work.”

341.content:
[Person: Michael Maier]
Canseliet says the Saint Marcel legend corresponds exactly to the 50th emblem of Maier's Atalanta Fugiens, where the dragon entwines a mature clothed woman lying inert in her violated grave.

Canseliet, in his preface: “It corresponds exactly to the 50th emblem of Michel Maier, in his Atalanta Fugiens”

342.content:
[Term: Microcosm]
Our microcosm is a tiny, imperfect particle of the macrocosm; we invent nothing, all is in all. Canseliet places the 'family drama' of mother and child in the alchemical-physical microcosm and speaks of the artist separating light from darkness in his 'petit monde'. The solar-cycle diagram at Hendaye joins the signs of macrocosm and microcosm.

Fulcanelli: “Our microcosm is only a tiny particle of the macrocosm, animate, thinking, more or less imperfect.”

343.content:
[Term: Millenarianism]
The Hendaye cross is called the most singular monument of primitive millenarianism, the rarest symbolic rendering of chiliasm. The doctrine, first accepted then opposed by Origen, saint Denys of Alexandria and saint Jerome, though never condemned by the Church, belonged to the esoteric traditions of the ancient philosophy of Hermes.

Fulcanelli: “It is known that this doctrine, first accepted then opposed by Origen, Saint Denys of Alexandria and Saint Jerome, although the Church had not condemned it, was part of the esoteric traditions of the ancient philosophy of Hermes.”

344.content:
[Person: Minotaur]
Theseus's combat with it was once shown at the centre of the Chartres labyrinth. Tristan's killing of the Morhout matches Theseus's killing of the Minotaur, a hieroglyph of making the Green Lion.

Fulcanelli: “At the centre of this figure one formerly saw the combat of Theseus and the Minotaur.” / “Tristan fights and kills the Morhout, Theseus the Minotaur.”

345.content:
[Term: Mirror of the Art]
Name of the first matter the artist must choose. On the second Notre-Dame medallion the Initiator holds a mirror: the mirror is the beginning of the work, the Tree of Life its end. Moras de Respour: through it one learned how metals are composed in the earth; the Cosmopolite: a mirror in which the whole world is seen; Basile Valentin: the body of Vitriol is a 'Mirror of philosophical Science' where Mercury, Sun and Moon shine. The sixth medallion's bust of Nature reflected in a mirror is the hieroglyph of the subject of the Sages. Canseliet: the hermetic star is first seen in the 'mirror of the art or mercury'; the star on the Virgin is an image reflected by the 'mirror of Wisdom'.

Fulcanelli: “Alchemically, the first matter, the one the artist must choose to begin the Work, is called the Mirror of the Art.” / “The mirror symbolises the beginning of the work, the tree of life marks its end, and the horn of plenty its result.”

Identified in the text with: First matter

346.content:
[Term: Modhallan]
Where the Arab authors place the fountain Holmat; the text says the root of the term means 'dark and gloomy Sea', which marks the elemental confusion the Sages attribute to their Chaos or first matter.

Fulcanelli: “They place the famous spring in the Modhallan, a term whose root means dark and gloomy Sea, which well marks the elemental confusion the Sages attribute to their Chaos or first matter.”

347.comment: Monograph on the Cathedral Church of Amiens (work; e445)
347.content:
[Work: Monograph on the Cathedral Church of Amiens (Monographie de l'Eglise Cathédrale d'Amiens)]
Work of G. Durand, Paris, A. Picard, 1901, source of the readings of the Amiens reliefs that Fulcanelli disputes.

Fulcanelli: “G. Durand, Monograph on the Cathedral Church of Amiens. Paris, A. Picard, 1901.”

348.content:
[Place: Monsieur Legris]
Popular name of a tall, narrow stone statue that stood on the Parvis of Notre-Dame, holding a book in one hand and a serpent in the other, part of a monumental fountain bearing a Latin distich on the Goddess who prepared the eternal waters. The people also called it Vendeur de gris and Grand Jeûneur de Notre-Dame. Fulcanelli calls Amédée de Ponthieu's explanation the best: a sacred monolith which the ancients named Phœbigène, son of Apollo (glossed 'engendered of the sun or of gold'), which the people later called Maître Pierre, meaning master stone, stone of power (glossed as the cornerstone already discussed), and messire Legris when gris meant fire, particularly firedamp, will-o'-the-wisp. Its features were variously read as Aesculapius, Mercury, the god Terminus, Archambaud, Guillaume de Paris, Jesus Christ or Saint Genevieve. It was removed in 1748 when the Parvis was enlarged. Fulcanelli later recalls having held back the esoteric sense of Saint Christopher when speaking of his statues and of this monolith.

Fulcanelli: “the people later named it Master Peter, meaning master stone, stone of power” / “it was also named Messire Legris, at a time when gris meant fire, and particularly firedamp, will-o'-the-wisp”

Identified in the text with: Cornerstone

349.content:
[Term: Moon]
In the symbolism of planetary metals the Virgin is the Moon, receiving the Sun's rays and keeping them secretly; she dispenses the passive substance that the solar spirit animates. On the disk of Philosophy, sun and moon (the moon hammered away) are sulphur and mercury, parents of the stone according to Hermes. The cow is consecrated to the moon; bull and cow, sun and moon, sulphur and mercury denote the contrary primitive natures before conjunction. The Moon stands for silver; in the Cosmopolite's scheme it is the lowest planet, corresponding to Saturn, the highest. The Virgin stands on the lunar crescent, always in blue, the colour of the night star. In Ceres's cult the Minister of the Altar represented the Moon.

Fulcanelli: “In the symbolism of the planetary metals, she is the Moon, which receives the rays of the Sun and keeps them secretly in her bosom.” / “The bull and the cow, the sun and the moon, sulphur and mercury are therefore hieroglyphs of identical meaning”

350.content:
[Person: Moras de Respour]
Cited for the name Mirror of Art given to the first matter: philosophers understand it so because through it one learned how the metals are composed in the veins of the earth. The footnote gives his work as Rares Expériences sur l'Esprit minéral, Paris, Langlois et Barbin, 1668, under the name De Respour.

Fulcanelli: “Commonly among the Philosophers, says Moras de Respour, it is meant by the Mirror of Art, because it is chiefly through it that one has learned the composition of the metals in the veins of the earth”

351.content:
[Person: Morien]
Cited master. Per an anonymous 18th-century manuscript Fulcanelli quotes, Morien says the corrupted matter must show some acidity and a smell of the sepulchre. Flamel quotes 'the wise Morien': this stone that is not a stone is animate, with power to procreate. Canseliet: with Raymond Lulle, he says the foul odour of the dark dissolution is followed by the sweetest perfume.

Fulcanelli: “Morien says: one must notice some acidity in it, and it must have some smell of the sepulchre.” / “Wherefore, says the wise Morien, this stone that is no stone is animate, having the power to procreate and engender.”

352.content:
[Term: Morning star]
Fulcanelli glosses Lucifer as 'who bears the light, — the morning star', the human form given to the initial matter of the Work in the devil figure Maistre Pierre du Coignet, symbol of the cornerstone. The letter to Fulcanelli says whoever has saluted the morning star is fascinated by 'this false light'. Canseliet, noting the apparent contradiction, explains: the star is first seen in the 'mirror of the art' or mercury before the chemical heaven; the celestial Virgin is called stella matutina, but that star is only an image reflected in the mirror of Wisdom, attesting the other. Limojon de Saint-Didier tells seekers to steer their route 'by the sight of the étoile du nord'. See also Star (e024).

Fulcanelli: “Now this figure, meant to represent the initial matter of the Work, humanised in the guise of Lucifer (who bears the light, — the morning star), was the symbol of our cornerstone”

Canseliet, in his preface: “One may almost say that whoever has saluted the morning star has lost forever the use of sight and reason, for he is fascinated by this false light and hurled into the abyss…”

Identified in the text with: Lucifer

353.content:
[Person: Mullachius]
Named as the last editor of Chalcidius, and the source for the statement that Chalcidius professed the worship of the Greek, Roman and foreign gods.

Fulcanelli: “the philosopher Chalcidius, who, as Mullachius, the last of his editors, says, professed that one should worship the gods of Greece, the gods of Rome and foreign Gods”

354.content:
[Term: Multiplication]
Cambriel says the multiplication of the white or red Sulphur is not shown on the Saint Anne pillar; Fulcanelli disagrees: multiplication is done only with mercury, the patient in the Work, by successive cookings or fixations, so its sign should be sought on the dragon, image of mercury. The solar circles covering the dragon mean it can transmute in quantity, a power gained by later cookings with the Sulphur or philosophical Gold, which make up the multiplications. The Chevalier Inconnu speaks of a third multiplication by adding the soul of the world.

Fulcanelli: “Multiplication, indeed, can only be achieved with the help of mercury, which plays the part of patient in the Work, and by successive cookings or fixations.”

355.content:
[Place: Musée de Cluny]
Where the original St Marcel pillar of Notre-Dame was kept, near the stair to the frigidarium of the Thermes de Julien. A later note says the itinerary is no longer valid: for about six years the pillar has been back in Notre-Dame's north tower, with most of the dragon amputated. Canseliet: Fulcanelli studied the statue there; it now sits in the north tower; the museum did not exist in the 16th century and has held it for about a century.

Fulcanelli: “Cross the Seine, enter the Cluny museum and you will have the satisfaction of finding it there, near the stair leading to the frigidarium of the Baths of Julian.”

356.content:
[Work: The Silent Book (Mutus Liber)]
Fulcanelli calls the Gothic temple itself a 'mutus Liber', of which the alchemy figure is the title-page. The gesture of silence of the figures of the Mutus Liber (and of Harpocrates) is not on the St Marcel statue. Its fishermen in a boat try to catch a dolphin with net and hook.

Fulcanelli: “Such is the chapter heading of this mutus Liber that is the Gothic temple; the frontispiece of this occult Bible with massive leaves of stone” / “It is, moreover, a dolphin that the fishermen in their boat in the Mutus Liber try to catch with net and hook.”

357.content:
[Term: Mysterious Fountain]
A bas-relief on the left buttress of the central portal shows the alchemist discovering the Mysterious Fountain described by the Trévisan: a stream of living water bubbling from an old hollow oak, its dissolving virtue and volatile essence attested by a bird (pl. IV). It is the powerful dissolvent able to penetrate all metals, gold above all, and to accomplish the whole work with the dissolved body. Mythology calls it Libethra; the Arab authors Holmat. Abraham the Jew's third figure shows it at the foot of a hollow oak. The tradition of the Fountain of Life or Youth is materialized in church wells. A quoted text calls it the Fountain of Trévisan, bath of King and Queen. Fulcanelli identifies the source at the foot of the sacred oak with what the philosophers named Mercury; the mercury is called Fountain of Youth.

Fulcanelli: “Of what nature is this powerful dissolvent, able to penetrate all metals, gold in particular, and to accomplish, with the help of the dissolved body, the whole great work?” / “That is our famous spring whose clear water flows at the foot of the sacred tree so venerated by the Druids, and which the old philosophers named Mercury”

358.content:
[Term: Mystic almond]
On Romanesque tympana Jesus sits, left hand on a book, right hand blessing, separated from the four animals by the ellipse called the mystic almond; this is the medieval form of the four phases of the cycle.

Fulcanelli: “There Jesus is shown seated, his left hand resting on a book, the right raised in blessing, and separated from the four animals escorting him by the ellipse called the mystic almond.”

359.content:
[Term: Natures]
The two contrary substances the alchemist works and joins. On the cubic socle of the Saint-Marcel pillar two raised bezants are the metallic matters or natures, subject and dissolvent, with which the Work must begin; the pair of natures, once united, yields the Saturn of the Sages, which the text calls an anagram of natures. The centre of the labyrinth is where the hard combat of the two natures takes place. The Sages figured the two natures by the Eagle (aerial, volatile force) and the Lion (earthly, fixed force), which fight until they become one body, the animated Mercury. At Notre-Dame they are shown as two quarrelling children, one dropping a pot, the other a stone. Bull and cow, sun and moon, sulphur and mercury all designate the contrary primitive natures before their conjunction. The two wheels of Amiens may also be read as the two natures in the conversion, a thesis the text says Pernety adopts.

Fulcanelli: “these are the metallic matters or natures, subject and dissolvent, with which the Work must be begun” / “the pair of natures the alchemist works, whose union yields the Saturn of the Sages, an anagrammatic name for natures”

Identified in the text with: Saturn

360.content:
[Person: Naxagoras]
Canseliet: with Blaise de Vigenère, he wrote at length on the value of a long preliminary coction of lead.

Canseliet, in his preface: “Blaise de Vigenère and Naxagoras, for instance, dwelt on the advisability of a long preliminary coction.”

361.content:
[Person: Nicolas Flamel]
Adept to whom the book of the Figures of Abraham the Jew is said to have belonged, displayed in his scribe's shop; its third figure shows the hollow oak and the fountain; he says 'Note this oak'. Abraham's serpent on a golden rod is in that book. He figured the combat of the two natures as eagle and lion and favoured the allegory of the Massacre of the Innocents. He covered his buildings with emblems: the portal of Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie (1389), houses for the poor (1407, 1410), the Saint-Gervais chapel, arcades at the Innocents' charnel (1389, 1407). Quoted on the hidden, despised stone; his parabolic pilgrimage to 'Monsieur Jacques de Galice'. Called 'the charitable Flamel'.

Fulcanelli: “Flamel liked to cover with emblems and hieroglyphs the buildings he raised on every side.” / “There is a hidden stone, concealed and buried in the depth of a fountain, which is vile, abject and not at all prized”

362.content:
[Person: Nicolas Rollin]
Chancellor of Philippe le Bon, founder of the hospital of Beaune, on whose tiled floor his motto was painted in 1477. The motto, given as a rebus ('Seule'), showed his science by the characteristic sign of the Work, the single star.

Fulcanelli: “This motto, presented in the manner of a rebus — Seule ('alone') — showed its owner's science by the characteristic sign of the Work, the unique, the single star.”

363.content:
[Person: Nicolas Valois]
Cited author (works with Nicolas Grosparmy, Arsenal manuscript). On the ladder held by Alchemy at Notre-Dame: patience is the ladder of the Philosophers, humility the door of their garden. On the subject: a stone that is a stone and not a stone, mineral, vegetable and animal, found everywhere. His epigraph opens the 1957 preface: the first who transmuted had no book but followed nature.

Fulcanelli: “'Patience is the ladder of the Philosophers,' Valois tells us, 'and humility is the door of their garden; for whoever perseveres without pride and without envy, God will show him mercy.'” / “There is a stone of great virtue, says Nicolas Valois in turn, and it is called stone and is not stone, and is mineral, vegetable and animal, which is found in all places and at all times, and with all persons.”

364.content:
[Term: Nostoc]
A gelatinous green cryptogam found in the countryside, swollen with night dew in spring mornings and vanishing in the sun; hence also called trémelles. Its sudden appearance, absorption of water, green colour and soft consistency let the Philosophers take it as hieroglyph of their matter; the mass absorbing celestial dew in an Amiens quatrefoil is such a heap, symbol of the Sages' mineral Magnesia. Its other names (Archée céleste, Crachat de Lune, Beurre de terre, Graisse de rosée, Vitriol végétal, Flos coeli) designated only their mineral principle; taken literally by ignorant puffers it discredited alchemy. The text derives the word from Greek νυξ, Latin nox: a thing born at night, needing night to develop and workable only at night; the following paragraphs argue that generation requires the total absence of sunlight.

Fulcanelli: “This word comes from the Greek νυξ, νυχτος, corresponding to the Latin nox, noctis, night. It is therefore a thing that is born at night, needs the night to develop, and can be worked only at night.” / “All these features combined — sudden appearance, absorption of water and swelling, green colour, soft and sticky consistency — allowed the Philosophers to take this alga as the hieroglyphic type of their matter.”

365.content:
[Place: Nostre-Dame de dessoubs terre]
A statuette of the Virgin in an underground gallery of the Paris Observatory, placed there in 1671 and invoked by this name in verses carved at its feet, as reported by Camille Flammarion. Fulcanelli says this little-known Paris Virgin personifies in the capital the mysterious subject of Hermes and seems a replica of the Chartres Virgin, 'la benoiste Dame souterraine'.

Fulcanelli: “This little-known Parisian Virgin, who personifies in the capital the mysterious subject of Hermes, appears to be a replica of the Chartres one, the blessed Lady beneath the earth.”

366.content:
[Place: Notre-Dame d'Amiens]
Its central porch, the porche du Sauveur, nearly reproduces the hermetic motifs of the Paris portal and their order, with shields instead of discs; Guillaume le Parisien's work influenced it. Built by Robert de Luzarches, Thomas and Renault de Cormont, and well preserved. Its labyrinth had a gold bar and half-circle figuring sunrise, later copper, then lost; 'Ariadne, the mystic spider, escaped from Amiens' left only the trace of her web. It keeps a bas-relief Saint Christopher.

Fulcanelli: “The singular fact, worth noting, is that the central porch of Notre-Dame d'Amiens — porch of the Saviour — is an almost faithful reproduction not only of the motifs that adorn the Paris portal” / “Ariadne, the mystic spider, escaped from Amiens, has left only the trace of her web on the pavement of the choir…”

367.content:
[Place: Notre-Dame de l'Epine]
A Gothic basilica in the Marne which, the text says, still has inside it a miraculous well called the Well of the Holy Virgin, an example of the sacred wells.

Fulcanelli: “There still exists today inside the Gothic basilica of Notre-Dame de l'Epine (Marne) a miraculous well, called the Well of the Holy Virgin”

368.content:
[Place: Notre-Dame de Limoux]
Church in the Aude with a well in the middle of the choir whose water, it is said, heals all illnesses. It bears the inscription 'Omnis qui bibit hanc aquam, si fidem addit, savus erit', which the book renders: whoever drinks this water, if he adds faith, will be well.

Fulcanelli: “Whoever drinks this water, if he joins faith to it, will be healthy. (the book's gloss of the Latin)”

369.content:
[Place: Notre-Dame de Paris]
The type chosen for the hermetic study of the cathedral. A 'philosophical church', one of the most perfect specimens; Victor Hugo called it the most satisfying summary of the hermetic science. Fourteenth-century alchemists met there weekly on Saturn's day. Dedicated to the Virgin-Mother; it keeps its alchemist on the gallery; its rose window keeps the original colours of the porch medallions, thanks to Guillaume de Paris. Its porches are read in PARIS.1–PARIS.7. Canseliet: setting of the St Marcel statue controversy.

Fulcanelli: “In this respect Notre-Dame de Paris, a philosophical church, is beyond question one of the most perfect specimens, and, as Victor Hugo said, 'the most satisfying summary of the hermetic science” / “Notre-Dame de Paris, indeed, keeps its alchemist.”

370.content:
[Place: Notre-Dame de Rocamadour]
Miraculous madonna and goal of a famous pilgrimage, already visited in 1166, traced by tradition to Zacchaeus; a wooden statuette blackened by time, clad in a robe of silver strips, over the altar of a chapel built in 1479; a quoted source links it to the hermit Saint Amateur or Amadour. At Rocamadour also stand a giant Saint Christopher, an old iron-bound coffer and a sword fragment said to be from Durandal.

Fulcanelli: “It is a wooden statuette, blackened by time, wrapped in a robe of silver strips that holds together its worm-eaten remains.”

371.content:
[Place: Notre-Dame de Strasbourg]
In its nave, per Witkowski, a capital shows a satirical procession of a pig with a holy-water stoup, asses in priestly robes, monkeys and a fox in a shrine: the Procession of the Fox or Feast of the Ass.

Fulcanelli: “the bas-relief of one of the capitals of the great pillars shows a satirical procession in which one makes out a pig carrying a holy-water stoup, followed by asses in priestly vestments and monkeys bearing various attributes of religion”

372.content:
[Place: Notre-Dame du Puy]
Black Virgin whose limbs are not visible; her robe, fastened at the neck and widening without a fold to the foot, gives her the figure of a triangle; it is decorated with vine stocks and ears of wheat, allegories of the eucharistic bread and wine, and at the level of the navel shows the Child's head, crowned as richly as the mother's.

Fulcanelli: “she takes the figure of a triangle, through her robe which girds her at the neck and flares without a fold down to the foot.”

373.content:
[Place: Notre-Dame-de-Confession]
Celebrated Black Virgin of the Saint-Victor crypts at Marseille, a fine specimen of ancient statuary, holding a sceptre in the right hand and crowned with a triple-fleuron crown (pl. I).

Fulcanelli: “This figure, full of nobility, holds a sceptre in her right hand, and her brow is girt with a crown of three fleurons”

374.content:
[Place: Notre-Dame-sous-Terre]
Black Virgin in the crypt of Chartres, seated on a throne whose socle bears Virgini parituræ. With her, Chartres passes for the oldest pilgrimage; originally an antique statuette of Isis 'carved before Jesus Christ', later replaced by a wooden statue burnt in 1793; the present image dates only from the end of the 18th century. The Paris Virgin of the Observatory seems a replica of her, 'la benoiste Dame souterraine'.

Fulcanelli: “one, designated by the expressive title of Our Lady under the Earth, in the crypt, sits on a throne whose socle bears the inscription already noted: Virgini parituræ”

375.content:
[Work: New Chemical Light (Nouvelle Lumière chymique)]
Work given in a footnote under the title Cosmopolite ou Nouvelle Lumière chymique. Its parts are cited: the Traité du Soufre (Paris, d'Houry, 1649) for the mirror in which the whole world is seen; the Traité du Mercure (Paris, Jean d'Houry, 1649) for the order of the planets and their mutations; and the Traité du Sel for the weights of water and earth and for the fish swimming in the philosophical sea (Paris, J. D'Houry, 1669).

Fulcanelli: “Cosmopolite or New Chemical Light. Treatise on Salt, p. 76. Paris, J. D'Houry, 1669.”

376.content:
[Person: Noël du Fail]
Quoted: Notre-Dame de Paris was the great meeting place of such 'academicians', the alchemists; source: Propos rustiques…, ch. X.

Fulcanelli: “and Noël du Fail says that 'the great meeting place of such academicians was at Notre-Dame de Paris'”

377.comment: Hail, O Cross, our only hope (work; e527)
377.content:
[Work: Hail, O Cross, our only hope (O crux ave spes unica)]
Carved on the Hendaye cross as OCRUXAVES / PESUNICA. Read as written, 'pes' (foot) with feminine 'unica' breaks grammar; the careful cutting excludes a slip, so the apparent error is a deliberate sign. The S, displaced on purpose, shows that the line must be read in the language of the gods or birds, by the rules of 'Diplomatique': read the Latin in French, with interchangeable vowels. The result: 'Il est écrit que la vie se réfugie en un seul espace' — there is a land where death will not reach man at the time of the double cataclysm. The text gives the result, not the step-by-step reading.

Fulcanelli: “Thus we receive this singular warning: It is written that life takes refuge in a single space, and we learn that there is a land where death will not reach man, at the terrible time of the double cataclysm.”

378.content:
[Term: Oak]
The water of the Mysterious Fountain springs from an old hollow oak; Flamel says 'Note this oak'; Abraham's third figure shows a fountain at the foot of a hollow oak. An oak branch on a Notre-Dame escutcheon reveals the material of the hermetic vessel; a quoted text reads the hollow oak as the oaken barrel in which the water is corrupted, and the vessel as of old oak. At Amiens the oak is the emblem of the subject from which the volatile cock is drawn. The old authors used the oak, by an à-peu-près, for the common name of the initial subject as found in the mine. Its gall leads via galla, Gallia, gallus to the cock, attribute of Mercury, and its kermès to Hermès. The old hermetic oak serves as mother to the secret mercury; a crown of oak leaves is the graphic sign of the subject's common name.

Fulcanelli: “you may say, without offending truth, that the old hermetic oak serves as mother to the secret mercury.” / “Now if we bring together three words of the same Latin family, galla, Gallia, gallus, we get gall, Gaul, cock.”

379.content:
[Term: Orient (East)]
Through Greek αρυω, rising of a star from the sea, αρυαν or ariane is the Orient, the rising sun, and also the magnet. Churches are oriented so that people entering from the West walk toward the side where the sun rises, the Orient, leaving darkness for light.

Fulcanelli: “walk straight to the sanctuary, facing the side where the sun rises, toward the Orient, Palestine, cradle of Christianity. They leave darkness and go toward the light.”

380.comment: The Original of the Desired Desire (work; e467)
380.content:
[Work: The Original of the Desired Desire (Original du Désir désiré)]
Work of Nicolas Flamel, also titled Thrésor de Philosophie (Paris, Hulpeau, 1629, p. 144); quoted among descriptions of the subject or first matter: a hidden, vile, despised stone in the depth of a fountain, given every name.

Fulcanelli: “There is an occult stone, hidden and buried in the depth of a fountain, which is vile, abject and not at all prized; and it is covered with dung and excrement”

381.content:
[Person: Osiris]
In Egyptian temples, a priest whispered to the candidate about to undergo the initiatory trials: 'Remember that Osiris is a black god!'. Portal, quoted by Dujols, says the black Osiris at the beginning of the funerary Ritual represents the soul's passage from night to day, from death to life. Horus fighting Typhon in the Osirian myth is listed among the combats figuring the making of the dissolvent.

Fulcanelli: “'Remember that Osiris is a black god!'”

382.content:
[Term: Our Lady]
Metropolitan cathedrals, dedicated to the Virgin Mary or Virgin-Mother, are popularly called Notre-Dame in France and Matrices in Sicily; they are temples to the Mother (Latin mater), the Matrone, a word corrupted into Madone (ma donna), my Lady, and by extension Our Lady. The Virgin-Mother, stripped of her symbolic veil, personifies the primitive substance.

Fulcanelli: “They are thus indeed temples dedicated to the Mother (Lat. mater, matris), to the Matron in the primitive sense, a word that by corruption became the Madonna (Lat. ma donna), my Lady, and by extension Our Lady.”

383.content:
[Person: P. H. Pfau]
Maker in 1702 of the alchemical stove whose paintings include an angler and a fine fish; the stove is kept at the Winterthur museum.

Fulcanelli: “Among the paintings of the alchemical stove made in 1702 by P. H. Pfau, one sees an angler coming out of the water and a fine fish.”

384.content:
[Term: Palace]
On the seventh lower medallion of Paris an old man, who is our Mercury, the secret agent, is about to cross the threshold of the mysterious Palace after tearing away its veil. The text says what the Palace stands for: living or philosophical gold, vile gold despised by the ignorant and hidden under rags. Entering it is the first step of practice, the discovery of the agent that reincrudates the fixed body; it is Philalethes' Entrance to the King's closed Palace. The interior of the Palace was once coloured purple, the old man green, a variant of the Green and Red Lions. At Amiens a fortified building may be the mysterious closed Palace of the king of the Art spoken of by Basile Valentin and Philalethes.

Fulcanelli: “As for the Palace, it represents living or philosophical gold, vile gold, despised by the ignorant, and hidden under rags that conceal it from the eyes”

385.content:
[Place: Palais Jacques-Cœur]
One of the two jewels of Bourges with the Hôtel Lallemant; once a true museum of hermetic emblems, its interior ruined by vandalism, only the façade kept in its original state. Built in the 15th century by Jacques Cœur; the scallop and heart recur on its decoration; the restored chapel is of little interest, and its most curious piece is the Tristan and Yseult corbel in the 'Trésor' room.

Fulcanelli: “Of the first, which was once a true museum of hermetic emblems, we shall say little.”

386.content:
[Person: Paracelsus]
Quoted from his Livre des Images on the colours of the Work: black is the root of the other colours; white follows black, yellow white, red yellow; matter reaching the fourth colour by reverberation is the tincture of things of its kind. Huginus à Barma says the old masters, Geber, Lulle, Paracelsus, each had his own process.

Fulcanelli: “Now, black is the root and origin of the other colours”

387.comment: Paraphrase of the First Epistle of Saint Peter (work; e164)
387.content:
[Work: Paraphrase of the First Epistle of Saint Peter (Paraphrase de la Première Epître de saint Pierre)]
Work by Amyraut (ch. II, v. 7), Saumur, Jean Lesnier, 1646, p. 27, source of the quotation on the corner stone.

Fulcanelli: “M. Amyraut, Paraphrase of the First Epistle of Saint Peter (ch. II, v. 7). Saumur, Jean Lesnier, 1646, p. 27.”

388.content:
[Person: Pegasus]
The text identifies the horse of the first lower medallion of Notre-Dame with the winged Pegasus of the fable, giving the root πηγη, 'spring'. Like it, Pegasus throws his riders, Perseus or Bellerophon, carries Perseus through the air to the Hesperides, and with a kick makes the Hippocrene spring gush on Mount Helicon. Perseus, mounted on Pegasus and killing the monster guarding Andromeda, is among the fables of the combat of the chemical bodies that yield the secret solvent.
