Fulcanelli: “The steed of Notre-Dame is the same as the winged Pegasus of the fable (root πηγη, spring).”

389.content:
[Person: Pernety]
Quoted: the Adepts say they draw their steel from the belly of Aries and also call this steel their magnet. In his Dictionnaire Mytho-Hermétique he does not cite the term 'Miroir de l'Art', either not knowing it or omitting it on purpose. He refuses to believe in two ways (dry and humid). He adopts the thesis that the two wheels of Amiens indicate the two natures in the conversion.

Fulcanelli: “The Adepts say they draw their steel from the belly of Aries, and they also call this steel their magnet.”

390.content:
[Person: Perseus]
Perseus is named with Bellerophon among the riders Pegasus throws, and Pegasus carries him through the air to the Hesperides. Perseus cutting off the Gorgon's head, and Perseus on Pegasus killing the monster that guarded Andromeda, belong to the many fables of the single combat of the chemical bodies whose combination gives the secret solvent; saint Michael, saint George and saint Marcel slaying the Dragon are called Christian replicas of him.

Fulcanelli: “saint Michael, saint George, saint Marcel slaying the Dragon, Christian replicas of Perseus killing the monster that guarded Andromeda, mounted on his horse Pegasus”

391.content:
[Person: Phidias]
Cited for his representation of Cybele seated on a throne between two lions, wearing a mural crown from which a veil descends.

Fulcanelli: “Phidias represents the goddess seated on a throne between two lions, with a mural crown on her head from which a veil descends.”

392.content:
[Person: Philalethes]
Adept often cited. The putrefaction must show 'fish eyes'; whoever knows the Regimen will be honoured by princes; the preparation of the flying Eagles is the first degree; seven to nine eagles are needed; the philosophical Mercury is the bird of Hermes, goose, swan or pheasant. In the Introitus, his way takes only a week. His Rules: tempered heat; one must boil, else it is digestion, not cooking. He describes the vessel by the Python fable; read the Philosophers 'with a grain of salt'. Canseliet: in his Entrée ouverte he dwelt most on practice and signals the hermetic star.

Fulcanelli: “'Whoever knows the Regimen,' writes Philalethes, 'will be honoured by the princes and great ones of the earth.'” / “For I assure you that if we do not make it boil, we can never call our work a cooking, but a digestion.”

393.content:
[Term: Philosopher by fire]
Jacques Cœur used a profusion of chosen symbols to accredit his 'true or supposed' quality of philosophe par le feu. Interpreted: an alchemist who practises the Work, as the next paragraph concludes he did.

Fulcanelli: “we must recognize that Jacques Cœur did everything to accredit, by a profusion of chosen symbols, his true or supposed quality of philosopher by fire.”

394.content:
[Term: Philosophers (Sages)]
The text's usual name for the alchemical masters and authors, also called Sages. They speak plainly only to turn the profane away, so their clear descriptions of colours are to be distrusted. The Sibyl defines a Philosopher as one who knows how to make glass. The disciple should not despise the works of the old Philosophers but study the classic texts. In the first preface Canseliet says no Philosopher, to his knowledge, has noted the colour that is the key.

Fulcanelli: “You will have read, in several places in your books, that the Philosophers speak clearly only when they wish to keep the profane away from their Round Table.” / “The Sibyl, asked what a Philosopher was, answered: 'It is he who knows how to make glass.'”

395.content:
[Term: Philosophers' stone]
The end product of the Work. The ancient alchemists called it the Absolute. Obtained as a red crystal or powder, volatile and fusible, it becomes penetrating and able to 'heal lepers', that is, transmute base metals into gold. The despised subject becomes the Tree of Life, Elixir or philosophers' stone, giving knowledge, fortune and health. Stone of the Philosophers and Philosophers' Stone are alike in kind and origin, the first raw, the second fully cooked and digested; the Golden Fleece names both the prepared matter and the result. The third repetition of one operation gives it as medicine of the third order, containing the virtues of Sulphur and Elixir multiplied. A legend says Guillaume de Paris hid it in a pillar of Notre-Dame.

Fulcanelli: “Stone of the Philosophers and Philosophers' Stone are therefore two similar things, in kind and in origin, but the first is raw, while the second, derived from it, is perfectly cooked and digested.” / “the philosophers' stone becomes penetrating and fit to heal lepers, that is, to transmute common metals into gold”

Identified in the text with: Absolute, Elixir, Tree of Life

396.content:
[Term: Philosophical earth]
At the start of the second work, while the Rebis decomposes in the Athanor, the seeds enclosed in the philosophical earth undergo the fermenting influence of moisture; this is the reign of Saturn. Canseliet: the alchemical earth, chaotic and inert, contains the philosophical heaven; separating the pure from the gross lets one know what the philosophical earth is.

Fulcanelli: “embryonic period in which the seeds, enclosed in the bosom of the philosophical earth, undergo the fermenting influence of moisture.”

397.content:
[Term: Philosophical Egg]
Stated: by 'œuf' the Sages mean their compound placed in its proper vessel, ready to undergo the transformations the fire will cause; it is an egg because its shell holds the Rebis, made of white and red in a proportion like that of a bird's egg. The secret vessel is generally called 'œuf philosophique' and 'Lion vert'. As to form, the egg may be spherical or ovoid, of clear transparent glass without bubbles, thick-walled (Lorraine glass is recommended), with a neck that can be sealed at the enameller's lamp. The Paris relief shows a section of the Athanor with the inner apparatus that supports the philosophical egg. The black colour follows the perfect mixing of 'les matières de l'Œuf'. The Philosophical Mercury is called 'l'oeuf vitriolé', needing only graduated cooking. At Amiens the tower of the 'church' is the secret furnace holding the philosophical egg; its contents end calcined, granular or powdery. The masters called the shell of the egg 'secretum secretorum'.

Fulcanelli: “By the term egg, the Sages mean their compound, placed in its proper vessel, and ready to undergo the transformations that the action of fire will cause in it.”

398.content:
[Term: Philosophical gold]
The dragon gains its power of transmuting in quantity by cookings with the Sulphur or philosophical Gold, the multiplications. The Palace of the seventh Paris medallion stands for living or philosophical gold, vile and despised. The Red Lion is the Green Lion brought to the quality of hermetic gold. The pure part of the subject is the dyeing Hermes that carries the mystic gold. In the RERE enigma, one RE is a dry matter, philosophical gold, the other a wet matter, philosophical mercury. The text distinguishes common gold, which has suffered neither exaltation nor transfusion.

Fulcanelli: “RE, a dry matter, philosophical gold; RE, a wet matter, philosophical mercury; RERE or REBIS, a double matter”

399.content:
[Term: Philosophical Mercury]
Shown on the Paris stylobate as a serpent coiled on a golden rod, the caduceus. The serpent is Mercury in its first state, dissolving and absorbing the metallic sulphur; the golden rod is the corporeal sulphur added; the resulting homogeneous body keeps the name Philosophical Mercury and the image of the caduceus. Stated: it is the matter or compound of the first order, 'l'oeuf vitriolé', which needs only graduated cooking to become red sulphur, then Elixir, then Universal Medicine. Philalèthe (quoted) calls it the bird of Hermes, Goose, Swan or Pheasant. It results from the absorption of a certain part of sulphur by a determined quantity of mercury, so the proportions must be known if one works by the old way. Sabine Stuart de Chevalier's claim to get it by dissolving common mercury is rejected. Lenglet-Dufresnoy (quoted) says the short way is done by the 'double mercure philosophique' in eight days. In the RERE reading, one RE is the humid matter, philosophical mercury. 'Celui qui sait faire l'Œuvre par le seul mercure a trouvé ce qu'il y a de plus parfait'. Identified with the Bird of Hermes (e317).

Fulcanelli: “but the resulting body, homogeneous and perfectly prepared, keeps the name of Philosophical Mercury and the image of the caduceus.” / “It is the matter or compound of the first order, the vitriolated egg, which now needs only a graduated cooking to change first into red sulphur, then into Elixir”

Identified in the text with: Bird of Hermes

400.content:
[Person: Philostratus]
Teller of the wonders of Apollonius of Tyana, which Fulcanelli says are of a chemical order.

Fulcanelli: “Hence the wonders told by Philostratus, being of a chemical order, cannot surprise us.”

401.content:
[Term: Phoenix]
In the Work: the cock, the volatile and living portion (Mercury) extracted from the subject, 'can become the Phoenix', but must first take the provisional fixity figured by the fox. Canseliet uses the 'phoenix of the poets' for the philosopher whose old self is consumed by the flame of Revelation and from whose ashes a new personality is reborn, 'so at least the philosophical Tradition will have it'.

Fulcanelli: “This cock, volatile as it is, can become the Phoenix. Yet it must first take on the state of provisional fixity characterised by the symbol of the goupil, our hermetic fox.”

Canseliet, in his preface: “And from these ashes, like the phoenix of the poets, a new personality is reborn.”

402.content:
[Term: Phrygian cap]
The alchemist of Notre-Dame wears it as the attribute of Adeptship. A footnote says it was worn by the sans-culottes as a protective talisman and was the distinctive sign of Initiates; Pierre Dujols is quoted that in the Eleusinian grade of Epopt a red cap was set on the candidate's head, that this headgear, called libéria in the Mithraic rites, once marked freed slaves, and was a masonic symbol and supreme mark of Initiation.

Fulcanelli: “The Phrygian cap, worn by the sans-culottes and serving as a kind of protective talisman amid the revolutionary slaughters, was the distinctive sign of the Initiates.” / “Cover yourself with this cap; it is worth more than a king's crown.”

403.content:
[Work: Natural Philosophy of Metals (Phylosophie naturelle de Métaux)]
Book of Bernard Trévisan, whose final Parable describes the Mysterious Fountain carved at Notre-Dame; cited from Mangin de Richebourg's Bibliothèque des Philosophes Chimiques (1741, t. II, traité VII). In the parable an 'old priest' knows the fountain's action on the 'king of the country', whom it loves, attracts and engulfs; a Notre-Dame medallion is compared to it.

Fulcanelli: “where the 'ancient priest of old age' shows himself so well versed in the properties of the hidden fountain and its action on the 'king of the country', whom it loves, attracts and engulfs.”

404.content:
[Place: PIERRE BELLE (house at Tousson)]
An old 18th-century house at Tousson, near Malesherbe (Seine-et-Oise), bearing on its façade an inscription, reproduced with its spelling, saying it was built by a 'Laboureur' who named it PIERRE BELLE, 1762. The note adds that alchemy was also called Celestial Agriculture and its Adepts 'Laboureurs'. The text makes no further reading of the name.

Fulcanelli: “By a Ploughman I was built. without self-interest and with zealous gift, he named me PIERRE BELLE (Fair Stone). 1762.”

405.content:
[Person: Pierre de Corbeil]
Called 'the initiate', archbishop of Sens; he composed the mass of the Feast of Fools according to pagan ritual, at which the flock of the year 1220 cried Evohé.

Fulcanelli: “Composed by the initiate Pierre de Corbeil, archbishop of Sens, according to the pagan ritual, and at which the flock of the year 1220 raised the joyful cry of the bacchanals: Evohe! Evohe!”

406.content:
[Person: Pierre de Montereau]
Named as the maker of the Sainte-Chapelle, a stone shrine built 1245-1248 for the relics of the Passion, whose south windows hold a large alchemical collection.

Fulcanelli: “The Sainte-Chapelle, masterpiece of Pierre de Montereau, a marvellous stone shrine raised from 1245 to 1248 to receive the relics of the Passion”

407.content:
[Person: Pierre Dujols]
Called 'the erudite' and 'the learned'. In his Bibliographie générale de l’Occulte he reports Elias Schadius's inscription to Isis and Bigarne's account of the Virgo paritura. Analysing Lombard's Histoire des Jacobins, he writes that in the Eleusinian grade of Epopt a red cap was placed on the candidate, and that this cap was a masonic symbol and supreme mark of Initiation. On the colour white he traces Hebrew hur, heur to heureux and bienheureux, equivalent of Initiate, noble, pure; Fulcanelli quotes him in support of his own reading.

Fulcanelli: “This term White, says Pierre Dujols, had been chosen for very deep philosophical reasons.”

408.content:
[Term: Planetary metals]
The seven circles on the sarcophagus of the Portal of the Virgin are the symbols of the seven planetary metals; a verse gives the pairs: sun gold, Mercury quicksilver, Saturn lead, Venus brass, Moon silver, Jupiter tin, Mars iron. The Cosmopolite teaches that planetary virtues descend, not ascend, so Mars turns easily into Venus and Jupiter into Mercury. The portal shows their correspondence of mutation: Sun in the centre, Saturn and Moon at the ends, then Jupiter and Mercury, then Mars and Venus. In the symbolism of the planetary metals the Virgin is the Moon, which keeps the sun's rays in her womb. At Amiens, dead trees under a faded sky refer to the first matters, planetary metals killed by fire and made inert by fusion, like trees in winter.

Fulcanelli: “The correspondence of mutation of the metallic planets among themselves is thus indicated, on the porch of Notre-Dame, in the most formal manner.”

409.content:
[Place: Plessis-Bourré]
A note cites its 15th-century painted soffit with initiatic subjects, comparable to the Lallemant chapel ceiling, referring to Deux Logis Alchimiques. Canseliet discussed its centaur, the 'man-horse', in Deux Logis alchimiques.

Fulcanelli: “the other, at Plessis-Bourré, made of paintings, of the 15th century (Two Alchemical Dwellings).”

410.content:
[Term: Pomegranate]
On the Lallemant ceiling, philosophic calcination is symbolized by a pomegranate under fire in a goldsmith's vase, with '3 R' above marking the three reiterations. Three flaming pomegranates crown the credence; stated: they represent fire corporified in the red salt that is philosophic Sulphur, and confirm that its calcination is reiterated three times. For how the triple operation is done, the text refers to the pomegranate roasting 'in a certain vase'.

Fulcanelli: “philosophic calcination, symbolized by a pomegranate subjected to the action of fire in a goldsmith's vessel” / “since they represent fire corporified in that red salt which is the philosophic Sulphur, we shall easily understand that the calcination of this body must be reiterated three times”

411.content:
[Person: Pontanus]
Author of De Lapide Philosphico (1614), recommended for the nature of the secret fire. He admits that before knowing the secret vessel he had begun the same work more than two hundred times without success, though working on the proper matters and by the regular method.

Fulcanelli: “Pontanus admits that before knowing this secret vessel he had begun the same work over again, without success, more than two hundred times”

412.content:
[Term: Pontic water]
After the sacred wells, the text promises to return to 'cette eau pontique' to which the philosophers gave many suggestive epithets. On the Paris portal the action of the pontic water on the heavy matter is shown by two quarrelling children, one dropping a pot, the other a stone. Interpreted: 'cette' points back to the water of the fountain and wells, i.e. the dissolvent of the Work; the medallion shows its action on the 'matière grave' in the Solution.

Fulcanelli: “We shall soon have occasion to return to this pontic water, to which the Philosophers have given a host of more or less suggestive epithets.” / “It is hardly possible to write with more clarity or simplicity the action of the pontic water on the heavy matter”

413.content:
[Place: Portal of Saint Anne]
The south portal of Notre-Dame de Paris; it offers a single motif, of great interest because it describes the shortest practice of the Science. Grillot de Givry reads its door, kept shut all year, as the non-vulgar path. Its trumeau bears the statue of saint Marcel, which Fulcanelli holds to have no secret meaning; only the dado and pedestal with the dragon, besants, king in the flames and athanor carry hermetic value. The pillar was remade and modified; the original went to the Cluny museum. Canseliet returns to the controversy over this statue in his third preface.

Fulcanelli: “Let us retrace our steps and stop at the south portal, also called the porch of Saint Anne. It offers us only one motif, but its interest is considerable, because it describes the shortest practice of our Science”

414.content:
[Place: Portal of the Judgement]
The great central portal of Notre-Dame de Paris. Its trumeau shows alchemy enthroned with sceptre, two books and the nine-rung ladder. The stylobate under the three porches is wholly devoted to 'our science'; two bas-reliefs on the buttresses show the Fountain and the Athanor. The hermetic subjects stand in two rows, twelve figures above and twelve medallions below; their original colours survive in the central rose. The central porch of Amiens reproduces it almost exactly. In the 14th century alchemists met weekly at the great porch.

Fulcanelli: “The stylobate of the façade, which runs beneath the three porches, is entirely devoted to our science” / “The hermetic subjects of the stylobate unfold in two superposed rows, to the right and left of the porch.”

415.content:
[Place: Portal of the Virgin]
The north portal of Notre-Dame de Paris. On its tympanum a sarcophagus bears seven circles, the symbols of the seven planetary metals. Its base carries the dog and doves, the lamb and the upside-down man; the Raven was once carved there. Its piers carry the zodiac, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, with Leo moved into Cancer's place. A small relief under the porch shows the Bath of the stars as a simplified Massacre of the Innocents.

Fulcanelli: “Let us leave the great porch and come to the north portal, or portal of the Virgin.”

416.comment: Philosophical Poem on the Truth of Mineral Physics (work; e190)
416.content:
[Work: Philosophical Poem on the Truth of Mineral Physics (Poème philosophic de la Vérité de la Phisique Minéralle)]
Poem by De Nuysement, printed in Traitez de l’Harmonie et Constitution generalle du Vray Sel (Paris, Périer et Buisard, 1620 and 1621, p. 254). The text cites from it eight lines on the wheel: the artist is to follow the tracks of the wheel and give an even heat, since too high burns the heaven and too low destroys the earth, while the middle course is surer.

Fulcanelli: “For by climbing too high you will burn the heaven,”

417.comment: Rustic Talk, Nonsense, Tales and Discourses of Eutrapel (work; e124)
417.content:
[Work: Rustic Talk, Nonsense, Tales and Discourses of Eutrapel (Propos rustiques, baliverneries, contes et discours d'Eutrapel)]
Work by Noël du Fail (ch. X, Paris, 1842), source of the statement that Notre-Dame was the alchemists' meeting place.

Fulcanelli: “Noël du Fail, Rustic Talk, Nonsense, Tales and Discourses of Eutrapel (ch. X). Paris, 1842.”

418.content:
[Person: Prudentius]
Saint Marcel was his pupil, disciple and successor. Fulcanelli mocks Cambriel's engraving that shows Prudence's pupil bearded.

Fulcanelli: “and, superb anachronism, Prudentius's pupil is bearded!”

419.content:
[Work: Precepts of Father Abraham (Préceptes du Père Abraham)]
Work of an anonymous author quoted on the primitive, celestial water to be drawn from the body where it is, expressed by seven letters, the first seed of all beings; it is the universal solvent, in which sun and moon bathe and resolve into water, their first origin.

Fulcanelli: “It is to this water that the Philosophers have given so many names, and it is the universal solvent, the life and health of all things.”

420.content:
[Term: Puffer]
Mostly the alchemist who works by the letter: Tollius addresses the souffleurs, slaves of the letter, who look for colours in their glass vessels; the 'tourbe des souffleurs' was drawn by the legend of the raven and its hidden treasure; ignorant souffleurs took the nostoc literally and brought ridicule on alchemy; the frauds of greedy souffleurs discredited hermetic truth. The word is also used neutrally: the 16th-century souffleur at Notre-Dame, the pilgrim's emblem popular among medieval souffleurs, the lightly clad 'souffleur chartrain' at the furnace.

Fulcanelli: “Thus you will better grasp the rebuke that Tollius addresses to the puffers, slaves of the letter” / “Let us remember that it is the trickery of greedy puffers, the senseless practices of charlatans, the inanities of ignorant and unscrupulous writers that have brought discredit on hermetic truth.”

421.content:
[Term: Putrefaction]
Decomposition of the matter, marked by black. The woman holding the raven personifies Putrefaction; the black colour is the first sign of decomposition after the perfect mixing of the matters of the Egg, the certain mark of success. Le Breton counts four putrefactions in the Work, each with its blackness; in the first putrefaction the corrupted matter must show acidity, a sepulchral smell, 'fish eyes'. Batsdorff: it separates pure from impure; its names include Occident, Darkness, Raven's Head, Death; its stench is sensible only to understanding. A winged skull at Bourges expresses a new generation issued from putrefaction. Canseliet: fertile putrefaction is necessary for life to continue in any matter.

Fulcanelli: “It is clear then that by this putrefaction the pure is separated from the impure.” / “there are four putrefactions in the philosophical Work.”

Identified in the text with: Raven's Head

422.content:
[Term: Python]
The anonymous author of the Clef du Cabinet Hermétique says Philalèthe describes the oak vessel needed for putrefying the water by the fable of the serpent Python that Cadmus pierced against an oak. Apollo's killing of Python is listed among fables of the combat that yields the secret dissolvent (and the vessel of the compound).

Fulcanelli: “Philalèthe describes it by the fable of the serpent Python, which Cadmus pierced right through against an oak.”

423.comment: Four Books of the Secrets of Medicine and Chemical Philosophy (work; e454)
423.content:
[Work: Four Books of the Secrets of Medicine and Chemical Philosophy (Quatre Livres des Secrets de Médecine et de la Philosophie Chimique)]
Treatise of Jean Liébaut, Paris, Jacques du Puys, containing the woodcuts of the Pyrotechnie that show furnaces as fortresses.

Fulcanelli: “Cf. Jean Liébaut, Four Books of the Secrets of Medicine and Chemical Philosophy. Paris, Jacques du Puys, pp. 17a and 19a.”

424.content:
[Term: Quicksilver]
Common quicksilver (mercure vulgaire) is distinguished from the Philosophers' mercury: some authors say that, purified and exalted, it would become a solvent, which Fulcanelli doubts, holding from experience that without its own agent it cannot become a water useful to the Work. In the verse on the planetary metals, quicksilver is marked by Mercury. The spring the old philosophers called Mercury has no likeness to common quicksilver: the water needed is dry and does not wet the hands.

Fulcanelli: “which the ancient philosophers named Mercury, although it has no appearance of common quicksilver. For the water we need is dry, does not wet the hands”

425.content:
[Term: Quintessence]
On the Saint Anne dado, beside the athanor and under the dragon's claws, five units are the quintessence, made of the three principles and the two natures, totalled under the number ten 'in which all ends'. Elsewhere the soul, metallic life and celestial Dew, freed by the death of the body, is called a quintessence which, put into a pure fixed body, gives birth to a new creature.

Fulcanelli: “the five units of the quintessence, comprising the three principles and the two natures, then their totalling under the number ten 'in which all finishes and ends'.”

426.content:
[Term: Ram (Aries)]
In the fourth motif of the Notre-Dame stylobate a man shows the Ram: the matter from which the dissolvent is prepared; per Pernety (QUOTED), Adepts draw their steel, their magnet, from the belly of Aries. That magnet must be taken at its birth; the steel is found in Aries, the beginning of spring. In the last medallion the ram shows the right season and substance were chosen. Aries opens the zodiac on the north portal, the spring months to begin work. Oak and ram are one thing under two aspects; the raw subject has the Ram as celestial hieroglyph. Hiram is the divine Ram.

Fulcanelli: “'The Adepts say they draw their steel from the belly of Aries, and they also call this steel their magnet.'” / “finally, this mineral has as its celestial hieroglyph the astronomical sign of the Ram (Aries).”

key: Rare Experiments on the Mineral Spirit
427.comment: Rare Experiments on the Mineral Spirit (work; e373)
427.content:
[Work: Rare Experiments on the Mineral Spirit (Rares Expériences sur l'Esprit minéral)]
Work of De Respour, Paris, Langlois et Barbin, 1668, the source of the passage on the Mirror of Art.

Fulcanelli: “De Respour, Rare Experiments on the Mineral Spirit. Paris, Langlois and Barbin, 1668.”

428.content:
[Term: Raven]
Stated: the raven is the symbol of the black colour; on the Paris stylobate it is held by a woman personifying Putrefaction. In the cooking of the Rebis it expresses the black colour, first appearance of the decomposition that follows the perfect mixing of the matters in the Egg; the philosophers call it the sure mark of success, and the text calls it the 'canonical seal' of the Work, as the star is the signature of the initial subject. The black bird appears several times, which lets authors confuse the order of operations; the Chevalier Inconnu calls the long putrefaction of the second operation 'Tête de Corbeau', and Batsdorff lists 'Teste de Corbeau' among its names. Descriptions of the raven of the coction are the most numerous. Tollius (quoted) mocks those who look for their 'noir corbeau' in glass vessels. A raven once sculpted on the north porch of Notre-Dame was 'l'hiéroglyphe majeur de notre pratique'; legend said its line of sight marked the pillar where Guillaume de Paris hid the philosophers' stone. At Bourges the dark blue or black colour of the dead body is assigned to the Raven, hieroglyph of the caput mortuum; a fiery raven pecks a skull on the chapel ceiling. Identified with the black colour (e291).

Fulcanelli: “The Raven is, in a way, the canonical seal of the Work, as the star is the signature of the initial subject.” / “It is in this part of the porch that the major hieroglyph of our practice was once carved: the Raven.”

Identified in the text with: Black colour

429.content:
[Term: Raven's Head]
A name for the putrefaction marked by blackness. Per the Chevalier Inconnu (QUOTED), in the second operation the putrefaction called the Raven's Head is very long. Batsdorff (QUOTED) lists 'Teste de Corbeau' among the Philosophers' names for putrefaction, which separates pure from impure.

Fulcanelli: “In this said operation the putrefaction, which they call the Raven's Head, is very long.” / “The Philosophers have given it various names and called it West, Darkness, Eclipse, Leprosy, Raven's Head, Death, Mortification of Mercury…”

Identified in the text with: Putrefaction

430.content:
[Person: Raymond Lull]
A note explains that 'Raymond' alone means Raymond Lulle, 'Docteur Illuminatus'; Bernard Trévisan (QUOTED) cites his 'eclipse of the sun' for the blackening. He spoke of weights; Huginus à Barma counts him among old masters each with his own process. Canseliet: with Morien, he says the foul odour of dissolution gives way to the sweetest perfume.

Fulcanelli: “By this first name alone the author means Raymond Lull (Doctor Illuminatus).” / “There is the eclipse of the sun of which Raymond speaks.”

431.content:
[Term: Realgar]
Offered only as a supposed example to explain RER: if RE were realgar, 'natural sulphide of arsenic', R could be its sulphur or its arsenic, and RER realgar increased by one of them. The text presents this as an illustration ('supposons'), not a statement of the matter.

Fulcanelli: “let us take an example and suppose that the matter represented by RE is realgar, or natural sulphide of arsenic.”

432.content:
[Term: Rebis]
The double matter of the Work, the compost. In its cooking, the black colour is the first sign of decomposition after the perfect mixture of the matters in the Egg. The Rebis enclosed in the athanor suffers dislocation at the first phase of the second work. The Egg's shell holds the rebis formed of white and red. Apollonius's name is an image of the 'rebis philosophal', union of brother and sister. At the Hôtel Lallemant RERE equals RE BIS: RE a dry matter, philosophical gold; RE a wet matter, philosophical mercury; together a double matter, amalgam of both. The text identifies it with the compost.

Fulcanelli: “To sum up. RE, a dry matter, philosophical gold; RE, a wet matter, philosophical mercury; RERE or REBIS, a double matter, at once wet and dry, an amalgam of philosophical gold and mercury” / “It is in this sense positively an egg, since its envelope or shell contains the philosophical rebis, formed of white and red in a proportion like that of a bird's egg.”

Identified in the text with: Compost, RERE

433.content:
[Term: Red]
The third and last principal colour. Stated: symbol of fire, it marks exaltation, the predominance of spirit over matter, sovereignty, power and apostolate. Obtained as red crystal or powder, volatile and fusible, the philosophers' stone becomes penetrating and able to 'heal lepers', i.e. to transmute common metals into gold. On the cathedral roses the colours end in 'la perfection de la lumière rubiconde'. In Paracelsus (quoted) red follows yellow and matter reaching it is the tincture. Christ is shown in red.

Fulcanelli: “As for red, symbol of fire, it marks exaltation, the predominance of spirit over matter, sovereignty, power and apostolate.” / “the philosophers' stone becomes penetrating and fit to heal lepers, that is, to transmute common metals into gold”

434.content:
[Term: Red Lion]
Stated (according to the philosophers): nothing other than the same matter, the Green Lion, brought by certain processes to the quality of hermetic gold. Basile Valentin (quoted) advises dissolving and feeding the true Lion with the blood of the Green Lion, both being of one nature. The occult salt of the Red Lion is extracted by the spirit of the Green Lion through repeated cohobation. The Palace and old man of the seventh medallion are a variant of the Green and Red Lions, dissolvent and body to dissolve.

Fulcanelli: “As for the Red Lion, it is nothing other, according to the Philosophers, than the same matter, or Green Lion, brought by certain processes to that special quality which characterises hermetic gold or Red Lion.” / “Dissolve and feed the true Lion with the blood of the Green Lion, for they are both of the same nature.”

435.content:
[Term: Regimen]
Stated: a régime is simply the way to make the stone vegetate, to maintain and increase the life it received at birth; a modus operandi, not necessarily shown by a succession of colours. The clear descriptions of régimes with emblematic colours are false; one must learn how one régime differs from the next. The Régime of the stone, i.e. its coction, contains several others, meaning repetitions of one way of working. Like a living body it needs food, graduated and changed (milk first, then meat), rest, and removal of excrements after each digestion. Philalèthe (quoted): who knows the Régime will be honoured by princes. The Bull is the first régime of elemental fire in the second work. Trévisan's 'second régime' begins with the blackness. The short way is called the 'Régime de Saturne'.

Fulcanelli: “Simply the way to make vegetate, to maintain and to increase the life your stone received at its birth.” / “the Regimen of the stone, that is, its coction, contains several others, meaning several repetitions of one same way of working.”

436.content:
[Term: Regimen of Saturn]
The text states that the sages named the short, veiled path the Regimen of Saturn; in it the cooking needs only a simple crucible instead of a glass vessel. This may explain the maxim: one vessel, one matter, one furnace.

Fulcanelli: “This shortened path, but covered with a thick veil, has been named by the Sages the Regimen of Saturn.”

437.content:
[Term: Reign of Saturn]
The old man numb with cold on the fourth lower medallion of Paris shows the first phase of the second work: the Rebis, shut in the Athanor, suffers the dislocation of its parts, at the gentle start of the wheel fire symbolised by cold and winter. The reign of Saturn that then appears is the emblem of radical dissolution, decomposition and the black colour. A different name, the Regimen of Saturn, is given to the short path.

Fulcanelli: “It is the reign of Saturn that is about to appear, emblem of radical dissolution, of decomposition and of the black colour.”

438.content:
[Term: Reincrudate]
The text defines it: to make raw, that is, to return to a state before maturity, to go backwards. The first step of practice is finding the agent able to reduce the fixed body, to reincrudate it into a form like its first substance; alchemists call this reanimating the corporifications, making dead metals live. The masters recommend reincrudating the planetary metals, killed by fire, by giving them back with the fluid form the proper agent they lost in metallurgical reduction. The rare solvent allows the reincrudation of natural gold, its softening and return to its first state as a friable, very fusible salt: the rejuvenation of the king.

Fulcanelli: “Hermetic technical term meaning to make raw, that is, to put back into a state prior to the one that characterises maturity, to go backwards.”

439.content:
[Term: Remora]
In the Conjunction the authors show the violent reaction by fights of unlike animals; in Fulcanelli's view the best and most initiatic description is the duel of the Remora and the Salamander witnessed by Cyrano Bergerac. The fight of the remora and the salamander is listed among the combats of the chemical bodies that give the secret solvent.

Fulcanelli: “the best description, the most initiatic above all, is the one left us by the great philosopher Cyrano Bergerac of the dreadful duel fought before his eyes by the Remora and the Salamander.”

440.content:
[Term: Renaissance]
For Fulcanelli, a decadence that took under François I the paradoxical name of Renaissance; its artists, ignorant of medieval symbolism, copied antique models counterfeited in Italy. Medieval builders built for Truth, anonymously; Renaissance ones for their own name: thought against fashion, genius against talent, spirit against matter. This antagonism explains the Renaissance's contempt for all that was Gothic and the mutilations of medieval work. The Classical School, 'imbued with the decadent principles of the Renaissance', derided Gothic as barbarous.

Fulcanelli: “Swept along by the great current of decadence which, under François I, took the paradoxical name of Renaissance” / “The Middle Ages owed its splendour to the originality of its creations; the Renaissance owed its vogue to the servile fidelity of its copies.”

441.content:
[Term: RER]
With RERE, the enigma written three times in the Lallemant credence. RE, ablative of res, is 'a thing'; RERE is 'two things in one', i.e. RE BIS, REBIS, the compost of philosophic gold (dry) and philosophic mercury (wet). RER holds a secret of capital importance concerning the vessel of the Work: it serves to cook, unite indissolubly and transform the compost RERE. R, half of RE, is half a thing; RER is a matter increased by half of another or of its own — a chemical combination, not a proportion; the text gives realgar plus its sulphur or arsenic as a supposed example. Seek RER, the vessel, first; RERE then follows.

Fulcanelli: “RER serves to cook, to unite radically and indissolubly, to bring about the transformations of the compost RERE.” / “R, which is half of RE, will mean half a thing, half a matter. RER is therefore a matter increased by the half of another, or of its own.”

442.content:
[Term: RERE]
One of two words, RERE and RER, each repeated three times in the niche of the credence of the Hôtel Lallemant chapel. The triple repetition indicates three repetitions of one technique, confirmed by the three flaming pomegranates (the calcination of the Sulphur reiterated three times, giving Sulphur, Elixir, Philosophers' Stone). Stated reading: RE is the Latin ablative of res, 'the thing'; RERE is 'two things in one', a double thing, and so equals RE BIS, the philosophers' REBIS or compost ready to undergo the fire; one RE is a dry matter, philosophical gold, the other a humid matter, philosophical mercury. The text advises seeking RER, the vessel, first; RERE will then be easily known.

Fulcanelli: “RERE or REBIS, a double matter, at once humid and dry, an amalgam of philosophical gold and mercury” / “since the word RERE is the joining of RE, a thing, and RE, another thing, we shall translate two things in one, or a double thing”

Identified in the text with: Rebis

443.content:
[Person: Ripley]
The first gate of Ripley, like Basile Valentin's and Philalethes' entrance to the King's Palace, is the first step of practice that must be opened. As 'Ripleus Anglois' he is cited at the start of his Douze Portes on the essence in which the sought spirit dwells. He is said to come closer to the truth on the Green Lion: a single unclean body enters the magistery, the means of joining the tinctures between sun and moon.

Fulcanelli: “Only one unclean body enters our magistery; the Philosophers commonly call it Green Lion.”

444.content:
[Person: Robert de Luzarches]
Named with Thomas and Renault de Cormont as the genius to whom the cathedral of Amiens is due.

Fulcanelli: “the admirable temple owed to the genius of Robert de Luzarches, of Thomas and Renault de Cormont”

445.content:
[Person: Roger Bacon]
Named, with the epithet Doctor admirabilis, among those with whom Jean Lallemant deserves to commune around the Holy Grail.

Fulcanelli: “deserves to take his place around the Holy Grail, to commune there with Geber (Magister magistrorum) and Roger Bacon (Doctor admirabilis).”

446.content:
[Term: Rose window]
Because of the fixed orientation of churches, of the three roses the northern is never lit by the sun, the southern blazes at noon, and the great western rose of the portal is lit by the setting sun; thus the colours of the Work unfold on the cathedral front in a circle from darkness (black) through white to the red of perfect light. In the Middle Ages the central rose was called Rota, the wheel, the hieroglyph of the time of coction. The rose alone represents the action of fire and its duration, and medieval decorators tried to render in their rose windows the movements of matter excited by fire. Some roses, emblematic of the compound, bear the six-pointed star; six-petalled star roses reproduce the Seal of Solomon. Guillaume de Paris had the medallions of the great porch reproduced in the glass of the central rose of Notre-Dame, which keeps their original colours.

Fulcanelli: “In the Middle Ages the central rose of porches was called Rota, the wheel.” / “The rose therefore represents, by itself alone, the action of the fire and its duration.”

447.content:
[Term: Rosicrucians]
After explaining the May Dew as the condensation of the universal spirit, formed at night in spring, Fulcanelli says it is no surprise that, per Thomas Corneille, the grand masters of the Rose-Croix were called Brothers of the Cooked Dew, the sense they gave their initials F. R. C..

Fulcanelli: “a meaning they themselves gave to the initials of their order: F. R. C.”

448.content:
[Term: Round Table]
The philosophers speak clearly only when they want to keep the profane from their Round Table. Stated: the romances of the Round Table cycle, to which Tristan and Yseult belongs, are traditional hermetic legends renewed from Greek fables, transmitting ancient science under fictions. Documents of the Hôtel Lallemant show Jean Lallemant belonged to the alchemical fraternity of the Knights of the Round Table; he deserves a place around the Holy Grail. The Knights of the Round Table are listed among initiation centres.

Fulcanelli: “The fine medieval poem belongs to the cycle of the romances of the Round Table, traditional hermetic legends renewed from the Greek fables.” / “the Philosophers speak clearly only when they want to keep the profane away from their Round Table.”

449.content:
[Person: Ruskin]
Named with his book The Bible of Amiens among those who read the wheel-fire quatrefoil as Ezekiel's vision. Durand cites him for the remark that the faithless fool is always barefoot in twelfth- and thirteenth-century miniatures.

Fulcanelli: “Ruskin observes that the faithless fool is always, in the miniatures of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, shown barefoot.”

450.comment: Rules of Philalethes for Conducting the Hermetic Work (work; e452)
450.content:
[Work: Rules of Philalethes for Conducting the Hermetic Work (Règles du Philalèthe)]
Printed in Lenglet-Dufresnoy's Histoire de la Philosophie hermétique, Paris, Coustelier, 1742, vol. II. Cited for the 'tempered heat', which may hold lead or tin molten and more, and for the fifteenth rule: the work must boil night and day, otherwise it is a digestion, not a cooking.

Fulcanelli: “For I assure you that if we do not boil, we can never call our work a cooking, but a digestion.”

451.content:
[Person: Sabine Stuart de Chevalier]
Author of the Discours philosophique sur les Trois Principes, or Clef du Sanctuaire philosophique, Paris, Quillau, 1781. Cited for the claim that philosophical mercury is had by dissolving common mercury without loss of weight into philosophical water, quickly. Fulcanelli rejects this, says so from experience, and advises reading this author with the whole salt-cellar rather than a grain of salt.

Fulcanelli: “If the Philosophers are to be read, as Philalethes advises, with a grain of salt, the whole salt-cellar should be used for the study of Stuart de Chevalier.”

452.content:
[Term: Sabot (top / clog)]
At Langres the choirboys whipped their humming sabots, spinning tops, out of the nave. The note calls it a top in the shape of a Tau or Cross; in cabala sabot equals cabot or chabot, Puss in Boots; the Epiphany cake sometimes holds a sabot instead of a bean. The little figure in the Kings' cake is called the bean, the sabot, the cradle or the cross of honour: the gold in its bath. A ceiling panel of the Hôtel Lallemant chapel shows a child urinating into his sabot.

Fulcanelli: “A top with the profile of a Tau or Cross. In cabala, sabot is equivalent to cabot or chabot, the Puss in Boots of the Tales of Mother Goose.” / “it is the gold in its bath, the bather; it is the bean, the sabot, the cradle or the cross of honour”

453.content:
[Term: Sacred Wells]
Wells possessed by most Gothic churches in the Middle Ages, in which, the text says, the esoteric tradition of the Fountain of Life or of Youth was materialised; their water often passed for curative. Examples: the well of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (Abbo), the well of Saint-Marcel in Paris (Gregory of Tours), the 'Puits de la Sainte-Vierge' at Notre-Dame de l'Epine and the well in the choir of Notre-Dame de Limoux with its Latin inscription. The text then announces it will return to this 'eau pontique'.

Fulcanelli: “The water drawn there was most often held to have healing virtues, and it was used in treating certain illnesses.”

454.content:
[Person: Saint Augustine]
The text attributes to him the 'Dispute avec Tryphon' (Dialogus cum Tryphone, 40), quoted on the paschal lamb as figure of Christ and, roasted whole on crossed spits, as symbol of the cross.

Fulcanelli: “Now this lamb, which the law prescribed to be roasted whole, was the symbol of the cross that Christ was to endure.”

455.content:
[Person: Saint Christopher]
A colossal grey-painted statue at Notre-Dame, erected 1413, was destroyed in 1781; others at Auxerre and Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie perished; Amiens and Seville keep theirs. Jacobus de Voragine gives his first name Offerus; for the people the name means 'who carries Christ', but phonetic cabala reads Chrysophe, 'who carries gold'. He is the hieroglyph of solar sulphur (Jesus) or nascent gold, raised on the mercurial waves and carried by Mercury to the power of the Elixir; he indicates the nature of the hidden matter. At the Hôtel Lallemant a painted stone bas-relief in the loggia follows the legend closely; his belt, marked with crossed lines, is the Sign of the canonically prepared mercurial dissolvent. He carries Jesus as the mercury carries the mystic gold.

Fulcanelli: “Christopher stands for Chrysophe: who carries gold” / “It is this belt that gives Saint Christopher his true esoteric character.”

456.content:
[Person: Saint Chrysostom]
A note gives the source of the Book of Seth legend about the star awaited by the Magi as the Opus imperfectum in Mattheum, printed with the works of St John Chrysostom. Canseliet: Chrysostom teaches that the sign that led the Magi came to rest on the Saviour's head before vanishing.

Fulcanelli: “Opus imperfectum in Mattheum, Homily II, printed with the Works of St John Chrysostom, Greek Patrology, vol. LVI, p. 637.”

Canseliet, in his preface: “The sign that led the magi to the cave of Bethlehem, St Chrysostom tells us, came before vanishing to rest on the Saviour's head and surround it with a luminous glory.”

457.content:
[Person: Saint Ignatius]
Quoted on the star of the Nativity: its light surpassed all others, its brightness was ineffable, and sun, moon and stars formed its chorus. Source given as the Epistle to the Ephesians, c. XIX. Fulcanelli notes that Huginus à Barma uses the same terms for the matter of the Great Work on which the star appears.

Fulcanelli: “The sun, the moon and the other stars formed the chorus of this star.”

458.content:
[Person: Saint John]
Fulcanelli quotes St John's vision of the four animals before the throne, matching Ezekiel's, in his account of the four ages of the world at Hendaye. Canseliet cites from St John the parable of the grain that must die to bear fruit, and the raising of Lazarus, against the Church's acceptance of cremation.

Canseliet, in his preface: “What an immense horizon is opened, however, by the parable of the grain entrusted to the soil, which St John reported”

459.content:
[Person: Saint Marcel]
Bishop of Paris, pupil of Prudence. On the Notre-Dame trumeau he is shown blessing, beardless, his crosier touching the dragon's mouth; the legend has him kill the dragon by touching it with his crosier. St Michael, St George and St Marcel slaying the Dragon are Christian replicas of Perseus, figures of the combat of chemical bodies yielding the secret dissolvent. A well near his tomb had curative water. Canseliet: he alone among saints touches the monster's head with his crosier; his legend of the serpent and the dead lady is a hermetic allegory of the dry and humid ways.

Fulcanelli: “He will see there the bishop killing the dragon by touching it with his crosier, as tradition reports.” / “St Michael, St George, St Marcel striking down the Dragon, Christian replicas of Perseus”

key: trumeau du porche de sainte Anne
460.content:
[Place: Saint Marcel pillar]
The trumeau of Notre-Dame's south (Sainte-Anne) portal, which 'describes the shortest practice of our Science'. The statue of St Marcel has no secret meaning; only the die and socle are hermetic. It was remade and altered, losing its key; the original went to Cluny. Reading: the bezants are the two natures, subject and dissolvent, turning into rosettes and calyxed flowers as their roots open; the die shows the king rising from the flames, the 'salt of the philosophers', with triple crown per Gobineau; the residue gives the mercurial salt or 'Babylonian Dragon'; the dragon covered with solar signs can transmute in quantity, by multiplications. Cambriel's account is rejected as faked. Canseliet defends this correction against Grillot de Givry.

Fulcanelli: “It offers us only one motif, but its interest is considerable, because it describes the shortest practice of our Science” / “The die and the socle alone have real hermetic value.”

461.content:
[Person: Saint Matthew]
His Gospel is that of the iron age. The text derives Matthæus from Greek Μαθημα, 'science', making it the Gospel according to Science, last of all but first for us, teaching that all but a few elect must perish. The angel is his attribute because science alone can give man wings to rise to God. His account of the Magi and the star is quoted in the introduction.

Fulcanelli: “It is the Gospel according to Science, the last of all, but the first for us, because it teaches us that, save a small number of elect, we must collectively perish.”

462.content:
[Person: Saint Paul]
Cited as witness that Jesus confided the Verbum dimissum to his Apostles; the quoted passage (Epistle to the Colossians I, 25–26) speaks of the secret hidden from all time and now shown to those judged worthy.

Fulcanelli: “That is to say the SECRET which has been hidden from all time and every age, but which he now makes manifest to those he judges worthy of it.”

463.content:
[Person: Saint Peter]
The cock is the attribute of saint Pierre, the true and flowing 'stone' on which the Christian edifice rests; after the third reiteration of the technique 'the cock will have crowed three times'. As first Apostle he holds the two crossed keys of solution and coagulation and is the symbol of the volatile stone that fire makes fixed and dense; the text adds that he was crucified head downward. In the third preface Canseliet speaks of occult forces aiming to destroy 'l’œuvre de Pierre'.

Fulcanelli: “Then the cock, attribute of Saint Peter, the true and flowing stone on which the Christian edifice rests, the cock will have crowed three times.” / “it is he who is the symbol of the volatile stone that fire makes fixed and dense by precipitating it.”

464.content:
[Person: Saint Thomas Aquinas]
An escutcheon attributed to him was imitated by Flamel on his arcade at the charnel house of the Innocents. The type escutcheon, less obscure than Flamel's, existed until the Revolution on a window lighting the chapel of Saint-Thomas-d'Aquin in the Jacobins' convent, beside which were the schools of the 'Angelic Doctor'. It was drawn and painted in 1787 from the window by a hermetist named Chaudet.

Fulcanelli: “The Curiositez de Paris, published in 1716 by Saugrain the elder, add that beside the church were the schools of the Angelic Doctor.”

465.content:
[Place: Saint-Germain-des-Prés]
The 'célèbre abbatiale' whose well, bored at the back of the sanctuary, had marvellous water according to Abbo. Witkowski (quoted) says a statue analogous to the Isis of Metz existed at Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

Fulcanelli: “which was bored at the back of the sanctuary of the famous abbey church.”

466.content:
[Place: Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie]
A Paris church that Victor Hugo called a complete hieroglyph of hermetic science. Flamel had its small portal built in 1389, covered with figures, including an angel holding a stone circle set with black marble and a fine gold cross (per abbé Vilain). Its statue of Saint Christopher perished with the building.

Fulcanelli: “Abbé Vilain tells us that the small portal of Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie, which the Adept had made in 1389, was covered with figures.”

467.content:
[Place: Sainte-Chapelle]
Masterpiece of Pierre de Montereau, built 1245–1248 to receive the relics of the Passion, presenting a remarkable alchemical ensemble. Its original portal, with two angels described by Victor Hugo (one with a hand in a vase, the other in a cloud), was remade, but its south windows survive intact. The text offers a specimen from the fifth bay, first mullion, on the Massacre of the Innocents and recommends the symbolic windows of the upper chapel and the great rose. Its splendid blue rose is listed among the six-petalled star roses.

Fulcanelli: “It seems hard to find anywhere else a larger collection on the formulas of alchemical esotericism than that of the Sainte-Chapelle.”

468.content:
[Term: Salamander]
The disc held by the figure of Calcination at Paris, the beast 'that lives in fire and feeds on fire'. Stated: this fabulous lizard designates nothing other than the central salt, incombustible and fixed, which keeps its nature even in the ashes of calcined metals, called by the Ancients metallic Seed. Cyrano Bergerac's duel of the Remora and the Salamander is, for Fulcanelli, the best and most initiatic description of the combat of the conjunction. The Porte-Rouge of Notre-Dame is decorated with salamanders. Identified with the central salt (e313).

Fulcanelli: “This fabulous lizard designates nothing other than the central salt, incombustible and fixed, which keeps its nature even in the ashes of calcined metals”

Identified in the text with: Central salt

469.content:
[Person: Salomon Trismosin]
Author of La Toyson d'Or. One figure of his book is almost the same as Abraham's third: an oak girdled at its foot by a golden crown gives birth to the hidden stream; white birds in its branches, a sleeping raven which a poorly dressed man on a ladder is about to seize, and two richly dressed sophists arguing without seeing the oak or the fountain. He is the 'auteur célèbre' quoted for the short way: the body buried in an earthen vessel, a fire made in the earth that holds the glass. His Toison d'Or comments the ludus puerorum, shown as a child on a hobby-horse.

Fulcanelli: “Let us also point out a figure of Trismosin's book, which is very nearly the same as the third of Abraham.”

470.content:
[Term: Salt]
Several salts are named. After putrefaction and calcination a pure salt is born, clothed by cooking with the occult power of fire; the three flaming pomegranates stand for fire corporified in the red salt that is the philosophic Sulphur. In the cohobation the occult salt of the Red Lion is extracted with the spirit of the Green Lion; the old man (dissolvent) meets the crowned king, the fixed, incombustible, pure metallic salt. The Sign on the prepared mercury is called Sel des Sages, 'Sel' standing for 'Scel' (seal). Elsewhere: the Salamander is the central salt, fixed and incombustible; the sel des philosophes is the king crowned with glory born in the fire; Sel céleste is the Philosophers' mercury in the dry way.

Fulcanelli: “a pure salt is then born, which the cooking clothes with the occult power of fire” / “And this sign the old authors called Seal of Hermes, Salt of the Sages (Sel put for Scel, seal) — which confuses the minds of seekers”

471.content:
[Term: Salt of the philosophers]
In the sublimation, the last fiery purification of the united compound, the pure incombustible principles rise in a different form: this is the salt of the philosophers, the king crowned with glory, born in the fire, who must rejoice in the following marriage. The text quotes Hermes: Rex ab igne veniet, ac conjugio gaudebit et occulta patebunt. On the Saint Anne dado only the king's head shows, rising from the flames; Gobineau de Montluisant says he wears a triple crown.

Fulcanelli: “This is the salt of the philosophers, the king crowned with glory, who is born in the fire and must rejoice in the subsequent marriage, so that, says Hermes, hidden things may become manifest.”

472.content:
[Term: Saturn]
Black was given to Saturn, in spagyrics the hieroglyph of lead. The 'reign of Saturn' at the start of the second work is the emblem of radical dissolution, decomposition and black. The old man of the seventh medallion, 'our Mercury', is identified by the texts with Saturn who devoured his children, once painted green; Saturn as dissolvent is very old (the god Sèr with green flesh). The short way is called the 'Regimen of Saturn'. The union of the two natures gives 'the Saturn of the Sages', an anagram of natures. The crude subject is called Son or Child of Saturn, Lead of the Sages. Canseliet quotes Philalèthe: Saturn sees his image in the mirror of Mars.

Fulcanelli: “the pair of natures the alchemist works, whose union yields the Saturn of the Sages, an anagrammatic name for natures.” / “It is the reign of Saturn that is about to appear, emblem of radical dissolution, of decomposition and of the black colour.”

Identified in the text with: Natures

473.content:
[Term: Scallop of Compostela]
The scallop (coquille Saint-Jacques), paired with the heart on Jacques Cœur's palace, was the badge of pilgrims to Saint-Jacques. Stated: in secret symbolism it designates the principle Mercury, also called Traveller or Pilgrim, and is carried mystically by all who undertake the work and seek the star (compos stella); Mercury is the Philosophers' blessed water, and large shells held holy water. Alchemists must make the long pilgrimage, half by land and half by sea, with staff and mérelle — 'pilgrims first, pilots after'. At the Hôtel Lallemant it recurs on the ceiling and on the credence, with wings and Neptune's trident, again marking the aqueous, volatile principle, the philosophic mercury.

Fulcanelli: “The Scallop of Compostela (pl. XXXIX), about which we would have many things to note, serves, in secret symbolism, to designate the principle Mercury, also called Traveller or Pilgrim.” / “It is worn mystically by all who undertake the work and seek to obtain the star (compos stella).”

474.content:
[Term: Seal of Hermes]
Stated: the 'Signe' that all philosophers recognise as marking outwardly the virtue, perfection and purity of their mercurial substance: crossed lines on the surface of the dissolvent when it has been canonically prepared, as on Saint Christopher's (Offerus's) belt at Bourges. The whole work of the art consists in raising this mercury until it bears this sign. Old authors called it Seal of Hermes, Salt of the Sages ('Sel' put for 'Scel', seal), the mark and imprint of the Almighty, his signature, Star of the Magi, Pole Star. The pattern appears more clearly when gold is dissolved in the mercury. The Epiphany cake is 'signée' like the matter. Interpreted: the 'sceau magique', the six-pointed Star of the Magi on the compost that shows the mixture was canonically prepared, is the same sign. The Raven is called by contrast the 'sceau canonique de l'Œuvre'.

Fulcanelli: “And this sign the old authors called the Seal of Hermes, Salt of the Sages (Salt put for Seal), which confuses seekers, the mark and imprint of the Almighty, his signature”

Identified in the text with: Star of the Magi

475.content:
[Term: Seal of Solomon]
The six-petalled star roses of several churches reproduce the traditional Seal of Solomon. A footnote says the plant called Seal of Solomon owes the name to its stem, whose cross-section is starred like the magic sign attributed to the king of the Israelites, son of David. On the Hôtel Lallemant chapel ceiling the starred seal of the king-magus Solomon on top of a pile of ingots fixes the sense of a ceiling panel: mercury below, the Absolute above. The union of the two triangles of fire and water, sulphur and mercury, generates the six-pointed star, hieroglyph of the Work and of the realized Philosophers' Stone.

Fulcanelli: “It is the union of the two triangles of fire and water, or of sulphur and mercury joined in a single body, that generates the six-pointed star, hieroglyph of the Work par excellence and of the realized Philosophers' Stone.”

476.content:
[Term: Secret fire]
The occult agent of the Work, distinct from common heat. Besides heat a second agent is needed, the 'secret or philosophical fire', which, excited by common heat, turns the wheel. Philosophical calcination needs this agent, more like water than flame: the vital spark given by the Creator to inert matter, the spirit enclosed in things; Fulcanelli calls it the highest secret, which stopped him twenty years, and names it 'aqueous fire' or 'igneous water'. Limojon: not actually hot, an igneous spirit put into a subject of the Stone's nature, which calcines, dissolves, sublimes. It is the 'secret fire enclosed in a water', the universal dissolvent; the only agent able to open, sublime and putrefy. As 'fire of nature' it is a spirit spread over the globe, to be captured in a receptive body. Canseliet: used with the universal spirit to separate heaven from earth.

Fulcanelli: “This fire, or this burning water, is the vital spark communicated by the Creator to inert matter; it is the spirit enclosed in things, the igneous ray, imperishable, shut in the depths of the dark, formless and frigid substance.” / “It is this latter fire, excited by common heat, that turns the wheel and brings about the various phenomena the artist observes in his vessel”

477.content:
[Term: Secret of Secrets]
Used twice for different points. At Amiens it names the great mystery of where to find the proper agent lost in metallurgical reduction, set beside the Verbum dimissum that Jesus confided to his Apostles according to saint Paul. At Bourges the masters of the Middle Ages are said to have called 'secretum secretorum' the shell of the egg, i.e. the vessel of the Work (RER), which one must fully understand before undertaking anything.

Fulcanelli: “What then can we say here, facing the Secret of Secrets, before that Verbum dimissum we have already mentioned, which Jesus confided to his Apostles, as Saint Paul testifies” / “Undertake nothing, therefore, until you have received full light on that shell of the egg which the masters of the Middle Ages called secretum secretorum.”

478.content:
[Person: Sendivogius]
Cited for the statement that prepared mercury looks like a stony, friable, flaky (feuilletée) mass, the basis of the names terre feuillée and livre aux feuillets.

Fulcanelli: “Sendivogius teaches us that the prepared mercury has the look and form of a stony, friable and flaky mass.”

479.content:
[Person: Senior Zadith]
Named twice as the more likely author of the Azoth, attributed to Basil Valentine.

Fulcanelli: “In the treatise of the Azoth, attributed to the famous monk of Erfurt, Basil Valentine, and which would rather be the work of Senior Zadith”

480.content:
[Term: Servus fugitivus (runaway slave)]
Name for the solvent needed in the Work. The text states what it is: a mineral and metallic water, solid, brittle, looking like a stone and very easily liquefied; this water coagulated as a stony mass is the Alkahest and the universal Solvent. It is set against common mercury, which Fulcanelli denies can become such a water.

Fulcanelli: “The servus fugitivus we need is a mineral and metallic water, solid, brittle, having the appearance of a stone and very easily liquefied.”

481.content:
[Person: The Sibyl]
Asked what a Philosopher is, she answered: one who knows how to make glass — quoted in the advice to seek and make the vessel RER first.

Fulcanelli: “The Sibyl, asked what a Philosopher was, answered: 'It is he who knows how to make glass.'”

482.content:
[Work: Seal of the Sages (Sigillum Sapientum)]
Image of Huginus à Barma in which the artist holds a balance whose one pan outweighs the other in the apparent ratio of one to two; the text says it would correspond to Basile Valentin's advice to give a white swan to the double fiery man.

Fulcanelli: “which would correspond to the Sigillum Sapientum of Huginus à Barma, where the artist holds a balance one pan of which outweighs the other in the apparent ratio of one to two”

483.content:
[Term: Solar sulphur]
What Saint Christopher signifies: the solar sulphur, identified in parentheses with Jesus, or nascent gold, raised on the mercurial waves and then carried by Mercury's own energy to the power of the Elixir.

Fulcanelli: “It is the hieroglyph of the solar sulphur (Jesus), or of nascent gold, raised on the mercurial waters and then carried, by the proper energy of this Mercury, to the degree of power the Elixir possesses.”

484.content:
[Term: Solar tree]
The tree on the twelfth lower medallion of Paris, with three huge round fruits, a ram at its foot and a bird in its branches, is the solar tree described by the Cosmopolite in the Parable of the Traité de la Nature, from which the water must be extracted. Saturn, says the Cosmopolite, put the fruit of the solar tree into ten parts of this water, the Water of life. The medallion illustrates the second solution, of the red or white Sulphur by the philosophical water.

Fulcanelli: “Here we find the solar tree described by the Cosmopolite in the Parable of the Treatise on Nature, a tree from which the water must be extracted.”

485.comment: Solve et coagula (dissolve and coagulate) (term; e069)
485.content:
[Term: Solve et coagula (dissolve and coagulate)]
Alchemical maxim. At Notre-Dame the 'overturned man' renders it: it teaches the elemental conversion by volatilising the fixed and fixing the volatile, as the quatrain says. At the Hôtel Lallemant an overturned vase slipping from a lion's mouth is 'an original version of the solve et coagula of Notre-Dame'. St Peter holds the two crossed keys of solution and coagulation. Canseliet: the ancient apophthegm gives the mode of operating.

Fulcanelli: “the overturned man, who best renders the alchemical apophthegm solve et coagula, which teaches how to carry out the elemental conversion by volatilising the fixed and fixing the volatile”

Canseliet, in his preface: “Solve et coagula; dissolve and coagulate. (French gloss is the book's.)”

486.content:
[Work: The Dream of Poliphilo (Songe de Polyphile)]
Named only as the work whose analysis by Grasset d'Orcet, in the Revue Britannique, sets out the rules for reading in the secret language.

Fulcanelli: “Some authors, and particularly Grasset d'Orcet, in the analysis of the Dream of Poliphilo published by the Revue Britannique, have given them clearly enough to spare us from speaking of them after them.”

487.content:
[Person: Soufflot]
His vandalism destroyed much of what the 16th-century souffleur could admire at Notre-Dame.

Fulcanelli: “Soufflot's vandalism destroyed in large part what the souffleur could admire in the 16th century.”

488.content:
[Term: Spagyric art]
The 'old Spagyrie' greets the visitor at Notre-Dame with hermetic Philosophy. The 'spagyric expression' of calcination is a likeness authors use; the Initiate's calcination differs fundamentally from the laboratory one. In spagyrics Saturn is the hieroglyph of lead; Paracelsus says black and white belong to the spagyric art. In spagyric notation crosses mark the imperfect metals; a graphic sign in the spagyric art stands for the vulgar name of the subject. Canseliet: 'lesser spagyric operations' beside the Great Work.

Fulcanelli: “Hermetic Philosophy, the old Spagyric art, bid him welcome into the Gothic church, the alchemical temple par excellence.” / “Such at least is the spagyric expression of calcination, a likeness the Authors use as an example of the general idea one should have of the hermetic work.”

489.content:
[Term: Star]
The sign of the Work. The star is the signature of the initial subject, as the Raven is the canonical seal of the Work. The six-pointed 'Star of the Magi' radiating on the compost is a magic seal showing the mixture was canonically prepared; the star guides the alchemist and announces the Saviour's birth. The crossed lines on a properly prepared dissolvent are the Sign called Seal of Hermes, Star of the Magi, Pole star. The six-pointed star, union of the fire and water triangles, is the hieroglyph of the Work and of the realised Stone. At Amiens a master shows three disciples the 'hermetic star', and Rollin's rebus 'Seule' means 'the single star'. Canseliet: the star is single yet double; one seen in the mirror, the other in the chemical heaven; it also appears in lesser operations, always signalling transformation; Fulcanelli dwelt on it from the start.

Fulcanelli: “The Raven is, so to speak, the canonical seal of the Work, as the star is the signature of the initial subject.” / “The master points out to three disciples the hermetic star on which we have already dwelt at length, the traditional star that guides the Philosophers and shows them the birth of the son of the sun”

490.content:
[Term: Star of the Magi]
A radiating six-pointed figure (digamma) that shines on the surface of the compound, that is, above the crib where Jesus the Child-King lies; this magic seal shows the artist he has followed the right path and that the philosophic mixture was prepared canonically. It is the star that guides the alchemist and announces the birth of the Saviour, whence the gathered texts on the Magi's star. Among the names of the Sign of crossed lines that marks the canonically prepared mercurial dissolvent, the text lists Seal of Hermes, Salt of the Sages, the mark and signature of the Almighty, Star of the Magi, Pole Star. Elsewhere the star is called the signature of the initial subject. Chalcidius is said to have preserved a mention of the star of the Magi.

Fulcanelli: “It is a radiating figure with six points (digamma), called Star of the Magi, which shines on the surface of the compound, that is, above the crib where Jesus, the Child-King, lies.” / “This magic seal reveals to the artist that he has followed the right path, and that the philosophic mixture has been prepared canonically.”

Identified in the text with: Seal of Hermes

491.content:
[Term: Steel]
Name the Adepts give to what they draw from the belly of Aries, also called their magnet (Pernety). The anonymous Clef du Cabinet hermétique: the Cosmopolite describes the water of the Work under the names steel and magnet, since it attracts the influences of heaven; this steel is found in Aries, the beginning of spring. Philalèthe's recipe speaks of 'our igneous dragon which hides our magic steel in its belly'.

Fulcanelli: “The Adepts say they draw their steel from the belly of Aries, and they also call this steel their magnet.” / “He says this steel is found in Aries, which also marks the beginning of Spring, when the sun passes through the sign of the Ram”

492.content:
[Term: Stone of the Philosophers]
Stated: Pierre des Philosophes and Pierre Philosophale are alike in kind and origin; the first is raw, the second, derived from it, is fully cooked and digested. The Golden Fleece names both the matter prepared for the Work and the final result. The fish is the hieroglyph of 'la pierre des Philosophes dans son premier état'.

Fulcanelli: “The Stone of the Philosophers and the Philosophers' Stone are thus two similar things, in kind and in origin, but the first is raw, whereas the second, which derives from it, is perfectly cooked and digested.”

493.content:
[Term: Stone to the white]
Stated: the gift of the stone to the white is the transmutation of base metals into silver, perhaps the source of Jacques Cœur's title argentier. Fulcanelli thinks Jacques Cœur made it, or saw it made, from 'essencified' iron cooked three times.

Fulcanelli: “in other words of the transmutation of base metals into silver. Whence, perhaps, his title of argentier.”

494.content:
[Term: Subject (of the Work)]
The first matter the artist must choose to begin the Work. The Black Virgins figure the primitive earth chosen as subject, the first matter as ore, black, heavy and brittle; the Paris Virgin of the Observatory personifies the mysterious subject of Hermes. The stylobate of Notre-Dame gives the lapidary name of the subject of the Sages; the mirror is its hieroglyph, and this vulgar, despised subject becomes the Tree of Life. The star is the signature of the initial subject. It contains the indispensable agent; a quoted commentator of the Lumière sortant des Ténèbres says it is to be sought in the mineral kingdom only. Old authors designated its common name, as found in the mine, by the oak; it is also called Magnesia lunarii, Lead of the Sages, Son of Saturn, Terra sancta, with Aries as its celestial sign. With the dissolvent it forms the two natures.

Fulcanelli: “All the descriptions the Philosophers have left us of their subject, or first matter containing the indispensable agent, are very confused and most mysterious.” / “the oak has always been used by the old authors to designate the common name of the initial subject, as it is found in the mine.”

495.content:
[Term: Sublimation]
Stated: the series of operations ending in the intimate union of sulphur and mercury; by the reiteration of the Eagles the exalted mercury sheds its gross, earthy parts and superfluous humidity and seizes a portion of the fixed body. True sublimation brings the light out of the tomb to the surface. Callimachus's swans describe these sublimations. The prepared compound must undergo sublimation, the last igneous purification: the pure principles rise as the 'sel des philosophes', the crowned king born of fire. Trismosin (quoted) calls his short method 'la vraye sublimation philosophique'. The Doves of Diana hide the spiritualisation and sublimation of mercury. The secret fire alone can open, sublime and putrefy (quoted). Identified with the Eagles (e344).

Fulcanelli: “It is by the reiteration of the Eagles or philosophical Sublimation that the exalted mercury strips off its gross and earthy parts, its superfluous humidity, and takes hold of a portion of the fixed body” / “The matters prepared and united in one compound must undergo sublimation or last igneous purification.”

Identified in the text with: Eagles

496.content:
[Term: Sulphur]
One of the two metallic principles: sulphur and mercury, sun and moon, are parents of the stone according to Hermes; the bull figures Sulphur, the male principle. The third water is called Mercury or Sulphur according to its quality or aspect. The mercury-serpent absorbs the metallic sulphur; the compost is cooked into red sulphur, then Elixir, then universal Medicine. The universal Spirit corporified in minerals is called Sulphur, agent of all metallic tinctures. Sulphur or philosophical gold serves the multiplications. The first of three identical operations yields Sulphur, medicine of the first order; the three grenades are fire corporified in this red salt. The text links soufre with Κυπρος, meaning dung.

Fulcanelli: “we will say, however, that the universal Spirit, corporified in minerals under the alchemical name of Sulphur, is the principle and effective agent of all metallic tinctures.” / “The first operation leads first to the Sulphur, or medicine of the first order”

497.content:
[Term: Sun]
Elias, the Sun, God the Father, is the emblem of the vital spirit; united with the Virgin (form) it gives living matter, Jesus. Hebrew Jes means fire, sun, divinity. The bull, consecrated to the sun, figures Sulphur, the male principle, since Hermes calls the sun the Father of the stone. The sun marks gold; on the north portal the central circle symbolizes the Sun among the seven planetary metals. At Amiens Fulcanelli argues that total absence of sunlight is the primordial condition of all generation, the sun destroying substances too young to resist it.

Fulcanelli: “since the sun is metaphorically called by Hermes the Father of the stone.” / “It is therefore important to remember that the sun is the destroyer par excellence of all substances too young, too weak to resist its fiery power.”

498.content:
[Work: The Emerald Tablet (Table d’Emeraude)]
Hermes' text, quoted for 'the wind carried it in its belly', which Fulcanelli glosses: the wind is the winged, volatile mercury carrying the reborn gold.

Fulcanelli: “'The wind — which is the winged and volatile mercury — carried it in its belly', Hermes tells us in his Emerald Tablet.”

499.content:
[Work: Testament (Testamentum)]
Work of Basile Valentin, cited for the statement that the whole body of Vitriol is to be recognised only as a Mirror of philosophical Science, in which our Mercury, Sun and Moon are seen to shine. Fulcanelli uses it with the Cosmopolite and Moras de Respour to support the name Mirror of Art for the first matter.

Fulcanelli: “The whole body of Vitriol must be recognised only as a Mirror of philosophical Science”

500.content:
[Person: Thales of Miletus]
Said to have shared Tiresias's knowledge of the Language of the Birds; the text calls him one of several fictitious persons whose names speak eloquently in this science. Named again among those able to understand the language of the gods.

Fulcanelli: “He shared it, they say, with Thales of Miletus, Melampus and Apollonius of Tyana, fictitious persons whose names speak eloquently in the science that concerns us”

501.content:
[Work: Chemical Theatre (Theatrum Chemicum)]
Named only as the collection whose vol. VI (Argentorati, 1613) contains Haymon's Epistola as treatise 192.

Fulcanelli: “Haymon, Epistola de Lapidibus Philosophicis. Treatise 192, vol. VI of the Theatrum Chemicum. Argentorati, 1613.”

502.content:
[Person: Theseus]
His fight with the Minotaur was shown at the centre of the Chartres labyrinth; Ariadne's thread let him succeed. The fable teaches true sublimation, 'making the eagle fly': Theseus is θεσ-ειος, organized, manifested light, separating from Ariadne, the spider, the empty husk. Tristan's myth replicates his: Tristan kills the Morhout as Theseus the Minotaur, hieroglyph of making the Green Lion.

Fulcanelli: “In this case Theseus is θεσ-ειος, organized, manifested light, which separates from Ariadne, the spider at the centre of her web” / “The myth of Tristan of Leonois is a replica of that of Theseus.”

503.content:
[Person: Thomas Corneille]
Cited as stating that the grand masters of the Rose-Croix were called Brothers of the Cooked Dew, a meaning they themselves gave to the initials F. R. C.; his work is the Dictionnaire des Arts et des Sciences, article Rose-Croix.

Fulcanelli: “So Thomas Corneille does not surprise us when he assures us that the grand masters of the Rose-Croix were called Brothers of the Cooked Dew”

504.content:
[Term: Three reiterations]
One same procedure repeated three times gives the three philosophic works, after Geber: the first gives the Sulphur (medicine of the first order), the second the Elixir (second order), the third the Philosophers' Stone (third order), differing in quality and power, not nature. Marked by '3 R' on the Lallemant ceiling, by RERE, RER written three times and the three pomegranates, and by the 'trois cuers' of Jacques Cœur's motto. At Amiens: a third reiteration of the cock-fox technique gives the stone, 'the cock will have crowed three times'. The closing advice: calcine, return the pure part, reiterate a third time.
